en: Om. The gods, indeed—Agni, Indra, Soma, Makha, Viṣṇu, and the Viśve Devās, with the exception of the Aśvins—sat down for a sacrificial session (sattra).
Kurukṣetra was their place of sacrifice for the gods; therefore they say, "Kurukṣetra is the gods' [place]."

"It is the place for sacrificing to the gods. Therefore, wherever one goes from Kurukṣetra, one thinks, "This is the place for sacrificing to the gods," for that is indeed the gods' place for sacrificing to the gods. 14.1.1.
[3] They sat down, thinking, "May we attain prosperity, may we be glorious, may we be eaters of food. And so too do these sit for the sacrificial session (*sattra*) for the sake of prosperity.

"Let us go so that we may have fame, so that we may be eaters of food. They said, "He among us who first reaches the conclusion of the sacrifice through toil, austerity, faith, sacrifice, and oblations—he shall be the best of us; let him be for all of us. "So be it," they replied.

Viṣṇu was the first to obtain it; he became the most excellent among the gods. Therefore they say, "Viṣṇu is the most excellent among the gods. That which is Viṣṇu is the sacrifice; that which is the sacrifice is yonder sun. And this glory is indeed Viṣṇu’s.

He was able to restrain it; even now, not everyone is indeed able to restrain their fame. Taking a bow with three arrows, he stepped aside and stood propping his head against the end of the bowstring. The gods, not daring to attack him, sat down all around him.
The ants said: "These are indeed ants, namely the upadīkas. If someone were to eat even the bowstring of this [bow], what would you give him?
We would give him food; even if he should find water in a desert, we would give him all kinds of food. They replied, "So be it. 14.1.1 [9]
Having approached him, they snapped his bowstring; and when that was severed, the two ends of the bow, snapping asunder, cut off the head of Viṣṇu.
It fell with a great crash; having fallen, it became that very sun, while the other [part of the body] was cast forward.

Because it fell with the sound "ghṛṅ," therefore it is called *gharma*; and because it was pushed forward (*prāvṛjyata*), therefore it is called *pravargya*. Those gods said, "A great hero (*vīra*) has indeed been given to us"; therefore he is the *mahāvīra*. The essence that flowed from him they rubbed together with their hands; therefore he is the *samrāj* (the sovereign).
The gods strove for him as those who intend to obtain a treasure do. Indra reached him first;
Aṅga followed after him. He seized him; having seized him, he became this glory that is here—namely, the glory that is Indra. Whoever knows this becomes glorious. 14.1.1. [13]

He indeed was Makha, he was Viṣṇu; from him Indra became Makhavat. Indeed, they call him Maghavan "Makhavat" cryptically, for the gods love the cryptic. 14.1.1. [14] To those ants they gave food; water, indeed, is all food.
For it is by means of these that they speak out repeatedly, as it were, when they speak of "this" (the world).
14.1.1.[15] Then the Vasus divided this Viṣṇu-sacrifice into three parts: the Vasus [took] the morning pressing, the Rudras the midday pressing, and the Ādityas the third pressing. 14.1.1.[16]
Agni [presides over] the morning pressing, Indra the midday pressing, and the All-gods the third pressing.
The Gāyatrī [meter presides over] the morning pressing, the Triṣṭubh the midday pressing, and the Jagatī the third pressing.
With that headless sacrifice, the gods moved about, praising and toiling.
Dadhyañc Ātharvaṇa indeed discovered this *śukra*, this sacrifice, so that the head of the sacrifice may be restored as it was, and so that this sacrifice becomes complete.
Indra said to him: "If you should teach this to anyone else, I shall cut off your head from that very spot."

Now this had been heard by the Aśvins: "Dadhyañc Ātharvaṇa indeed knows this *śukra*, this sacrifice—how this head of the sacrifice is restored, and how this sacrifice becomes complete. They both went to him and said, "We will come to you as pupils. He asked, "What do you intend to recite? [They replied: "This *śukra*, this sacrifice."
"In whatever way this head of the sacrifice is restored, so that this sacrifice becomes complete.
He said, "Indra has indeed told me: 'If you should teach this to anyone else, I shall cut off your head from that very spot.
Therefore, I am afraid; lest he should cut off my head, I will not initiate you."
The two of them said, "We two shall protect you from that. He asked, "How will you protect me?

They replied, "When they lead you up, we shall then cut off your head and set it aside elsewhere; then, having brought the horse's head, we shall replace yours with it, and with that you will recite for us.
When you have recited for us, then they will cut off your [real] head. And so it happened.

"Let us bring our own heads and replace yours with them," they said. "So be it," he replied. He initiated them both. When he had initiated them, he cut off his head and set it aside elsewhere; then, having brought the head of a horse, they replaced his head with it. With that [new head], he recited the Veda to them both. When he had recited it to them, then—his [original head].
Indra cut off that head; then, having brought his own head, they two restored it to him.
Therefore, this was declared by the seer: "When Dadhyañc, the son of Atharvan, spoke to you two with the horse's head—that honey—what he spoke then, he spoke it truly.
Thus indeed was it spoken.
One should not recite it for everyone, for that would be a sin; moreover, one should think, "Lest Indra cut off my head.
One should indeed recite it only for someone who is well-known, or for one who is learned in the Vedas, or for one who is dear to him—but certainly not for just anyone.
One should recite it for one who has lived with him for a year; for he who shines yonder is indeed the Year, and he is also...
The Pravargya is this very [Sun]; it is him that he thus gratifies. Therefore, one should recite [the formulas] for one who has lived [in seclusion] for a year.

(14.1.1 [28]) He observes the vow for three nights. There are indeed three seasons in the year; and this one who shines yonder is the year, and he is the Pravargya. It is him that he thus gratifies. Therefore, he observes the vow for three nights. (14.1.1 [29])
"The ascetic drinks from a heated vessel; 'the ascetic recites,' so he says when he recites while abstaining from meat.

[14.1.1.30] "He drinks from a non-clay vessel; for there is something in this earth as if mixed together—namely, that untruth which one speaks upon it—therefore he drinks from a non-clay vessel. [14.1.1.31]

One who is not a Śūdra should avoid impurity. This indeed is dharma: he who shines yonder; this is prosperity; truth is light, while falsehood is woman, a Śūdra, a dog, and a black bird—one should not look at these. One should not [look at] prosperity and evil together, nor light and darkness, nor should one mingle truth and falsehood. 14.1.1. [32]
Now, this indeed is glory: he who shines yonder. In that the sun is glory, it is indeed the sacrifice that is that glory;

in that the sacrifice is glory, it is indeed the sacrificer that is that glory; in that the sacrificer is glory, it is indeed the officiating priests that are that glory; in that the officiating priests are glory, it is indeed the sacrificial fee that is that glory. Therefore, whatever [is given] to him...

They should bring the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*). He should not bestow it upon another immediately, thinking, "Lest I should transfer this glory that has come to me immediately to another. Rather, on the next day or after two days have passed, having placed that glory within himself, he gives whatever it may be—gold, a cow, a garment, or a horse. 14.1.1. [33]

Now, indeed, he who either recites this or consumes it enters this life and this light. His rule of conduct is as follows: he should not expose himself to the heat, thinking, "Lest I should become hidden from him"; he should not spit while exposed to the heat, thinking, "Lest I should spit upon him"; and he should not urinate while exposed to the heat, thinking, "Lest I should urinate upon him."
"As long as this [sun] shines, so long is this [fire]; let me not injure it with these [flames].

Having thus illuminated it, he should eat at night; thereby the form of that which shines is produced. Regarding this, Āsuri said: "The gods indeed observe one vow, namely truth; therefore, one should speak only the truth. 14.1.2. [1]

He indeed gathers the ritual requisites (sambhāra). Insofar as he gathers these here and there, that is the reason for their being called "requisites" (sambhāratva). He gathers them from wherever they are deposited within the sacrifice.
He prepares the black antelope skin; the black antelope skin is indeed the sacrifice; thus he prepares him within the sacrifice itself.

It is with the hair-side up, for the hairs are the meters; thus he prepares him within the meters. To the north, for the northern direction belongs to men; with the neck toward the east, for that is the way among the gods.
The spade is a thunderbolt; the thunderbolt is indeed vigor. By means of vigor, he thus causes this [sacrifice] to prosper and makes it complete.
It is made of Udumbara wood; the Udumbara is indeed strength and sap. By means of that strength and sap, he causes this to prosper.
He makes it complete.
Furthermore, [the ladle] is made of *vaikaṅkata* wood. That which Prajāpati offered as the first oblation—having offered it, where he wiped his hands, from that the *vikaṅkata* tree arose.
The oblation is indeed the sacrifice, and the *vikaṅkata* is the sacrifice.

By means of the sacrifice, he thus causes this [altar] to prosper and makes it complete. (14.1.2.6) It is one cubit (*aratni*) in measure; for the cubit is the arm, and by the arm indeed is valor performed. Thus it becomes commensurate with valor;
by means of valor, he causes this to prosper and makes it complete. (14.1.2.7)

He takes it up with the formula: "At the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins, with the hands of Pūṣan, I take thee; thou art a woman. The significance of this is exactly as before. Having placed it in his left hand and touched it with his right, he murmurs: "They harness the mind and they harness the thoughts."
"The inspired ones have established the priestly offices of the great, inspired, wise one; he alone, who knows the ways, has ordained them.
Great is the praise of the god Savitṛ"—the significance of this is the same as before.
Then, with a wooden shovel on the south side and with his hand on the north side, he takes up a lump of clay, [saying]: "O Goddess..."

When the head of the sacrifice had been cut off, its sap flowed away; it went into these two, heaven and earth—that which is the clay is this [earth], and that which is the water is yonder [heaven]. From the clay and from the waters, the *mahāvīra* vessels are made.
By means of that very sap, he thus completes him and makes him whole. Therefore he says, "O divine Heaven and Earth."
"May I today accomplish the head of Makha for you"—Makha is indeed the sacrifice; thus he says, "May I today accomplish the head of the sacrifice for you.
"On the earth’s place of divine worship"—for he gathers it on the earth’s place of divine worship.
"For Makha thee! For the head of Makha thee!"—Makha is indeed the sacrifice; thus he says, "For the sacrifice thee! For the head of the sacrifice thee!"

"Of the head," he says; this is what he means. Now, as for the ant-hill: "O divine ants"—for they indeed performed this service when the head of the sacrifice was cut off. By means of them, he now makes this [sacrifice] complete and perfects it; [it is] the first-born of existence.

Thus, this earth is indeed the first-born of what has come to be; by means of her he thus makes him prosper and makes him complete. "May I today accomplish the head of Makha on the earth’s place of divine sacrifice; for Makha thee! For the head of Makha thee!"—the significance of this is the same as before. 14.1.2. [11]
Then [he says], "Was it struck down by a boar? Was it this large at first? For this earth was indeed this large at first, only a span in size;

a boar, thinking "This is mine," dug her up. He, Prajāpati, is her lord. By means of that very pair, his own dear abode, he thus causes him to prosper and makes him complete. "May I today succeed in the head of Makha for thee."
"On the place of sacrifice of the earth, for Makha thee; for the head of Makha thee"—the significance of this is the same as before.

Then [he lays down] the *ādāra* bricks with the formula, "The vigor of Indra. When indeed Indra encompassed him with his vigor, then the sap of him, being thus encompassed, flowed out. It lay there as if putrefying. He said, "Alas, this has burst open for me!"
Because the essence (rasa) praised him, they are called *ādāra*; and because it lay as if putrid, they are called *pūtīka*.

Therefore, when offered as an oblation into the fire, they blaze up; and therefore they are fragrant, for they were produced from the essence of the sacrifice. And because Indra then encompassed it with his might (*ojas*), therefore one says, "The might of Indra."
"May I today obtain the head of Makha for you at the place of sacrifice on earth; for Makha, you!
For the head of Makha, you!"—the significance of this is the same as before.
14.1.2. [13] Now, as for the goat's milk: when the sacrifice had its head cut off, its heat (śuc) departed, and from that [heat] the goat was born.
By means of this very completeness, he thus endows him and makes him whole. "For Makha thee!
For the head of Makha thee!"—the significance of this is the same as before.
Now, he gathers these five materials; for the sacrifice is fivefold, the animal is fivefold, and the seasons are five.
The year is this very one that shines yonder; and this Pravargya is indeed that year. Thus, he gratifies him.

He touches those [materials] when they have been gathered together, saying: "For Makha thee! For the head of Makha thee!"—the significance of this is the same as before. 14.1.2. Then there is an enclosure to the north; approaching it, they mutter: "May Brahmanaspati go forward!"—this is he.
Verily, he who shines yonder is Brahmaṇaspati, and he is indeed the Pravargya; thus he gratifies him.

Therefore he says, "Let Brahmaṇaspati come forth. "Let the divine Sūnṛtā come forth," for she is indeed the divine Sūnṛtā. "And [let her bring] the hero, the manly one, whose gifts are fivefold"—thus he praises him and magnifies him. "May the gods lead the sacrifice for us."
He thus makes all these gods his protectors. It is enclosed; for the gods were afraid, thinking, "Lest the *rakṣases* and *nāṣṭrās* should slay this one here";
they therefore encircled him with this fortress. In the same way, this [sacrificer] now encircles him with this fortress.

Then he places [the clay] on the donkey with the formula, "For Makha thee! For the head of Makha thee!"—the significance of this is the same as before. Then, having taken a lump of clay, he fashions the Mahāvīra vessel with the formula, "For Makha thee! For the head of Makha thee!"—the significance of this is the same as before. It should be a span high, for the head is, as it were, a span high; it is constricted in the middle, for the head is constricted in the middle.
For he raises the face three finger-breadths above the head as if it were tucked away;

he thus places the nose upon it. When it is completed, he touches it with the formula, "Thou art the head of Makha," for this is indeed the head of the gentle Makha. In the same way, the other two [pans] are silent; the two *pinvana* pans are silent, and the two *rauhiṇa* potsherds are silent. 14.1.2. [18]

This sacrifice is indeed Prajāpati. For Prajāpati is both the defined and the undefined, the limited and the unlimited. Thus, when he performs an act with a sacrificial formula (*yajus*), he thereby perfects that form of his which is defined and limited; and when he acts silently, he thereby perfects that form of his which is undefined and unlimited.

With that he prepares it; indeed, he who, knowing this, performs it in this manner, prepares this entire Prajāpati in his completeness. Then he leaves over a lump for the *upashayā* (the lying brick) for the sake of expiations. Then he impels [the clay] with *gavedhukā* grass. When the sacrifice had its head cut off, its sap flowed away, and from that these plants [arose].
They were born from that very essence; with that same essence he thus causes him to prosper and makes him whole.
"For Makha thee! For the head of Makha thee!"—this is the significance of the formula; the other two are likewise. The two *pinvana* vessels are silent, as are the two *rauhiṇaka* potsherds.
Then he fumigates them, saying: "With the dung of the stallion, the bull, I fumigate thee. The horse is indeed a bull, and virility is indeed [the dung].

By means of the bull, he thus endows him with vigor and makes him complete. "On the earth’s place of sacrifice, for Makha thee! For Makha’s head thee!"—the significance of this is the same as before; likewise for the other two. Silently [he places] the two *pinvana* vessels;
silently the two *rauhiṇaka* potsherds. 14.1.2. [21]
Then he cooks them, for what has been cooked belongs to the gods. He cooks them with bricks; indeed, the gods did this very thing:
by means of those [bricks], they restored that part of the sacrifice which had been severed from its head; thus he now restores it and makes it whole.
Therefore, he should cook them in such a way that they are well-cooked; then, having placed the cooking-vessel down, he places the Mahāvīra pot upon it.

"For Makha thee! For the head of Makha thee!"—this is the significance of that very [formula]; so too for the other two. Silently [he places] the two *pinvana* vessels; silently the two *rauhiṇaka* potsherds. He should place them on the day [of the sacrifice], and he should take them off on the day [of the sacrifice], for the day belongs to the gods.
He takes them off with the formula, "For the straight one thee! This world is indeed the straight one, for truth is straight; and this [sun] which shines yonder is truth. It is he who shines yonder.

The first Pravargya is this very one; he thus gratifies it. Therefore he says, "For speed (java) thee! [14.1.2.23]. "The good (sādhu) thee! This one who blows here is indeed the good, for as the perfected one (*siddha*), he blows through these worlds.
He is also the second Pravargya; he thus gratifies him. Therefore he says, "For the good thee! [14.1.2.24].
"For a good dwelling (sukṣiti) for thee"—this world is indeed the good dwelling, for in this world all beings dwell;
moreover, Agni is the good dwelling, for Agni indeed dwells in this world as all beings. This is the third Pravargya;
it is him he thus gratifies. Therefore he says, "For a good dwelling for thee," [and] silently [he pours] into the two milking vessels, silently.
[Regarding] the two Rauhiṇa-pans (14.1.2.25):

Then he moistens them with the milk of a she-goat, [saying], "For Makha thee! For the head of Makha thee!"—the significance of this is the same as before; in the same way for the other two. [He moistens] the two *pinvana* vessels silently, and the two Rauhiṇa-pans silently. (14.1.2.26)
Now, indeed, he who either recites this or consumes it enters this life and this light.
His observance of the vow is the same as that prescribed for the *sṛṣṭi* [offering].
When he proceeds with the *ātithya* ceremony, then, intending to perform the *pravargya*, he goes before the *upasad*s.
Having strewn *kuśa* grass pointing eastward from the *gārhapatya* fire, he places the vessels in pairs:

the supporting ladle (*upayamanī*), the *mahāvīra*, the two *parīṣās*, the two milking pots (*pinvana*), the two *rauhiṇa* potsherds, the two *rauhiṇa* offering-spoons (*havanyau*), and whatever else there may be.
That makes ten; for the *virāj* consists of ten syllables, and the *virāj* is indeed...

This sacrifice, he thus completes as the Virāj. Now, as for the pairs: a pair is indeed vigor; when two people exert themselves together, then they perform a vigorous act. A pair is a productive union; by means of this productive union, he thus causes it to prosper and makes it complete. 14.1.3. [2]

Then the Adhvaryu, taking up the sprinkling waters and rising, says: "O Brahman, we shall proceed; O Hotṛ, recite the praises! The Brahman sits to the south of the sacrifice as its guardian; it is to him that he thus says, "Sit alert; we shall restore the head of the sacrifice. "O Hotṛ, recite the praises"—for the sacrifice is [the body].
The Hotṛ indeed says this very thing: "Restore the head of the sacrifice. Thus the Hotṛ begins.

"The Brahman was born first in the east"—the Brahman is yonder sun; day after day it is born in the east, and this Pravargya is that very [sun]. It is him he thus gratifies; therefore he says, "The Brahman was born."
"First from the front"—this is the sprinkling; the significance of this is the same as before.

He sprinkles with the formula, "For Yama thee! This one who shines yonder is indeed Yama, for he restrains all this, and by him all this is restrained. And this Pravargya is that very [sun]; thus he gratifies him. Therefore he says [the formula].
"Unto Yama thee! [14.1.3.5]. "Unto Makha thee!"—Makha is indeed he who shines yonder; he is also the Pravargya. Thus, he gratifies him;
therefore he says, "Unto Makha thee! [14.1.3.6].
"Of the heat of the sun, thee!"—for he who shines yonder is indeed the sun, and he is the Pravargya;
thus he gratifies him. Therefore he says, "Of the heat of the sun, thee.
Having removed the pillar by the eastern door, they fix it in the ground to the south, so that...
The Hotṛ, while praising, should look away; for the Hotṛ is indeed the sacrifice. He thus places the sacrifice within her, and so she causes the Gharma to swell.
Having carried the throne-seat (āsandī) of the Sovereign (samrāj) around the front of the Āhavanīya fire, he sets it down to the south, facing east, with its northern side [turned toward the fire].
The king’s throne-seat is made of Udumbara wood. The Udumbara is indeed strength and sap; verily, he thus endows him with strength and sap and makes him complete.
It reaches up to the shoulders; for this head is established upon the shoulders, and thus he establishes this head upon the shoulders.
It is woven with cords of *balvaja* grass; when the sacrifice had its head cut off, its sap flowed away, and from that these [cords] arose.

The plants were born from him; with that very sap he thus endows it, making it whole. Now, as to why he places it to the north: Soma is the sacrifice and the Pravargya is the head; since the head is higher, therefore he places it to the north.
Furthermore, Soma is a king and the Pravargya is an emperor; and the emperor is indeed higher than the king. Therefore he places it to the north. 14.1.3. [12]

From the kingdom he attains imperial sovereignty from that [kingdom], moving further upward. 14.1.3. When the Hotṛ recites this verse, "Him the sages anoint as they spread him out," then he anoints this Mahāvīra vessel used for the ritual performance with clarified butter, saying, "May the god Savitṛ anoint thee with honey. For Savitṛ is indeed the impeller (*prasavitṛ*) of the gods.
All this indeed is honey—whatever exists here. He thus anoints him with all this;
therefore Savitṛ, the Impeller, impels him for this purpose. Hence he says: "May the divine Savitṛ anoint you with honey.
Then, to the north, sand has been scattered. Thereupon, he places a piece of silver beneath it, [saying]: "From the earth..."
"Touching it, he says, 'May you protect! For the gods were afraid, thinking, 'Lest the Rakṣases, the destroyers, should strike this [Agni] from below.

Gold is indeed the seed of Agni; [he does this] for the purpose of warding off the destroyers and the Rakṣases. Moreover, the Earth was indeed afraid of him, thinking, 'Lest he, being heated and glowing, should injure me'; [he does this] for her sake."

He hides this; it is made of silver, for this earth is indeed silver. 14.1.3.[15] When the Hotṛ recites this verse, "Sit down, O great one; you are great," then on both sides there are blazing tufts of Muñja grass. Having placed them near, he pours the essence of the sacrifice—which was severed from its head—into them.

It flowed forth, and from it these plants were born; by means of that very sap he thus causes him to prosper and makes him complete. Now, as to why they are kindled on both sides: it is so that the *rakṣases* and *nāṣṭrās* [demons] may be driven away from all directions.
While he is being enkindled, the wife covers her head. "For he becomes heated and glowing;

[she does this] lest he, being heated and glowing, should rob me of my sight. He enkindles it with: "Thou art flame, thou art glow, thou art heat. For he who shines yonder is indeed the *gharma*; everything indeed—

This is that; he thus gratifies this very [fire]. Therefore he says: "Thou art radiance, thou art glow, thou art heat. (14.1.3.18) Then he invokes blessings upon this [earth]. For this earth is indeed the sacrifice; it is upon her that he invokes these blessings, and she fulfills them all for him. (14.1.3.19)

"Unassailable from the front"—for she is indeed unassailable from the front by the *rakṣases* and *nāṣṭrās* under the overlordship of Agni; thus he makes Agni her overlord for the warding off of the *nāṣṭrās* and *rakṣases*. "Give me life"—thus he bestows life upon himself, and so he attains a full span of life. 14.1.3 [20]

"Possessing sons on the right"—there is nothing here that is obscure. "Under the sovereignty of Indra"—he thus makes Indra her sovereign for the warding off of destructive spirits and demons. "Grant me offspring"—he thereby bestows upon himself offspring and cattle;
thus he becomes possessed of sons and cattle. 14.1.3. [21]

"Easy to sit upon from behind,"—there is nothing hidden here; "by the overlordship of the god Savitṛ"—he thus makes the god Savitṛ the overlord for her, for the warding off of destructive spirits and demons. "Give me sight,"—he thus bestows sight upon himself, and so he becomes possessed of sight. 14.1.3. [22]
"May there be hearing from the north," he says; by this he means "may he cause [the announcement] to be heard from the north. "By the power of Dhātṛ," he says;

he thus makes Dhātṛ her overlord for the warding off of the destructive Rākṣasas. "Grant me increase of wealth," he says; he thereby bestows upon himself wealth and prosperity, and so he becomes possessed of wealth and prosperity. 14.1.3. [23]

"Supporting from above"—by saying this, he means "supporting from above. "Under the lordship of Bṛhaspati"—he thereby makes Bṛhaspati her lord for the warding off of destructive spirits and Rākṣasas. "Give me vigor"—he thus bestows vigor upon himself; so he becomes vigorous and strong. 14.1.3 [24]

Then, with his right hand turned upward, he makes atonement on the south side, saying: "Protect me from all destructive powers. By this he means: "Guard me from all calamities. When the head of the sacrifice was cut off, its sap flowed away and went to the Fathers. There are three kinds of Fathers; it is with them that he thus provides for him and makes him whole. 14.1.3. [25]
Then, having touched this [earth], he mutters: "Thou art the horse of Manu. For indeed, having become a mare, she bore Manu;
he is her lord, Prajāpati. By means of that very pair, his beloved abode, he thus causes him to prosper and makes him whole. 14.1.3. [26]
Then he encloses [the fire] with two splinters of *vaikaṅkata* wood, pointing eastward, with the formula: "Svāhā! Be enclosed by the Maruts!
He places the *svāhā*-utterance first and the deity last; for this indeed is the *svāhā*-utterance, namely that which shines yonder (the sun), and that is also the *pravargya*.
Thus he gratifies him. Therefore, he places the *svāhā*-utterance first and the deity last. 14.1.3. [27]

"Be thou encompassed by the Maruts!"—the Maruts are indeed the people (viś); thus he makes the nobility (kṣatra) prosper through the people. Therefore, this nobility is encompassed on both sides by the people. [He places them] silently facing north, silently facing east, silently facing north, silently facing east. 14.1.3. [28]
He prepares thirteen [materials]. There are indeed thirteen months in a year;
this one who shines yonder is the year, and he is the Pravargya. Thus, he thereby gratifies him. Therefore, he prepares thirteen.
Then he places a piece of gold on top, saying, "Protect it from touching the sky. For this, O gods...

They were afraid that the *rakṣases* and *nāṣṭrās* might strike him from above; for gold is indeed the seed of Agni, and it serves to ward off the *nāṣṭrās* and *rakṣases*. Moreover, the Sky was afraid of him, thinking, "Lest this one, heated and glowing, should injure me"; thus he places this yellow [gold] between himself and the Sky.
For the sky becomes like a doe.
Then he fans it with fans, saying "Honey, honey" three times. Honey is indeed breath;
he thus bestows breath upon this [sacrificial fire]. There are three [fans], for there are three breaths: out-breath (prāṇa), up-breath (udāna), and—
By means of the vyāna breath, he thus bestows those very [vital powers] upon him.
14.1.3. [31] Then they shake [the horse] three times from left to right. When the sacrifice had its head cut off, its sap flowed away and went to the Pitṛs.
There are indeed three kinds of Pitṛs; it is by means of them that he thus causes this [horse] to breathe forth. 14.1.3. [32]
The vital breaths indeed depart from those who perform the shaking at the sacrifice.

They shake [the ladles] three times toward the right; thus they become six. For there are these six vital breaths in the head; it is these he thereby places in him. They cook the two Rauhiṇa cakes. When the flame arises, then he takes up the gold. 14.1.3. [33]

When the Hotṛ recites this verse, "O Aśvins, may our speech be effective," the Adhvaryu, rising up, says, "The Gharma has shone. If it has indeed shone, he should know that the sacrificer will become more prosperous; but if it has not shone, he should know that he will become worse off; and if neither...
"One should know: 'Whether it is pleasing or not pleasing, it will be neither better nor worse. Indeed, one should blow upon it in such a way that it becomes pleasing.
14.1.3 [34] Now, he who recites this section for another enters this very breath, this very light. "The consumer," [he says].
Or rather, his practice of the vow is as it was at the beginning of creation. When the Adhvaryu priest stands up and says, "The Gharma has been relished," [that is the time].
Having risen toward it, they worship with the *avakāśa* formulas. The *avakāśas* are indeed the vital breaths; thus he bestows the vital breaths upon him.

Six of them worship, for there are these six vital breaths in the head; it is those very breaths that he bestows upon him. "The embryo of the gods"—he who shines yonder is indeed the embryo of the gods, for he is all this.
"By means of this he grasps all this; indeed, this is the Pravargya, and it is him whom he thus gratifies. Therefore he says:
'The embryo of the gods' (14.1.4.3).
'The father of thoughts'—for he is indeed the father of thoughts; 'the lord of creatures'—for he is indeed the lord of creatures" (14.1.4.4).

"The god has come together with the god Savitṛ"—for indeed, the god has come together with the god Savitṛ; "he shines together with Sūrya"—for indeed, he shines together with Sūrya; "Agni has come together with Agni"—for indeed, Agni has come together with Agni; "together with the divine Savitṛ"—for indeed, [he has come] together with the divine [Savitṛ].
"Thou hast come together with Savitṛ; thou hast shone forth with Sūrya," for he indeed has shone forth with Sūrya. "Svāhā!

Agni has come together with fervor," for Agni indeed has come together with fervor. He utters the *svāhā* call for the lower [deity]; the significance of the higher deity is the same as before. "Together with the divine Savitṛ," for he has indeed come together with the divine Savitṛ. Together...
"He has shone forth with the sun"—for he indeed has shone forth with the sun.
These three spaces come into being; for there are indeed three vital breaths: prāṇa, udāna, and vyāna. It is by means of these that he thus places [the breaths] in him.

"He shines as the upholder of heaven and earth through his fervor"—for he indeed shines as the upholder of heaven and earth through his fervor. "The immortal god, born of fervor, is the upholder of the gods"—for he indeed is the immortal god, born of fervor, the upholder of the gods.
"Bestow upon us speech that yearns for the gods"—sacrifice is indeed speech; bestow upon us the sacrifice by which [we may prosper].

"Delighting the gods," he thereby says. "I saw the herdsman, never resting"—this one who shines yonder is indeed the herdsman, for he protects all this; moreover, he never rests; therefore he says, "I saw the herdsman, never resting. (14.1.4.9–10)
"Moving hither and thither along the paths"—for he indeed moves hither and thither along the paths with the gods;

"clothing himself in those converging and diverging"—for he clothes himself in the directions that are both converging and diverging, as well as in the rays; "he revolves repeatedly within the worlds"—for he indeed revolves again and again in these worlds.
He moves about, being repeatedly turned.
O Lord of all beings, Lord of every mind, Lord of every word, Lord of all speech—O Lord of all this! O God, you who hear the gods, O divine Gharma, you are a god.
"Protect the gods"—in this there is nothing hidden.

"Here they have helped you both for the feast of the gods"—this he says specifically regarding the Aśvins; for it was the Aśvins who restored the head of the sacrifice, and it is them he thus gratifies. Therefore he says here: "Here they have helped you both for the feast of the gods."

"Honey for the two Mādhvīs, honey for the two Mādhūcīs. For Dadhyañc Ātharvaṇa indeed spoke this Brāhmaṇa named "Honey" to these two; that is their beloved abode, and by this he approaches that very abode of theirs.
Therefore he says: "Honey for the two Mādhvīs, honey for the two Mādhūcīs. 14.1.4. [14]

"For the heart thee, for the mind thee, for the sky thee, for the sun thee; standing erect, place the sacrifice among the gods in heaven"—in this there is nothing, as it were, obscure. "Thou art our father, be thou mindful of us as a father"—he who shines yonder is indeed the father, and he is...
The Pravargya is this; thus he gratifies this very one. Therefore he says: "Thou art our father; be thou mindful of us as a father. "Homage be to thee;
do not harm me"—thus he invokes this very blessing.
Then, having uncovered the head of the wife, he makes her recite while she gazes at the Mahāvīra: "May we serve thee, accompanied by Tvaṣṭṛ."
The Pravargya is indeed a bull, and the wife is a female; thus, this procreative union is brought about.

Now, he who either teaches this [rite] or partakes of it enters this very life-span and this very light. His observance of the vow is as follows: *Note: The text fragment provided ends abruptly with "yā" (of which), indicating the sentence is incomplete.*
Regarding the *Sṛṣṭi* [offerings], 14.2.1.[1]:

Now, therefore, he offers to Rohiṇī with both of these *yajus* formulas: "May Day, with its banner, enjoy [the offering]; may the well-luminous one [enjoy it] with light, *svāhā*!"—with this *yajus* at dawn; and "May Night, with its banner, enjoy [the offering]; may the well-luminous one [enjoy it] with light, *svāhā*!"—with this *yajus* in the evening. 14.2.1.[2]
Now, as to why he offers the two *rauhiṇa* oblations: Agni and Āditya are indeed the two *rauhiṇas*, for by means of these two deities the sacrificers ascend to the heavenly world.
Moreover, the two *rauhiṇas* are day and night, and the *pravargya* is Āditya; thus, he [places] that Āditya between day and night.

He encompasses it; therefore, this [sacrifice] is encompassed by day and night. Furthermore, these two worlds are indeed the *rauhiṇas*, and the *pravargya* is the sun; he thus encompasses that sun with these two worlds, and therefore it is encompassed by these two worlds.
Now, the two *rauhiṇa* cakes are indeed the eyes, and the *pravargya* is the head; he thus places the eye in the head.

14.2.1.[6] Then he takes up the cord with [the formula]: "At the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins, with the hands of Pūṣan, I take thee; thou art a girdle. Its significance is the same as before. 14.2.1.[7]
Then he calls the cow from behind the *gārhapatya* fire with the words: "O *iḍā*, come! O *aditi*, come! O *sarasvatī*, come!
For the cow is indeed *iḍā*, the cow is indeed *aditi*, and the cow is indeed *sarasvatī*. Then he calls her by name three times: "O so-and-so, come! O so-and-so, come! (14.2.1).
When she has arrived, he addresses her with: "Thou art the girdle of Aditi, the turban of Indrāṇī. For Indrāṇī is indeed the beloved wife of Indra.
"The wife is his [the Pravargya's] turban; 'thou art the most manifold in form'—thus he says, and thereby he makes him such.
14.2.1.[9] Then he drives up the calf with "Thou art Pūṣan. This one who blows here (the wind) is indeed Pūṣan, for he nourishes (*puṣyati*) all this;
and this is the Pravargya. Thus he gratifies him; therefore he says, "Thou art Pūṣan. 14.2.1.[10]
Then he says, "Heat it for the *gharma*; give [it]! For here, the *gharma* is indeed the essence which she (the cow) swells;
thus he says, "Have mercy on her.
Then he causes it to swell in the *pinvana* vessel, saying, "Swell for the Aśvins! He thereby speaks to the Aśvins; for the Aśvins...
"May these two restore the head of the sacrifice"—it is them he thus gratifies; therefore he says, "Swell for the Aśvins!
[14.2.1.12] "Swell for Sarasvatī"—Sarasvatī is indeed speech; by means of speech the Aśvins restored the head of the sacrifice;
it is them he thus gratifies; therefore he says, "Swell for Sarasvatī! [14.2.1.13]

"Swell for Indra!"—Indra is indeed the deity of the sacrifice; by that very deity who is the deity of the sacrifice, the Aśvins restored the head of the sacrifice. It is them he thus gratifies; therefore he says, "Swell for Indra. 14.2.1. [14]

Then he consecrates the drops with the formula: "Svāhā, like Indra! Svāhā, like Indra! Indra is indeed the deity of the sacrifice; thus he gratifies that very deity who is the deity of the sacrifice. Therefore he says, "Svāhā, like Indra! Svāhā, like Indra! He says it three times, for the sacrifice is threefold. He utters the *svāhā*-call first and the deity afterwards; such is the significance. 14.2.1. [15]
Then he applies his mouth to her breast with the verse, "That breast of thine which is inexhaustible, which is refreshing...

By this he means, "that breast of thine which is placed in secret. "...which bestows jewels, which finds wealth, and is easy to give"—by this he means, "which is the giver of riches, the finder of wealth, and worthy of praise. "...wherewith thou nourishest all desirable things"—by this he means, "wherewith thou [nourishest] all the gods and all..."
"Thou bearest the beings"—this is what he says. "O Sarasvatī, make him here fit for the sacrificial offering"—Sarasvatī is indeed Speech; she is this very milch-cow of the Gharma.
"Grant us the sacrifice by which we may gratify the gods"—this is what he says. Now...

He goes toward half of the *gārhapatya* fire with the formula, "I follow the wide atmosphere"; the significance of this is the same as before. Then he takes up the two plow-shares with the formulas, "Thou art the *gāyatrī* metre; thou art the *triṣṭubh* metre.
He thus takes them up with both the *gāyatrī* and the *triṣṭubh* metres. With the formula, "I enclose thee from heaven and earth," [he takes them] from these two.

The two *pariśās* are indeed Heaven and Earth, and the *pravargya* is the sun; he thus encloses that sun with these two, Heaven and Earth. Then he wipes it with a *vedī* made of muñja grass; the significance of this is the same as before. 14.2.1. [17] Then he supports it with the *udayamanī* [ladle], saying, "I support thee with the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*). Indeed, it is the intermediate space.

With the *upayamanī* [ladle], he says, "I support with the intermediate space. For by means of the intermediate space, all this is supported; or rather, the *upayamanī* is the belly, for by means of the belly all this food is supported. Therefore he says, "I support with the intermediate space.
(14.2.1) Then he brings goat's milk. For that [fire] is indeed heated and glowing; he thus cools it, and when it has cooled...
"He brings cow's milk. [Regarding the formula] "O Indra and Aśvins": Indra is indeed the deity of the sacrifice;
thus he gratifies that very deity who is the deity of the sacrifice. By saying "O Aśvins," he refers to the two Aśvins, for it was the two Aśvins who restored the head of this sacrifice.
He thus gratifies those two; therefore he says, "O Indra and Aśvins.
"Of the honey of the bee"—this honey indeed belongs to the bees; "drink the gharma," he thereby says, "drink the essence.
"O Vasus"—these are indeed the Vasus, for they cause all this to dwell; "sacrifice, vaṭ! he says.
It is just as when an oblation is offered with the cry of *vaṣaṭ*; so it becomes for him.

"Svāhā to the rain-bringing ray of the Sun!"—for indeed, one ray of the Sun is named "rain-bringer" by which he sustains all these creatures; it is that very one he gratifies thereby. Therefore he says: "Svāhā to the ray of the Sun! 14.2.1.[21]
He utters the lower *svāhā* call as "vṛṣṭivanaye" (to the one who wins the rain); this is the supreme deity; the significance of this is the same [as before]. 14.2.1.
[22] Now, he who either recites this or consumes it enters this life-span and this light; such is his [fate].
Regarding the performance of the vow:
at the point in the creation [of the sacrifice] when the Hotṛ recites this verse, "May Brahmaṇaspati go forth; may Sūnṛtā, the goddess, go forth," then the Adhvaryu...

He offers the names of the winds while moving eastward. For the gods were afraid, thinking, "Lest the *rakṣases* and *nāṣṭrās* strike him down in this interval. They offered him with the utterance of *svāhā* even before he had reached the Āhavanīya fire; they offered him into the fire only after he had already been offered.
In the same way, this sacrificer now offers him with the utterance of *svāhā* even before he has reached the Āhavanīya fire. Him...
He offers that which is already offered into the fire:
"To the ocean, to Vāta, svāhā! This one who blows here is indeed the ocean;
from this ocean, all the gods and all beings surge forth. It is into this very one that he offers it; therefore he says [the formula].

"To the ocean-going wind, svāhā! 14.2.2.[3] To the surging wind, svāhā! This one who blows here is indeed the surging one (*sariṛa*). From this surging one, all the gods and all beings prevail; it is for him that he offers this [oblation]. Therefore he says: "To the surging wind, svāhā!"

Svāhā! 14.2.2.[4] "To the invincible wind, svāhā! To the unassailable wind, svāhā! Indeed, this one who blows here is the invincible and the unassailable; it is to him that he offers this oblation. Therefore, he says, "To the invincible..."
"To Vāta for assistance, svāhā! To Vāta the unassailable, svāhā!

(14.2.2.5) "To Vāta who seeks aid, svāhā! To Vāta who is free from disease, svāhā! He indeed is the one who seeks aid and is free from disease who blows here; it is to him that he offers this oblation. Therefore he says: "To Vāta who seeks aid, svāhā! To Vāta who is free from disease, svāhā!"
"Svāhā! [14.2.2.6] "To Indra, accompanied by the Vasus and the Rudras, svāhā! This one who blows here is indeed Indra;
it is to him that he offers this oblation. Therefore he says, "To Indra," and "accompanied by the Vasus and the Rudras"; thus he follows after Indra as well as the Vasus.
He partakes of the Rudras; thus, this form of both the morning pressing and the midday pressing is performed.
"To Indra accompanied by the Ādityas, svāhā!"—Indra is indeed he who blows here; it is to him that he offers this.
Therefore they say, "For Indra thee," [and then] "for the one possessed of the Ādityas. Thus he causes the Ādityas to share in Indra;
moreover, this is made as a form of the third pressing.
"For Indra, the slayer of the adversary, thee, Svāhā!"—this wind that blows here is indeed Indra; it is for him that he offers this.

Therefore he says, "To Indra thee, the slayer of the overweening! For the overweening one is indeed the rival; thus he says, "To Indra thee, the slayer of rivals! This is his special portion (*uddhāra*); just as there is a special portion for the chief, so is this his, apart from the gods.
"To Savitṛ thee, accompanied by the Ṛbhus, accompanied by the Vibhus, accompanied by Vāja, Svāhā! He who purifies here is indeed Savitṛ.
Therefore he offers it to him; therefore he says, "To Savitṛ thee! [and] "To Ṛbhumat, Vibhumat, Vājavat thee!"—thereby he causes all the gods to share in this [oblation].
"To Bṛhaspati, accompanied by the Viśvedevas, svāhā!"—Bṛhaspati is indeed this wind that blows here; therefore...

He offers it with this [formula]; therefore he says, "To Bṛhaspati thee! and "Belonging to the Viśve Devas!"—thereby he causes all the Viśve Devas to share in it. (14.2.2) "To Yama, accompanied by the Aṅgirases and the Pitṛs, svāhā!"—Yama is indeed this wind that blows; to him he offers it.

He offers it; therefore he says, "To Yama, thee, accompanied by the Aṅgirases and the Pitṛs. When the head of the sacrifice was cut off, its sap flowed away and went to the Pitṛs. There are indeed three kinds of Pitṛs; it is to them that he thus gives a share. 14.2.2.12.
These names are twelve; there are indeed twelve months in a year, and this one who shines yonder is the year, and he is the Pravargya. Thus he gratifies him; therefore, there are twelve. 14.2.2.
[13] Then he pours from the supporting ladle into the Mahāvīra vessel with the words, "Svāhā to Gharma! For he who shines yonder is indeed Gharma.
This Pravargya indeed blazes; thus he gratifies it. Therefore he says, "Svāhā to the Gharma!
He utters the *svāhā* first and the deity last; the significance of this is the same as before.
When it has been brought forward, he mutters: "Svāhā! The Gharma for the Father. When the head of the sacrifice was cut off, its essence flowed away.
The ancestors indeed go to the three worlds; it is these very ones that he gratifies here. He makes the *svāhā*-utterance last [in the sequence];
the significance for the supreme deity is the same as before.
(14.2.2) He does not recite an invitatory verse (*anuvākyā*), for they have indeed once and for all departed.

Therefore, the *pitaras* do not recite the invitatory verse (*anuvākyā*). Having passed over [the offering], and having called for the *śrauṣaṭ*, he says, "Recite the offering prayer (*yajya*) for the *gharma*. When the *vaṣaṭ* is uttered, he makes the oblation with the verse: "To all the quarters, seated in the south"—by this he means "to all the quarters, seated in the south"; "he has sacrificed here to all the gods"—by this he means "he has sacrificed here to all the gods"; "of the honeyed *gharma* consecrated by *svāhā*..."

"Drink, O Aśvins!"—he says this specifically to the two Aśvins, for it was the two Aśvins who restored the head of the sacrifice; he thus gratifies them. He performs the *svāhā*-utterance first, [and then offers] to the deity afterwards; the significance of this is the same as before. (14.2.2) Then, having offered, he shakes it upwards, saying: "Place this sacrifice in heaven! Place this sacrifice in heaven!"—this refers to that [world].
Or rather, the *gharma* is the sun, the sacrifice; he is placed in heaven, established in heaven. It is him he thus gratifies.

Therefore he says, "Place this sacrifice in heaven; place this sacrifice in heaven. At the secondary *vaṣaṭ*-call, he offers with the words, "Svāhā to Agni, the worthy of sacrifice! That is the portion for the *sviṣṭakṛt*; for Agni is the *sviṣṭakṛt*, and [the offering is made] from the *yajus* formulas.

For by means of the *yajus* formulas he is established in this world; it is these very ones that he thus gratifies. He performs the *svāhā*-utterance first; the higher deity [is addressed later]—this is the significance. 14.2.2.

[19] Then the *brahmán* priest pronounces the consecratory formula (*anumantrayate*). For the *brahmán* is indeed the best physician among the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*); therefore, he who is the best among the officiating priests...
"He is the best of physicians; with him he thus heals this sacrifice.
(14.2.2.20) "O Aśvins, drink the hot offering!"—he says this to the two Aśvins, for it was the two Aśvins who restored the head of the sacrifice;
it is them he thus gratifies. (14.2.2.21)
"With aids that are great by day and great by night"—this is undefined; for Prajāpati is undefined, and the sacrifice is Prajāpati;
thus he heals Prajāpati, the sacrifice.
"The extenders"—he who shines yonder is indeed the extender. This...
"He traverses these worlds as if following a warp-thread; this Pravargya is that very [warp-thread], and it is him he thus gratifies.
Therefore he says, 'O weavers' (tantrāyiṇaḥ).
'Homage to Heaven and Earth!'—thus he pays homage to those two, Heaven and Earth, from whom this [world] exists."
[All Adhi 14.2.2.24] Now, as for the sacrificer: the sacrificer is indeed the sacrifice; it is by means of the sacrifice that he thus heals the sacrifice.
[14.2.2.25] "The Aśvins have drunk the Gharma"—by this he speaks of the two Aśvins, for the Aśvins are indeed the head of this sacrifice.
He thus provides these two with support; he gratifies them.
"May Heaven and Earth approve," he says; by this he addresses these two, Heaven and Earth, upon whom all this rests.
"May there be gifts right here," he says; by this he means, "May our riches be right here."
Then he consecrates the swelling [milk] with the mantra: "Swell for food! By saying "Swell for food," he speaks for the sake of rain.

"Swell for strength!"—by this he speaks for that vigorous sap which is produced from rain. "Swell for the *brahman*!"—by this he speaks for the *brahman*. "Swell for the *kṣatra*!"—by this he speaks for the *kṣatra*. "Swell for Heaven and Earth!"—[by this he speaks for Heaven and Earth].

Then he says [the offering] for these two, heaven and earth, upon whom all this rests. When it overflows upwards, that overflows for the sacrificer; when eastward, that for the gods; when southward, that for the ancestors; when westward, that for the cattle; when northward, that for his offspring—it is indeed never-failing.

For he causes it to swell upward for the sacrificer; moreover, he causes that very direction toward which it swells to swell. When the drops have subsided, he steps out toward the northeast, saying, "Thou art Dharma, the Good Dharma. For he who shines yonder is indeed Dharma; he is...
"Verily, this [sun] sustains all this; by it all this is sustained. This indeed is the Pravargya; thus he gratifies him. Therefore he says: 'Thou art Dharma, the good Dharma.
(14.2.2) Then he places it on the mound, saying: "May it sustain manly powers for us; may it not make us angry, but bestow riches upon us."
"Support," he says this; "support the Brahman, support the Kṣatra, support the Viś"—he says this, "support all this. 14.2.2.
[31] Then he offers with the wood-shavings (śākala); the wood-shavings are indeed the vital breaths; thus he bestows the vital breaths upon him. 14.2.2. [32]

"Svāhā to Pūṣan, to the arrow! This one who blows here is indeed Pūṣan, for he nourishes (*puṣyati*) all this; he is also the breath (*prāṇa*). He thus places breath into him. Therefore he says, "Svāhā to Pūṣan, to the arrow. He makes the utterance of *svāhā* first and the deity last; the significance of this is the same as before. Having offered the oblation, he leans it against the middle enclosing-stick. 14.2.2 [33]

"Svāhā to the pressing-stones!"—the pressing-stones are indeed the vital breaths; he thus bestows the vital breaths upon him. Having offered the oblation, he leans it against the middle enclosing-stick.
"Svāhā to the echoes!"—the echoes are indeed the vital breaths, for by the vital breaths all this is made to resound.
He thus bestows the vital breaths upon him. Having offered the oblation, he leans it against the middle enclosing-stick (paridhi).

[Saying: "Svāhā to the fathers who have spread the sacrificial grass, who drink the Gharma!"—without having offered it, while looking toward the north, he hides it within the southern half of the sacrificial grass. [The essence of the sacrifice, when its head was cut off, flowed away...]

The ancestors indeed go to the three worlds; it is them that he thus gratifies. Now, as to why he does not look [back]: for the ancestors have once and for all turned away. "Svāhā to Heaven and Earth!"—Heaven and Earth are indeed the out-breath and the up-breath.
He thus bestows heaven and earth, as well as the out-breath and the up-breath, upon him. Having offered the oblation, he leans it against the middle enclosing-stick, saying:
"Svāhā to the All-Gods! The All-Gods are indeed the vital breaths; he thus bestows the vital breaths upon him. Having offered the oblation...

He places it upon the middle enclosing-stick (paridhi) with the formula, "Svāhā to Rudra, the invoker of Rudra" (14.2.2). Without having offered it, while looking toward the south, he hands it to the Pratiprasthātṛ; the latter throws it out toward the north from the northern side of the hall, for this is the [proper] direction for that deity.
He thus gratifies him in each of the quarters; and as to why he does not look [at the fire], it is lest Rudra should harm him.

These offerings amount to seven; for there are these seven vital breaths in the head, and it is these he thereby places in him. Then he pours from the Mahāvīra into the Upayamanī [ladle] with the formula, "Svāhā! Light with light! For light indeed...
In the one [offering] there is milk, in the other light; for these two lights meet together. He makes the *svāhā*-utterance first and the deity last; this is the bond. 14.2.2.
[41] Then he offers the two *rauhiṇa* oblations: "May the day be pleased with its banner, the fair-lighted with light, *svāhā*!"—this is the bond.
"May Night with its banner rejoice in the fair light, through the light, Svāhā!"—the significance of this is the same as before.

Then he hands the remainder of the *gharma* to the sacrificer; having sought permission, he consumes it, saying: "The honey has been offered into the most Indra-like Agni. By this he means: "The honey has been offered into the Agni who possesses the most *indriya* (vital power); may we partake of thee."
"O divine Gharma, homage be to you; do not harm me"—with these words he invokes this very blessing.
Then, sand is strewn to the south; they perform the purification there, for whatever significance belongs to the *mārjālīya* altar applies here as well.
He throws the wood-shavings into the fire, and then they proceed with the *upasad* rites; thus is the head of the sacrifice prepared.
Just as the Aśvins restored it for him then, so one should not perform the Pravargya at his first sacrifice; for that would be a sin, and moreover, lest Indra should cut off his head.
Rather, he should do it at the second or the third sacrifice, for in the beginning the gods were worshipping with a headless sacrifice.
They performed [the rite] while exerting themselves; therefore, it should be done on the second or the third day. For this [fire], once heated, becomes glowing.

(14.2.2.45) If one were to heat it at the first pressing, this fire, being heated and glowing, would burn up his offspring and cattle, and furthermore, the sacrificer would be liable to die prematurely. Therefore, it should be done on the second or the third day. (14.2.2.46)
One should not perform the Pravargya for just anyone; for the Pravargya is everything, and [one should think], "Lest I do everything for just anyone.
One should indeed perform it for one who is well-known, or for one who is dear to him, or for one who is learned in the Vedas and might attain him through his recitation. 14.2.2. [47]

One should pour it out at a sacrifice of a thousand; for a thousand is everything, and this [offering] is everything. One should pour it out at a *sarvavedasa* sacrifice; for a *sarvavedasa* is everything, and this is everything. One should pour it out at the *viśvajit* with all the *pṛṣṭha* chants; for the *viśvajit* with all the *pṛṣṭha* chants is everything, and this is everything. One should pour it out at the *vājapeya* and the *rājasūya*; for that is everything, as is the *sattrā*.
One should perform the Pravargya rite; for the Sattra is indeed everything, and all these [elements] are its Pravargyas, and not otherwise.

14.2.2.[48] Regarding this they say: "If the Apravargya sacrifice is headless, then by what does his Agnihotra become possessed of a head? One should reply: "By the Āhavanīya fire. "And how do the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices [become so]? "By means of the clarified butter (ājya)."

"If one asks, 'How [is it performed] with the *puroḍāśa*? one should say, 'With the *payasyā*. If one asks, 'How [are] the *Cāturmāsya* sacrifices? one should say, 'With the *payasyā*. If one asks, 'How [is] the animal sacrifice (*paśubandha*)?
one should say, 'With both the animal and the *puroḍāśa*. If one asks, 'How [is] the *Saumya-adhvara*? one should say, 'With the *havirdhāna* [shed]. Now they also say:
"When the head of the sacrifice was cut off, the gods restored its head by means of this *Ātithya* [offering]. Indeed, it is not so.
He who knows this has sacrificed with a sacrifice that is headless by some measure.

14.2.2.[50] Regarding this they say: "Since they lead forward the *praṇītā* waters at the sacrifice, why then does one not lead them forward here? The *praṇītā* waters are indeed the head of the sacrifice, and the *pravargya* is the head; [one does not lead them forward] lest one should place the head upon the head. 14.2.2.[51]

Regarding this they say: "Since the *prayāja*s and *anuyāja*s occur elsewhere, why do they not occur here? The *prayāja*s and *anuyāja*s are indeed the vital breaths (*prāṇa*); the *avakāśa* bricks are the vital breaths; the *śākala* chips are the vital breaths. [They omit them] thinking, "Lest I should cause the vital breaths to mount upon the vital breaths. Regarding this they say: "Since they offer the two *ājyabhāga* oblations elsewhere, why do they not offer them here? These two are indeed the eyes.
"The two *rauhiṇa* offerings are the eyes of the sacrifice; [he offers them] so that he may not cause the eye to ascend by means of the eye.
14.2.2. [53] Regarding this they say: "Since they offer to the gods with wooden vessels, why does he offer this one with an earthen vessel?
When the sacrifice had its head cut off, its sap flowed out; it went to these two, heaven and earth—and that which was on this earth was the clay.

Now, when that [cup] is made of clay—which is water—and the great heroes (mahāvīra) are made of water, he thereby provides it with that very essence and makes it complete. If it were made of wood, it would burn; if it were made of gold, it would melt; if it were made of iron, it would be consumed.

If it were made of iron, it would overflow; if it were made of clay, it would burn up the vessel. But this [oblation] stands firm because it is made of earth; therefore, one offers it with something made of earth alone. Now, he who either recites or partakes of this [rite] enters this life and this light.
Or rather,
his practice of the vow extends into the future.
On the third day, or the sixth, or the twelfth, he combines the Pravargya and Upasad rites.

He puts away the Pravargya vessels; for this head is, as it were, put away. Taking all that which is around it, they go together to the front of the hall and enter within the altar. Then the Āgnīdhra prepares three bundles of splinters at the Āhavanīya fire; having kindled one of them—
Holding it at the level of the mouth, he offers. When the sacrifice had its head cut off, its pain (śuc) went forth and entered these worlds; with that very pain he thus endows it and makes it whole.
Now, as to why [he holds it] at the level of the mouth: that which is at the level of the mouth is, as it were, above; and that which is yonder [the sun] is, as it were, above.
The world—that pain which entered this world—he thus satisfies with that very pain and makes it whole.

(14.3.1.4) "O Gharma, that pain of thine which is celestial"—that which is indeed the celestial pain; "which is in the Gāyatrī, in the Havirdhāna"—that which is indeed in the Gāyatrī and in the Havirdhāna;
"may that swell for thee, may it expand; to that of thine, Svāhā!"—in this there is nothing hidden, as it were. (14.3.1.5)

Then, having kindled a second [fire-brand] and holding it at the height of the navel, he offers. That which is at the height of the navel is indeed like the middle; the intermediate region (antarikṣaloka) is like the middle. Thus, by means of that very heat (śuc) which entered the intermediate region, he endows this [sacrifice] with that heat and makes it complete. 14.3.1. [6]

"O Gharma, that heat which has gone into the atmosphere—by means of that *triṣṭubh* verse which is in the atmosphere, [and] that which is in the *āgnīdhra* hearth—may it swell for thee, may it expand for thee; to that of thine, *svāhā*! There is nothing here that is obscure. Then, having added a third piece of wood, sitting upon it, he offers the oblation. For that which is sitting is, as it were, below; and below indeed is this [earth].
Now, that which is this world—that grief entered this world; with that very grief he thus completes him, making him whole.
"O Gharma, that grief of thine which is on the earth"—that which is on the earth; "which is in the Jagatī [meter], in the Sadas"—that which is...

"May she, the assembly on earth, prosper for thee and extend for thee; to her, to thee, Svāhā!"—in this there is nothing hidden, as it were. 14.3.1 [9] Then he steps out with the formula, "For the supreme protection of the Kṣatra. That which shines yonder is indeed the divine Kṣatra;
by saying this, he means, "For the supreme lordship over this human Kṣatra," [and thus] the body of the Brahman.

"Protect," he says; this means "protect yourself, O Brahman. "The clans [viśas] with their law [dharmaṇā], we," he says; the clan is indeed the sacrifice; thus he means "for the safety of the sacrifice. "We step forward for new prosperity," he says; this means "for the safety and security of the sacrifice. 14.3.1. [10]

Then he says, "Sing the *sāman*," or "Recite the *sāman*," but he should rather say, "Sing," for they sing the *sāman*. Now, as to why he sings the *sāman*: it is so that these malevolent spirits (*nāṣṭrā rakṣāṃsi*) may not injure the limbs of the sacrifice from the outside; for the *sāman* is the repeller of the malevolent spirits and the *rakṣases*. 14.3.1. [11]
He sings in the Āgneyī [meter], for Agni is the repeller of the *rakṣases*. He sings in the *aticandas* [meter]; this *aticandas* indeed contains all the meters;
therefore he sings in the *aticandas*. He sings: "Agni burns, he strikes back, ahāva! ahāva!"—for those are indeed the *nāṣṭrās*.
Therefore, they ward off the *rakṣas* from this place. They go out toward the north, first by way of the *cātvāla* pit and then by way of the *āgnīdhra* shed, for this is the door of the sacrifice.
They proceed in whatever direction water is found there.
One should extinguish it in a pool. For this [fire] becomes heated and glowing;
if he were to extinguish it on this earth, its heat would enter this earth; if he were to extinguish it in water, its heat would enter the water.
But when he extinguishes it in a pool, in that way he harms neither the waters nor this earth, since he does not cast it into the waters.
Therefore, he does not harm the waters; and since the waters surround him on all sides, and the waters are peace (*śānti*), therefore he does not harm this [earth].
For that reason, one should set it down near a flowing stream.
But rather, one should set it down on the *uttaravedi* (high altar). The *uttaravedi* is indeed the sacrifice, and the *pravargya* is the head; thus, it is the head of the sacrifice itself.
He replaces it. He sets aside the first *pravargya* vessel so that it touches the northern *nābhi*. The northern *nābhi* is speech, and the *pravargya* is the head; thus he places speech in the head.
"Four-cornered," he says; for he who shines yonder is indeed four-cornered, since the quarters are his corners; therefore he says, "four-cornered.
"The navel of *ṛta*, far-extending"—*ṛta* is truth, and the navel of truth is far-extending; this is what he thereby says. He [is] our...
"Viśvāyuḥ saprathāḥ"—by this he means "May he be for us all-living and far-reaching.

(14.3.1.19) "Apa dveṣo apa hvaraḥ"—in this there is nothing hidden; "saścima anyavratasya"—for his vow is one thing and that of human beings is another; therefore he says, "We follow him whose vow is other [than ours]. The other two [verses] are likewise directed forward.
That [wood] is threefold; this head is threefold.

He places the clay for the side-lying brick in front; verily he thus bestows flesh upon him. On both sides of that are the two *parīśas*; verily he thus bestows the two arms upon him. On both sides further are the two *rauhiṇa* offering-spoons.
He places these two [the spade and the throne] in his hands;
for he places the spade to the north, since that is its proper place; the royal throne to the south, since that is its proper place;
the black antelope skin to the north, since that is its proper place; and fanning-purses on all sides—for they are indeed the vital breaths.

He thus bestows the vital breaths upon him; there are three fans, for there are indeed three vital breaths—the out-breath, the up-breath, and the through-breath—and it is these he thereby bestows upon him. Then, having placed this cord-fastening upon the supporting ladle (upayamanī), he sets it down.

He places [the two cups] towards the east; he thus bestows the belly upon him. On both sides of that, he places the two *pinvana* vessels; he thus bestows the two testicles upon him, for by means of the testicles the bull is filled with semen. Behind them, he places the post-hole pegs; he thus bestows the thighs upon him. Behind those, he places the two *rauhiṇa* potsherds; he thus bestows the knees upon him. These...
As for the two [stones] being on a single potsherd: these two knees are, as it were, on a single potsherd;
he thus places the two feet upon this [altar]. For with the feet one strikes firmly;
the two *khara* stones are used for moving forward from the north, for that is their place; the *mārjālīya* is to the south, for that is its place. 14.3.1. [23]
Then he pours milk into this [mixture], saying, "O Gharma, this is thy filler (purīṣa). Food indeed is the filler;
verily, he thus bestows food upon it. "By this, do thou grow and swell,"—there is nothing here that is obscure.
"And may we grow and may we swell"—verily, with this he invokes a blessing. 14.3.1. [24]

He should not bring all [the food] at once, lest there be food apart from the sacrificer; he leaves over half or more. In the afternoon, having poured out the fast-food for the sacrificer, he hands it to him. Thus he bestows this food upon the sacrificer himself, and so food does not depart from the sacrificer. 14.3.1. [25]
Then he sprinkles it all around with water. Water is indeed peace; he thus pacifies it.
He sprinkles it all around from every side; he thus pacifies it from every side. He sprinkles three times, for the sacrifice is threefold.
Then he says, "He sings the Vārṣāhara Sāman. This one who shines yonder is indeed the tawny bull (vṛṣā hariḥ). And this one...
The Pravargya is this; it is him whom he thus gratifies. Therefore he says: "He sings the Vārṣāhara Sāman.
(14.3.1) Then they purify themselves at the Cātvāla pit. With the formula, "May the waters and plants be friendly to us," he takes water with his joined palms.
The waters are indeed a thunderbolt; by means of the thunderbolt, he thus establishes friendship. [With the formula,] "May they be unfriendly to him who hates us and whom we hate..."
And thinking, "We hate him," if he should have someone whom he hates in a certain direction, he should pour it out toward that direction; by that very act, he brings about his defeat.
Then, as if facing east, he steps out toward the north with the verse, "Up from the darkness we... Darkness is indeed evil; [thus] he [casts off] evil itself.
"Driving away the darkness, we behold the sun, the highest light"—for this world is indeed higher than the waters; thus he establishes himself in this very world.

"To the god among gods, to Sūrya, we have gone, to the highest light"—for the heavenly world is indeed the sun, the highest light; thus he finally establishes himself in the heavenly world. Having reached [the fire] without looking back, he [places it] in the Āhavanīya.
He places a fuel-stick on the fire with the formula, "Thou art a fuel-stick; thou art splendor; bestow splendor upon me. By this, he indeed invokes a blessing.

(14.3.1) Now, when the Soma has been pressed, they proceed with the Dadhigharma offering. Soma is the sacrifice, and the Pravargya is the head; thus he restores the head to the sacrifice itself. This occurs at the midday pressing, for that is Indra’s exclusive pressing.

By [offering] at the midday pressing, he thus gratifies him in his own portion. When the Mādhyandina Pavamāna has been chanted—the Mādhyandina Pavamāna being indeed the vital breath—he thereby places vital breath into him. With the Agnihotra-ladle, for this is the mouth of sacrifices.
The Agnihotra is the head; he thereby places the mouth [upon it]. 14.3.1.
[30] When it is being brought forward, he says, "O Hotṛ, speak what is to be spoken by you," for here the Hotṛ indeed speaks.
Then, rising up, he says, "The oblation is cooked," for it has indeed been cooked. Having passed by, and having called for the *śrauṣaṭ*, he says...
He says, "Sacrifice the curd-heat offering (*dadhigharma*). At the *vaṣaṭ*-call he offers it;
at the subsequent *vaṣaṭ*-call he brings it back and hands it to the sacrificer for consumption.
Having sought permission, he consumes it with the verse, "In me be that great power (*indriya*)," for that indeed is the great power.
"Heat shines within me, skill within me"—thus he places *kratu* (will) and *dakṣa* (skill) within himself.
"The Gharma, three-pointed, shines forth"—for this Gharma indeed shines forth, three-pointed. "Together with the Virāj, with light"—for it indeed shines together with the Virāj and with light.
"Together with the Brahman, with splendor"—for it indeed shines together with the Brahman and with splendor. "The seed of milk..."
"It has been brought"—for this seed of milk has indeed been brought; "may we obtain its milking year after year"—with these words he invokes this very blessing.
Then they purify themselves at the *cātvāla* pit; the significance of that is the same as before.
Now, therefore, regarding the sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*s): he gives a hundred-measure weight of gold to the Brahman priest, for the Brahman priest is seated.
He gives fame, gold, and therefore a *suvarṇa*—a hundred-measure weight of gold—to the Brahman priest.
(14.3.1.33) Now, as for this cow that milks the *gharma*, he gives her to the Adhvaryu.
For the *gharma* is indeed heated, and the Adhvaryu steps out as if heated; therefore, he gives her to the Adhvaryu. (14.3.1.34)

Now, that cow which provides the sacrificial food for the sacrificer, he gives her to the Hotṛ; for the Hotṛ is the sacrifice and the sacrificer is the sacrifice—therefore he gives her to the Hotṛ. Then, that cow which provides the sacrificial food for the wife, he gives her to the Udgātṛs; for here they indeed perform the duties of the wife.
Because the Udgātṛs perform it, he therefore gives that [cow] to the Udgātṛs. 14.3.1.
[36] Now, indeed, he who either recites this or consumes it enters this life-span and this light; his observance of the vow is the same as that at the Sṛṣṭi [offering]. 14.3.2. [1]

The sacrifice is indeed the self of all beings and of all the gods; following its success, the sacrificer prospers with offspring and cattle. But he whose *gharma* vessel breaks is deprived of offspring and cattle;
in that case, there is this expiation. 14.3.2. [2]
He offers the full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*). The full is indeed everything; by means of everything he thus heals whatever in the sacrifice has been torn asunder.
"Svāhā to the vital breaths together with their overlord!"—the mind, indeed, is the overlord of the vital breaths, for all [the breaths] are in the mind. 14.3.2. [3]
The vital breaths are established therein; it is by means of that mind alone that he heals whatever in the sacrifice has been torn asunder.
"Svāhā to the Earth!"—the earth, indeed, is the abode of all the gods; thus, by means of all those deities, he heals whatever in the sacrifice has been torn asunder. 14.3.2 [4–5]

‘To Agni, svāhā!’—Agni, indeed, is the self of all the gods; thus he heals with all these deities whatever in the sacrifice has been torn asunder. ‘To the intermediate space, svāhā!’—The intermediate space, indeed, is the abode of all the gods; thus [he heals] with all [the deities].

"Vāyave svāhā!"—Vāyu, indeed, is the self of all the gods; therefore, [he offers] for the sake of all of them. "Dive svāhā!"—Dyaus, indeed, is the abode of all the gods; therefore, [he offers] for the sake of all of them. "Sūryāya svāhā!"—Sūrya, indeed, is the self of all the gods; therefore, [he offers] for the sake of all of them.

"To the quarters, svāhā!"—the quarters indeed are the abode of all the gods; that [is for] all. "To the Moon, svāhā!"—the Moon indeed is the self of all the gods; that [is for] all. "To the constellations, svāhā!"—the constellations indeed are the abode of all the gods; that [is for] all.

"To the waters, svāhā!"—the waters, indeed, are the abode of all the gods; thus [he offers] to all of them. "To Varuṇa, svāhā!"—Varuṇa, indeed, is the self of all the gods; thus [he offers] to all of them. "To the navel, svāhā! To the purified one, svāhā!"—this is undefined; Prajāpati, indeed, is undefined.
Prajāpati is the sacrifice; thus he heals this very Prajāpati, the sacrifice.

(14.3.2.16) These oblations are thirteen; there are indeed thirteen months in a year, and the year is Prajāpati, and Prajāpati is the sacrifice; thus he heals this very Prajāpati, the sacrifice. (14.3.2.17)

"To Speech, Svāhā!"—with this he bestows the mouth upon him. "To Breath, Svāhā! To Breath, Svāhā!"—with this he bestows the two nostrils upon him. "To Sight, Svāhā! To Sight, Svāhā!"—with this he bestows the two eyes upon him. "To Hearing, Svāhā! To Hearing, Svāhā!"—with this he bestows the two ears upon him. 14.3.2 [18]
There are these seven oblations; for there are these seven vital breaths in the head, and it is these he thereby places in him.
He offers the final full-oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*); the full is indeed everything, and by means of everything he thus heals whatever in the sacrifice has been torn asunder. 14.3.2. [19]

"May [the gods grant] the desire and intention of the mind"—for by the mind indeed all this is attained; he heals with the mind itself whatever in the sacrifice has been torn asunder. "May [the gods grant] the truth of speech"—for by speech indeed all this is attained; he heals with speech itself whatever [in the sacrifice has been torn asunder]. 14.3.2. [20]
"The increased form of the sacrifice, the essence of cattle, food, glory, and fortune—may it rest upon me, svāhā! With this, he indeed invokes a blessing.
(14.3.2) Then, having ground that [clay] and the clay for the secondary brick, and having mixed them with moist clay, he fashions them according to the prescribed ritual procedure.
He cooks it for the purpose of cleansing; then, he should proceed with whichever of the two spare bricks (*upaśaya*) is firm.

The *Pravargya* is indeed the year; the year is everything, and the *Pravargya* is everything. When it is heated, that is spring; when it has become red-hot, that is summer; when it has swelled, that is the rainy season; and when the rains have come...

They swell, and then all the gods and all beings live upon them; indeed, rain swells for that person who knows this. These worlds are the Pravargya; these worlds are everything, and the Pravargya is everything. 14.3.2. [23]

What it flowed forth from is this world; what it delighted in is the intermediate space; what it swelled is that world. Indeed, when that world swells, then all the gods and all beings subsist upon it. That world indeed swells for him who knows this thus. 14.3.2. [24]

These deities indeed are the Pravargya: Agni, Vāyu, and Āditya. All these deities are indeed the Pravargya; all is the Pravargya. When it is heated (pravṛkta), that is Agni; when it has shone forth (rucita), that is Vāyu; when it has swelled (pinvita), that is yonder Āditya.
And when yonder Āditya swells, then all the gods and all beings subsist upon him. Verily, he causes [the sacrificer] to swell.

"That is the sun—he who knows this thus. 14.3.2.[25] The Pravargya is indeed the sacrificer; his self is his offspring and his cattle. The sacrificer is everything, and the Pravargya is everything. When it is set forth (*pravṛkta*), that is his self; when it has been heated (*rukita*), that is his offspring; when it has been swollen (*pinvita*), that is his cattle. When, indeed...

The cattle swell, and then all the gods and all beings live upon them; indeed, the cattle swell for him who knows this. The Agnihotra is the Pravargya, for the Agnihotra is everything and the Pravargya is everything. That which has been placed upon the fire...

What is drawn up from it is what he has increased; what is offered is what he has pleased; what is poured out is what he has made swell. When the *agnihotra* swells, then all the gods and all beings subsist upon it. Indeed, the *agnihotra* swells for that man who knows this thus. 14.3.2. [27]

The *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices are indeed the *pravargya*; the *darśapūrṇamāsa* are everything, and the *pravargya* is everything. When [the milk] has been placed on the fire, that is the *pravṛkta*; when it has been set down, that is the *rucita*; when it has been offered, that is the *pinvita*. Indeed, when the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices overflow (*pinvete*), then all the gods and all beings subsist upon them; they indeed overflow.
Or rather, the New and Full Moon sacrifices belong to him who knows this thus.

(14.3.2 [28]) The Cāturmāsya sacrifices are indeed the Pravargya; the Cāturmāsya sacrifices are everything, and the Pravargya is everything. When it has been placed on the fire, that is the *pravṛkta* (the one set forth); when it has been set down, that is the *rug*.
