Cito That which is offered (*huta*) is that which swells (*pinvita*). When the *Cāturmāsya* sacrifices swell, then all the gods and all [the sacrificial elements] swell.
"Beings live depending on them; indeed, the Cāturmāsya sacrifices swell for him who knows this thus.

(14.3.2) "The Pravargya is indeed the Animal Sacrifice (Paśubandha). The Animal Sacrifice is everything, and the Pravargya is everything. When it has been placed upon the fire, that is the 'Pravṛkta' (the one set forth); when it has been set down, that is the 'Rucita' (the one made radiant); when it has been offered, that is the 'Pinvita' (the one made to swell). When indeed..."
The animal sacrifice swells, and then all the gods and all beings subsist upon it; indeed, the animal sacrifice swells for him who knows this.
Soma is the Pravargya; Soma is everything, and the Pravargya is everything. That...

When it is pressed, that is its being "set forth" (*pravṛkta*); when it is drawn up, that is its being "pleasing" (*rucita*); when it is offered, that is its being "swollen" (*pinvita*). For when Soma swells, then all the gods and all beings partake of him. Indeed, Soma swells for that man who knows this; and for him, no sacrifice remains unperformed that is without the *pravargya* rite.

Thus he knows this (ChU 14.3.2.31). Now, he who either teaches or consumes this [food] enters this very life-span and this very light. His observance of the vow is the same as that prescribed for the creation [of the world]. (ChU 14.4.1.1)
There were two classes of Prajāpati’s offspring: the gods and the Asuras. Of these, the gods were fewer, while the Asuras were more numerous; they contended with one another for these worlds.
Then the gods said, "Come, let us overcome the Asuras at the sacrifice by means of the Udgītha."

They said to Speech, "Do you sing the Udgītha for us. "So be it," she replied. Speech sang the Udgītha for them; whatever enjoyment was in speech, that she obtained for the gods, and whatever is auspicious that one speaks, that she obtained for herself. They perceived, "Verily, they will surpass us by means of this singer. They rushed upon him and pierced him with evil. That which is that evil—
"That which he speaks here that is improper—that indeed is that evil.
Then they said to the breath, "Sing for us as the Udgātṛ. "So be it," [said] the breath. For them, the breath sang;
whatever enjoyment there is in the breath, that it sang for the gods, and whatever is auspicious that one smells, that it sang for itself. They understood: "By this indeed we..."
Thinking, "The Udgātṛ will surpass us," they rushed toward him and pierced him with evil.
That which is this evil is precisely that which one smells here as something unseemly; that indeed is that evil.
Then they said to the eye, "Do you sing the Udgītha for us. "So be it," it said, and the eye sang the Udgītha for them. Whatever [evil] was in the eye...

The *bhoga* (enjoyment) sang it out for the gods, while that which he sees as auspicious, he sang out for himself. They perceived this and, thinking, "By means of this Udgātṛ priest, they will surely surpass us," they rushed at him and pierced him with evil.
That which is evil is precisely that which one sees here as unseemly; that itself is that evil. 14.4.1.6
Then they said to the ear, "Do you sing the Udgītha for us. "So be it," [said the ear]. For them, the ear sang the Udgītha;

it sang for the gods whatever enjoyment was in the ear, and for itself whatever was pleasant that it hears. They perceived, "With this singer, they will surely surpass us. Having rushed upon it, they pierced it with evil. That which is that evil—
Whatever unpleasant thing he hears here, that is indeed that evil.
Then they said to the mind, "Chant the Udgītha for us. "So be it," [it replied]. Mind chanted the Udgītha for them;

whatever enjoyment is in the mind, that it secured for the gods, and whatever is auspicious in its volition, that it secured for itself. They understood: "By this, indeed, we have not been surpassed."
Thinking, "The Udgātṛ will pass us by," they rushed toward him and pierced him with evil.

That which is that evil is this very thing that one conceives here as improper; that indeed is that evil. In this same way, they indeed beset these deities with evils and pierced them with evil. 14.4.1.8
Then they said to the breath in the mouth, "Do you sing the Udgītha for us. "So be it," he replied. This breath sang the Udgītha for them.
They perceived, "With this singer, they will surely overcome us. They rushed at him and sought to strike him with evil.
Just as a clod of earth would shatter upon hitting a stone, even so did they perish, scattering in all directions. Thereupon—
The gods became superior and the asuras were defeated; he who knows this becomes superior himself, and his hateful rival is defeated.
They said, "Where indeed has he gone, who thus adhered to us?"—"He is here within the mouth.
He is Ayāsya Āṅgirasa, for he is the essence (*rasa*) of the limbs (*aṅga*).

This deity is indeed named *dūr* (the Far), for death is far from her; and indeed, death becomes far from him who knows this. This very deity, having struck away the evil—the death—from these deities, [went] where they...

He sent them forth toward the quarters; he then deposited their evils therein. Therefore, one should not go to a person nor to the edge of a place, thinking, "Lest I fall into evil, into death. That deity, having struck away the evil and death from these deities, then [proceeded].
He carried Speech across death first. When Speech was released from death, it became this fire. This very fire, having transcended death on the far side, shines forth.
Then Prāṇa carried him across. When he was released from death, he became Vāyu;
this very Vāyu blows, having passed beyond death. Then Cakṣus carried him across. When it was released from death, it became Āditya; that is yonder Āditya.
Beyond that, he transcended death; he burned away [the sin]. Then he carried the sense of hearing across. When it was released from death, it became these quarters;
these quarters are beyond death, having transcended it.
Then Mind carried him across. When it was released from death, it became the moon.
That moon shines having transcended death beyond. Indeed, this deity carries across death in the same way for one who knows this. 14.4.1.18
Then he sang for himself the right to food. For whatever food is eaten here, it is eaten by him alone;
thus he is established in this world.
14.4.1.19 The gods said, "This entire universe is only as much as food; you have sung that all of it for yourself. Let us have a share in this food."
"Share with us," they said; "Enter into me," he replied; "So be it," they said, and they entered around him on all sides.

Therefore, whatever food one eats with this [breath], by that these [other breaths] are satisfied. Thus indeed do his own people enter into him who knows this—he becomes the supporter of his own, the best, the leader, the eater of food, and the sovereign. 14.4.1.20
And whoever among his own people seeks to be a rival to one who knows this, he is by no means able to support his dependents;
but whoever follows him, or whoever desires to support dependents by following him, he indeed is able to support his dependents.
This is Ayāsya Āṅgirasa, for he is the essence (*rasa*) of the limbs. Indeed, the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is the essence of the limbs; for the vital breath is the essence of the limbs.
Therefore, from whichever limb the vital breath departs, that very limb withers, for it is indeed the vital breath that is the essence of the limbs. 14.4.1.22
He is indeed Bṛhaspati. Vāc is the Bṛhatī; he is her lord, therefore he is Bṛhaspati. (14.4.1.23) He is indeed Brahmaṇaspati. Vāc is Brahman; he is its lord, therefore he is Brahmaṇaspati.
(14.4.1.24) He is indeed Sāman. Vāc is Sāman; he is both *sā* and *ama*, and that is the essence of the name Sāman. Furthermore, because he is equal (*sama*), [he is Sāman]. (14.4.1.25)
It is equal to a flea, equal to a mosquito, equal to an elephant, equal to these three worlds, and equal to this entire universe;

therefore, indeed, one attains the Sāman, attaining union with and residence in the same world as the Sāman, who thus knows this Sāman. This, moreover, is the Udgītha: breath is "ut," for by breath all this is upheld; speech is "gīthā," and it is called so because it sings.

And because it is sung (*gīthā*), it is the *udgītha*. Regarding this, Brahmadatta Caikitāneya, while consuming the King [Soma], said: "May this king have his head split apart, since Āyāsya Āṅgirasa sang the *udgītha* for him with something other than this! For he [sang] by means of speech alone.
"And he sang [the Udgītha] with breath. Regarding this very Sāman, he who knows its property (sva) indeed acquires property. Its property, verily, is tone (svara).
Therefore, one intending to perform the office of a priest (ārtvijya) should desire tone in his speech; for with that speech endowed with tone, one performs the office of a priest.
Therefore, one should make the sacrifice possess a tone (*svara*); they desire to see it indeed, and furthermore, he who possesses his own property (*sva*) succeeds;

for he who thus knows this "own" (*sva*) of the *sāman* possesses his own property. 14.4.1.28 He who knows the gold (*suvarṇa*) of this very *sāman* possesses gold; for its gold is indeed the tone (*svara*).

His becomes gold—he who thus knows this "gold" (*suvarṇa*) of the *sāman*. Now, he who knows the support (*pratiṣṭhā*) of this *sāman* indeed finds his support. Speech, verily, is its support; for it is upon speech that this vital breath (*prāṇa*) is supported when it is sung. Some, however, say it is upon food.
Now, therefore, follows the ascent of the Pavamāna chants. The Prastotṛ indeed chants the Sāman;
when he begins the Prastāva, at that moment he should mutter these [mantras]: "Lead me from non-existence to existence; lead me from darkness to light; lead me from death to immortality. (14.4.1.31)
When he says, "Lead me from the unreal to the real," the unreal is indeed death and the real is immortality; thus he says, "Lead me from death to immortality;
make me immortal. When he says, "Lead me from darkness to light," darkness is indeed death and light is immortality; [thus he says], "Lead me from death to immortality..."
"Make me immortal"—this is what he says; "lead me from death to immortality"—in this there is nothing hidden, as it were.

Now, regarding those other chants (*stotra*s), one should sing for oneself the attainment of food. Therefore, in those [chants], one should choose a boon—whatever desire one may wish for. This Udgātṛ who knows thus [obtains] whatever desire for himself or for the sacrificer.
Whatever one desires, that he sings for; and this very Sāman is indeed world-conquering. For one who knows this Sāman thus, there is no hope of not attaining the worlds.
In the beginning, this was only the Self (Ātman) in the form of a person (puruṣavidha). He looked around.
He saw nothing other than himself; he first uttered, "I am," and from that the name "I" (Aham) arose.
Therefore, even now, when addressed, one first says, "It is I," and then utters whatever other name one may have.
Because he burnt away all evils prior to all this, he is called *Puruṣa*. Indeed, he who knows this burns away such a person.

He who desires to be before me—he who knows thus. 14.4.2.[3] He was afraid; therefore, one who is alone is afraid. He reflected: "Since there is nothing other than myself, of what am I afraid? Then his fear departed from him. For of what would he have been afraid? Indeed, fear arises from a second [entity].
He did not find delight. Therefore, one who is alone does not find delight. He desired a second. He was as large as a man and a woman in close embrace.
He split this very self into two parts; from that, there came to be a husband and a wife.
Therefore, Yājñavalkya used to say, "This body is, as it were, only half of oneself. Thus, this void is filled by a woman. He united with her, and from that, human beings were born. 14.4.2. [6]
He reflected: "How indeed can it be that he, having produced himself alone, comes into being? Well, let me disappear.
He became a cow, and the other became a bull; he united with her, and from that cows were born.

One became a mare, the other a stallion; one became a she-ass, the other a donkey. He united with her, and from that, the single-hoofed animal was born. One became a goat, the other a ram; one became a ewe, the other a male sheep. He united with her...
He ate her; from that, goats and sheep were born. In this very way, he created everything whatsoever exists here, down to the ants.
He thought, "I alone am the creation, for I have created all this. Thus he became the creation (*sṛṣṭi*). In the creation...
Laughter arises for him who knows this. 14.4.2.[11] Then he rubbed [the breath] together; from the mouth as the womb and from his hands, he emitted fire.
Therefore, both of these are hairless on the inside, for the womb is hairless on the inside. 14.4.2.[12]
Now, as for what they say, "Sacrifice to this one, sacrifice to that one"—each individual deity is but an emanation of this very [Self], for he alone is all the gods.
(14.4.2) Furthermore, whatever here is moist, that was created from semen; that is Soma. Indeed, all this food is only so much.
And indeed, Soma is the eater of food and Agni is the food.
This is the "extra-creation" (atisṛṣṭi) of Brahman: that he created the gods, who are superior; and that, though being mortal himself, he created those who are immortal.
Therefore it is called the extra-creation. He who knows this becomes a participant in this extra-creation.
In the beginning, this was indeed undifferentiated; it was differentiated by name and form alone, as "this has such a name" and "this has such a form.
Even now, this is likewise differentiated by name and form alone, as "this has such a name" and "this has such a form. 14.4.2 [16]

This very Self has entered here, even to the tips of the fingernails, as a razor might be hidden in a razor-case, or as fire in the hearth of the fire-drill. They do not see it, for it is incomplete [when perceived through its functions]. When breathing, it is called breath; when speaking, speech; when seeing, sight; when hearing, hearing; when thinking, mind. 14.4.2. [17]
These are merely names for his actions; he who venerates them one by one does not know him, for he is incomplete when regarded through any one of these alone.
One should venerate him simply as the Self (*ātman*), for in this all these become one. This is the way to reach this All.

For when one knows this Self by means of this [Self], one knows all this. Just as one might find [something lost] by following a footprint, so does he who knows this find fame and praise. 14.4.2. This very Self is dearer than a son, dearer than wealth, dearer than everything else—this Self which is within.
If one were to say to another who speaks of what is dear to himself, "That which is dear to you will perish," it would indeed happen exactly so; therefore, one should worship the Self alone as dear.
He who worships the Self alone as dear—his own dear ones do not come to ruin. 14.4.2. [20]

Regarding this they say: "What indeed was that Brahman which, when known, became all this, on account of which men think, 'We shall become all through the knowledge of Brahman'? (14.4.2) In the beginning, this was indeed Brahman. It knew only itself: "I am Brahman."

Therefore, all that came to be; whosoever among the gods awakened to this, he alone became That, as did so it with the seers and likewise with human beings. Seeing this, the seer Vāmadeva realized: "I was Manu and I was Sūrya."
Even now, whoever knows this—"I am Brahman"—he becomes all this. Indeed, not even the gods have power over his failure to attain this state, for he becomes their very Self.
But he who worships another deity, thinking "He is one and I am another," does not know; he is like an animal to the gods, just as...
Indeed, many animals serve a single human; in the same way, each individual person serves the gods. When even a single animal is taken away, it becomes unpleasant; how much more so when many are?
Therefore, that which humans might learn is not pleasing to them. 14.4.2 [23]

In the beginning, this universe was indeed Brahman alone; being alone, it did not flourish. It created from itself a superior form, the Kṣatra—the various ruling powers among the gods, namely Indra, Varuṇa, Soma, Rudra, Parjanya, Yama, Mṛtyu, and Īśāna. Therefore, there is nothing higher than the Kṣatra; for this reason, the Brāhmaṇa sits below the Kṣatriya and pays him homage.
In the Rājasūya sacrifice, he thus bestows that glory upon the Kṣatriya alone; for the Brahman is the womb of the Kṣatriya.

Therefore, even though a king may attain the highest state, in the end he resorts to the Brahman as his own womb. But he who harms him destroys his own womb; he becomes worse off, just as one who has harmed a superior. 14.4.2 [24]
He did not multiply; he created the Vaiśya class—those classes of gods that are designated in groups:
the Vasus, the Rudras, the Ādityas, the Viśvedevas, and the Maruts.
He did not multiply; he created the Śūdra caste, [namely] Pūṣan. This earth, indeed, is Pūṣan, for she nourishes all this.
It nourishes everything that exists here.
He did not yet multiply; he created from himself that form which is Dharma. This Dharma is the sovereign power (*kṣatra*) of sovereign power;
therefore there is nothing higher than Dharma. Moreover, the weaker man overcomes the stronger by means of it.

Just as one praises a king according to his righteousness (*dharma*), so indeed is that which is *dharma*; it is truth (*satya*). Therefore, they say of one who speaks truth, "He speaks *dharma*," and of one who speaks *dharma*, "He speaks truth."

"He speaks"—this indeed constitutes both of these. This very thing is the Brahmin, the Kṣatriya, the Vaiśya, and the Śūdra. Among the gods, he became the Brahman through Agni; among humans, he became a Brāhmaṇa through Agni, a Kṣatriya through the Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya through the Vaiśya, and a Śūdra through the Śūdra. Therefore, [it is] in Agni alone...
Among the gods they desire the world, and among men, the Brahmin; for through these two forms, Brahman came to be.

Now, whoever departs from this world without having seen his own world, it does not protect him, being unknown to him—just as a Veda that has not been studied, or any other work that has not been performed. Even if one who lacks such knowledge performs a great meritorious deed...

That indeed perishes in the end for him. One should meditate upon the Self alone as the world. He who meditates upon the Self alone as the world—his work does not perish; for from this very Self, whatever he desires, that he creates. Moreover, this Self is indeed the world of all beings. When he offers oblations and when he sacrifices, by that he [satisfies] the gods.
Now, that which he recites for the world belongs to the Ṛṣis;
that which he offers to the ancestors belongs to the Pitṛs; that by which he causes men to dwell and gives them food belongs to men;
that by which he provides grass and water for animals belongs to the animals; and whatever wild beasts and birds [subsist] in his house...

They depend on ants for their livelihood; therefore, that world belongs to them. Just as one would desire safety for one's own world, even so do all beings always desire safety for one who knows this. This, indeed, has been known and investigated. In the beginning, this was only the Self (ātman), one alone. He desired: "May I have a wife, so that I may procreate; and may I have wealth. 14.4.2 [30]
"Perhaps I might perform ritual action"—this is indeed the desire; one does not find anything more than this.

Therefore even now a single person desires: "May I have a wife, may I procreate, may I possess wealth, and may I perform ritual action. As long as he does not obtain even one of these, he remains incomplete.
To that extent, he considers his completeness.
His mind is his self; his speech is his wife; his breath is his offspring; his sight is his human wealth—for one finds it through sight;
his hearing is his divine wealth—for one hears it through hearing; and his very self is his action—for one performs action by means of the self.
This sacrifice is fivefold; the animal is fivefold; man is fivefold; whatever exists here is fivefold.
He who knows this obtains all this, whatever exists here.
When the Father, through wisdom and austerity, produced the seven kinds of food, he made one common to all, and two he assigned to the gods.
He made three for himself and gave one to the animals; in that [one], everything is established—both that which breathes and that which does not.

Why is it that these [foods] are never exhausted, though they are being eaten constantly? He who knows that imperishability eats food with his face [the mouth]; he goes even unto the gods; he lives upon vital strength (*ūrj*). These are the verses (Ślokas). 14.4.3. [2]

"That the Father generated the seven foods by means of wisdom and austerity"—for indeed, the Father generated them by means of wisdom and austerity. "One of these is common to all"—this very food which is eaten here is that one which is common to all. He who venerates this [food] does not turn away from evil, for it is mixed. 14.4.3. [3]

"He assigned two [portions] to the gods," namely the *huta* (the offering made into the fire) and the *prahuta* (the offering made elsewhere); therefore, they offer into the fire for the gods and also offer elsewhere.
Furthermore, they say it refers to the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*); therefore, one should not be a frequent performer of animal sacrifices (*iṣṭiyājuka*).
"He bestowed one [portion] upon the cattle"; that was milk, for it is indeed milk that humans and cattle first subsist upon.

Therefore, when a boy is born, they first cause him to lick clarified butter or they suckle him at the breast. (14.4.3.5) Now, regarding a calf that has been born, they say, "It is a non-grazer. For everything is established in it—both that which breathes and that which does not; for indeed, all this is established in milk—both that which breathes and that which does not. (14.4.3.6)
Regarding what they say: "By offering milk for a year, one overcomes repeated death"—one should not understand it thus.

On whatever day he offers it, on that very day he overcomes repeated death, for one who knows this gives all food to the gods. [Question: Why do those [foods], though being eaten constantly, never perish? 14.4.3. [7]

The person (*puruṣa*) is indeed the imperishable; for he generates this food again and again. "He who knows that imperishable"—the person is indeed the imperishable, for he generates this food through every act of thought and by means of ritual actions; for if he did not do this, it would surely perish. "He eats the food with his face" (*pratīkena*); "face" (*pratīka*) means the mouth; thus, [he eats] with the mouth. He...
"He goes even to the gods; he lives upon vital strength"—this is the praise.
"He made three for himself": namely, mind, speech, and breath; these he made for himself. "I was elsewhere in mind, I did not see;
I was elsewhere in mind, I did not hear. For it is with the mind alone that one sees, and with the mind that one hears.
Desire, volition, doubt, faith, lack of faith, steadfastness, lack of steadfastness, shame, intelligence, and fear—all these are indeed the mind.
Therefore, even when touched from behind, one perceives it through the mind.
Whatever sound there is, that is speech alone; for this [speech] is bound to its end, and it is not the prāṇa, apāna, vyāna, or udāna.

"Samāno 'naḥ"—all this is indeed the vital breath (*prāṇa*). This self consists of speech, consists of mind, and consists of vital breath. (14.4.3.11) These three worlds are these very [three]: speech is this world, mind is the intermediate world, and vital breath is yonder world. (14.4.3.12)

The three Vedas are these very [three]: speech is the Ṛgveda, the mind is the Yajurveda, and the breath is the Sāmaveda. (14.4.3.13) The gods, the ancestors, and human beings are these very [three]: speech indeed is the gods, the mind is the ancestors, and the breath is human beings. (14.4.3.14) The father, the mother, and the offspring are these very [three]: the mind indeed is the father, speech is the mother, and the breath is the offspring. (14.4.3.15)
The known, the object of desire to know, and the unknown—these are indeed [the forms]. Whatever is known, that is the form of speech;

for speech is the knower. Having become that, speech protects him. 14.4.3.[16] Whatever is the object of desire to know, that is the form of the mind; for the mind is the object of desire to know. Having become that, the mind protects him. 14.4.3.[17]

Whatever is unknown is the form of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), for the vital breath is indeed unknown; having become that very thing, the vital breath protects it. 14.4.3 [18] The earth is the body of that speech, and its luminous form is this fire. As far as speech extends, so far extends the earth, and so far extends this fire. 14.4.3 [19]
Now, heaven is the body of this mind, and its form is light—that is yonder sun. As far as the mind extends, so far extends heaven, and so great is yonder sun.
These two united in sexual union, and from that Prāṇa was born; he is Indra. He is indeed without a rival. For a rival is truly a second person; he who knows this has no rival. 14.4.3 [20]

Now, water is the body of this vital breath (*prāṇa*), and that moon is its form of light. As far as the vital breath extends, so far extend the waters, and so far extends that moon. These—all of them—are equal and all are infinite. He who meditates upon these as finite reaches a finite world.
Now, he who worships these as infinite conquers an infinite world. 14.4.3.

[22] This very year is Prajāpati with sixteen parts; its fifteen parts are the nights, and its sixteenth part is the constant one. By means of the nights it waxes and by them it wanes. At the new moon (amāvāsyā),...
Having entered into all these living beings by means of this sixteenth part during this night, it is born again in the morning;
therefore, during this night, one should not cut off the breath of any living being, even that of a lizard, out of reverence for this very deity. 14.4.3 [23]

That Prajāpati who is the year and consists of sixteen parts is indeed this very person who knows thus. His wealth constitutes fifteen parts, while his self is the sixteenth part. By means of his wealth he waxes and wanes; that which is the self is the nave, and the wealth is the felly. Therefore, even if one suffers the loss of everything—

"If one conquers by means of the self, one truly lives; they say he has conquered by means of the rim. 14.4.3 [24] Now, there are indeed three worlds: the world of men, the world of the fathers, and the world of the gods.

This world of men is to be won only by a son, and not by any other ritual act; the world of the fathers by [the performance of] rites; and the world of the gods by knowledge. Of all the worlds, the world of the gods is indeed the best.

Therefore, they praise knowledge as the best. Now, therefore, follows the transmission: when he thinks he is about to depart this world, he says to his son, "Thou art the Brahman, thou art the sacrifice, thou art the world. The son replies, "I am the Brahman, I am the sacrifice, I am the world."

Whatever has been spoken, all that is unified in "Brahman"; whatever sacrifices there are, all those are unified in "Sacrifice"; whatever worlds there are, all those are unified in "World. All this that exists is indeed this much. "May he not enjoy me from here while I am thus deprived of everything," [thinking this,] one instructs a son.

Therefore, they say he is "the world" (loka), and for that reason they instruct him. When one who knows this departs from this world, he enters his son together with these very vital breaths (*prāṇa*). Whatever has been done wrongly by him through this [body], from all that the son delivers him; therefore he is called "son" (*putra*). By means of the son alone, he remains in this world.

He becomes firmly established; then these divine, immortal vital breaths enter him. 14.4.3 [27] Divine speech enters him from the earth and from fire. That indeed is divine speech by which whatever one speaks comes to be exactly so. 14.4.3 [28]
From the day and from the sun, the divine mind enters him; that indeed is the divine mind by which one becomes truly blissful and does not grieve.
From the waters and from the moon, the divine vital breath enters him; that indeed is the divine vital breath which...
Whether moving or not moving, he is neither distressed nor harmed. He who knows thus becomes the self of all beings, just as this deity is.
As all beings protect this deity, so do all beings protect him who knows thus—whatever these creatures may be.
They mourn for this world alone; that [merit] of theirs goes to the other world. Indeed, evil does not go to the gods. 14.4.3.
Now, therefore, follows the inquiry into vows. Prajāpati created the organs of action. Once created, they vied with one another:
"I shall speak," said Speech; "I shall see," said the Eye; "I shall hear," said the Ear.
In the same way, the other organs [were seized by death], each according to its function.
Death, becoming weariness, took possession of them; having reached them, death held them captive.
Therefore, speech indeed becomes weary, the eye becomes weary, and the ear becomes weary. But he whom this [breath] is, it did not reach.
The middle vital breath (prāṇa). 14.4.3 [32].

They resolved to know these: "This one among us is indeed the best, for whether moving or not moving, he neither falters nor suffers harm. Come, let us all assume his very form. Thus they all became his forms.

They became forms (*rūpa*); therefore, they are called by this name "vital breaths" (*prāṇāḥ*). Indeed, that family is named after him who knows this and belongs to such a family; and whoever competes with one who knows thus eventually dies of consumption. This is with reference to the self (*adhyātma*). 14.4.3. [33]
Then, with respect to the deities, Fire conceived: "I alone shall blaze"; the Sun conceived: "I shall burn";
the Moon conceived: "I shall shine. In this manner, the other deities [conceived] according to their respective domains.
Just as among these vital breaths (prāṇas) the middle breath is the chief, so among these deities is Vāyu. For the other deities set, but Vāyu does not set.
This very deity, which never sets, is Vāyu.

Regarding this, there is this verse: "From whence the sun rises and where it goes to set"—it indeed rises from the vital breath (prāṇa) and sets in the vital breath. The gods made that their law: "That same one exists today, and that same one tomorrow. Or rather...
These [ancients] performed this very rite even then, and they do so even today. Therefore, one should observe only a single vow:
while breathing out and breathing in, one should think, "Lest evil death should overtake me.
If one should perform it, he should desire to complete it; he who knows thus wins union with and residence in the same world as that deity. 14.4.4. [1]
This world consists of three things: name, form, and action. Of these names, speech is their *uktha*;
for from it all names arise. It is their *sāman*; for it is equal to all names. It is their *brahman*; for it sustains all names. 14.4.4. [2]
Now, regarding forms, "the eye" is their *uktha*, for from it all forms arise;
this is their *sāman*, for it is equal to all forms; this is their *brahman*, for it sustains all forms.
Now, regarding actions, "the self" (*ātman*) is their *uktha*, for from it all actions arise; this is their...
For this is equal to all ritual acts; this Brahman among them is indeed that which sustains all ritual acts.

These three, being real, are one—this Self; and this Self, being one, is these three. This is the immortal covered by the real. Breath is the immortal; name and form are the real; by these two, this breath is covered. 14.5.1. [1]
There was once a learned man named Gārgya Bālāki. He said to Ajātaśatru, the king of Kāśī, "I shall tell you about Brahman.
Ajātaśatru replied, "We give a thousand [cows] for such a speech; indeed, people run toward one who says 'Janaka, Janaka'!
Gārgya said, "That person who is yonder in the sun—that very one I worship as Brahman. He [Ajātaśatru] said:

Ajātaśatru said: "Do not converse with me about him. I meditate upon him as the one who stands over all beings, the head, the king. He who meditates upon him in this way becomes one who stands over all beings, the head, the king. 14.5.1. [3]

Gārgya said: "The person who is yonder in the moon—that is the very one I meditate upon as Brahman. Ajātaśatru said: "Do not talk to me about him! I meditate upon him as the Great One, clad in white, King Soma. He who meditates upon him as such has his soma pressed and poured out day after day; there is no lack of food for him."
[It] perishes. 14.5.1.[4] Gārgya said: "The person who is right here in lightning—that very one I venerate as Brahman.
Ajātaśatru said: "Do not talk to me about him! I venerate him rather as 'the Radiant' (tejasvin). As for him—
"He who worships him thus becomes radiant, and his offspring becomes radiant.
Gārgya said: "The person who is here in space—that very one I worship as Brahman.
Ajātaśatru said: "Do not talk to me about him! I worship him rather as the 'Full' that does not circulate."
He who venerates him thus is filled with offspring and cattle; his progeny does not perish from this world.
Gārgya said: "This very person who is here in the wind—that is the one I venerate as Brahman.
Ajātaśatru said: "Do not talk to me about him! He is Indra Vaikuṇṭha, the invincible army."

"I venerate him as 'the victorious'. He who venerates him thus becomes victorious and invincible; he conquers the offspring of others. Gārgya said: "The person who is here in the fire—that very one I venerate as Brahman.
Ajātaśatru said: "Do not speak to me about him! I venerate him rather as 'the all-subduing' (*viṣāsahi*). He who...
"He who worships him thus becomes a conqueror; his offspring indeed become conquerors. Gārgya said: "That person who is here in the waters—that very one I worship as Brahman.
Ajātaśatru said: "Do not talk to me about him! I worship him rather as 'The Counterpart' (Pratirūpa). As for him who...
"He who worships him thus, to him only a corresponding form comes, not a non-corresponding one;
moreover, a corresponding son is born from him. 14.5.1.
[9] Gārgya said: "This person who is here in the mirror—that very one I worship as Brahman. He said: ...
Ajātaśatru said, "Do not converse with me about him. I meditate upon him as the Radiant One (*rociṣṇu*).
He who meditates upon him thus becomes radiant; his offspring become radiant; and moreover, whoever he encounters, he outshines them all. 14.5.1 [10]
Gārgya said: "The person who is here in the quarters—him indeed I meditate upon as Brahman.

Ajātaśatru said: "Do not talk to me about him! I meditate upon him as the 'Inseparable Companion' (Anapaga), for he is indeed a companion. He who meditates upon him thus becomes possessed of a companion; his retinue does not depart from him. 14.5.1. [11]
Gārgya said: "This very one who, as a sound, follows after a person walking—this indeed I worship as Brahman.

Ajātaśatru said: "Do not talk to me about him! I worship him rather as 'Life' (asu). He who worships him thus reaches the full span of life in this world; his vital breath does not leave him before his time. 14.5.1 [12]
Gārgya said: "The person who is here in the fire—that very one I meditate upon as Brahman.

Ajātaśatru said: "Do not talk to me about him! I meditate upon him as Death. He who meditates upon him as such reaches the full span of life in this world; death does not come to him before his time. 14.5.1 [13]

Gārgya said: "The person who is here in the self—that very one I worship as Brahman. Ajātaśatru said: "Do not talk to me about him! I worship him rather as 'the embodied one' (ātmanvī). He who worships him thus becomes embodied himself, and his offspring become embodied; then Gārgya became silent.
Gārgya said: 14.5.1 [14] Ajātaśatru replied: "Is that all? "That is all," he said. "By that much alone, it is not known," [Ajātaśatru replied].
Gārgya said: "Let me come to you as a pupil. 14.5.1 [15]
Ajātaśatru said: "It would indeed be contrary to the natural order for a Brāhmaṇa to approach a Kṣatriya thinking, 'He will teach me the Brahman.
Rather, I shall make you understand it. Taking him by the hand, he rose up. They both went to a man who was asleep. He addressed him by these names: "Bṛhan! Pāṇḍaravāsa! Soma!"
"O King! he said, but [Ajātaśatru] did not rise; he woke him by pressing him with his hand, and then he rose.
Ajātaśatru said: "When this person consisting of consciousness was thus asleep, where was he then, and from whence did he return? Gārgya did not know that.

Ajātaśatru said: "When this person was asleep there—this person who consists of consciousness—he takes the consciousness of these vital breaths by means of his own consciousness and lies in that space which is within the heart. When he seizes them, then it is said that the person sleeps; at that time, the vital breath is indeed seized, and [the senses] are seized.
Speech is withdrawn, the eye is withdrawn, the ear is withdrawn, and the mind is withdrawn.
When he moves about in this state of sleep, these indeed are his worlds; then he becomes, as it were, a great king, or as it were a great Brahmin, or he experiences various high and low states.

Just as a great king, having taken hold of the people of his realm, moves about as he pleases within his own kingdom, even so this [self], having taken hold of the vital breaths, moves about as it pleases within its own body.
Now, when one is fast asleep— when one knows nothing of anything— there are seventy-two thousand channels called *hitā*.
Thousands [of channels] extend from the heart toward the pericardium; through them he slips out and lies within the pericardium.
Just as a young boy or a great Brahmin might lie down after reaching the height of bliss, even so does he lie there.
Just as a spider moves along with its thread, or as tiny sparks fly out from a fire,
even so from this Self all vital breaths, all worlds, all gods, and all beings emerge.
All these selves emerge from him; his secret name (*upaniṣad*) is "the Truth of truth. The vital breaths (*prāṇāḥ*) are indeed truth, and he is their truth.
Whoever knows the infant together with its support, its foundation, its pillar, and its cord, he surely conquers his seven enemies.
He holds back his rivals.

This very one who is the middle vital breath (prāṇa) is indeed the child; this [chest] is its support, this [lower abdomen] is its counter-support, the vital breath is the pillar, and food is the rope. These seven imperishables wait upon it.

Now, those reddish-brown streaks on the axle—Rudra is dependent upon them; those waters on the axle—Parjanya is dependent upon them; the pupil of the eye—Āditya is dependent upon it; that which is white—Agni is dependent upon it; that which is black—Indra is dependent upon it; by its lower track the earth is dependent upon it, and by its upper track the sky is dependent upon it. The food of one who knows this does not fail. 14.5.2. [4]
Regarding this, there is this verse: "A bowl with its opening below and its bottom above—in it is placed glory of every form.
Upon its bank sit the seven seers; Vāk is the eighth, attaining union with Brahman.
"The bowl with its opening below and its bottom above"—this refers to this head, for this head is indeed a bowl with its opening below.
"Upon it is the upward-pointing base; in it glory, omniform, is deposited. Glory, indeed, is the vital breaths (prāṇas);
he thereby refers to the vital breaths. "Of that, the seven seers are on the shore. The seers, indeed, are the vital breaths; he thereby refers to the vital breaths.
"Speech is the eighth, attaining union with Brahman. For speech, as the eighth, attains union with Brahman. 14.5.2 [6]
These two are indeed Gotama and Bharadvāja—this one is Gotama and this one is Bharadvāja;
these two are indeed Viśvāmitra and Jamadagni—this one is Viśvāmitra and this one is Jamadagni;
these two are indeed Vasiṣṭha and Kaśyapa—this one is Vasiṣṭha and this one is Kaśyapa; Atri is speech, for by speech [he is so called].

For food is eaten; indeed, "Atri" is the name for this very thing. He who knows thus becomes the eater of all, and everything becomes his food. (14.5.3) There are indeed two forms of Brahman: the formed and the formless, the mortal and the immortal, the stationary and that which moves.
And this is the truth:
that which is other than the wind and the intermediate space is this formed [entity], this mortal, this stationary, this existent.
Of this formed, this mortal, this stationary, this existent, the essence is he who shines yonder.
For this is the essence of the Real (sat). Now, that which is formless consists of wind and the intermediate space; this is immortal, this is the Real (tya).
Of this formless, of this immortal, of this real, this is the essence: namely, he who is this [person in the sun].

"In this maṇḍala is the person; for he is its essence"—thus with respect to the deities (adhidevatam). 14.5.3.[6] Now with respect to the self (adhyātmam): that which is corporeal, other than the vital breath (prāṇa) and that which is the space within the self—this is mortal, this is stationary, this is existent (sat). 14.5.3.[7]

Of this very one that is embodied, that is mortal, that is stationary, that is existent—of this, the eye is the essence; for it is the essence of the existent. 14.5.3[8] Now, that which is unembodied—the breath and this space within the self—that is immortal, that is the Real. 14.5.3[9]
Of this formless one, of this immortal one, of this undecaying one, of this unchanging one, this is the essence:
namely, this person who is in the right eye; for he is indeed the essence of that [unmanifest]. The form of this person is like a saffron-dyed garment, like a white woolen cloth.
As a firefly, as a flame of fire, as a white lotus, or as a flash of lightning—just like a flash of lightning, indeed, does his splendor become for one who knows this. 14.5.3.
[11] Now, therefore, follows the instruction: "Not this, not this. For there is nothing else higher than this "not this. Furthermore, its name is the Truth of Truth.

"Truth," he said. "The vital breaths (*prāṇa*) are indeed truth; of them, this [Self] is the Truth. "Maitreyī," Yājñavalkya said, "I am indeed about to depart from this state. Come, let me make a final settlement for you with this Kātyāyanī."

Maitreyī said: "If, O Venerable Sir, this entire earth filled with wealth were mine, would I become immortal by means of it? "No," said Yājñavalkya, "your life would be just like the life of those who possess worldly means; there is no hope for immortality through wealth. 14.5.4. [3]
Maitreyī said: "What indeed should I do with that by which I might not become immortal? Tell me only that which the Blessed One knows.
Yājñavalkya said: "Truly, you speak what is dear to us, you who are yourself dear. Come, sit down; I shall explain it to you."

"But as I explain this to you, please meditate upon it," he said. "Let the Blessed One speak. Yājñavalkya replied: "Truly, my dear, it is not out of love for the husband that the husband is dear; rather, it is out of love for the Self that the husband is dear. Truly, my dear, it is not out of love for the wife that the wife is dear; rather, it is out of love for the Self..."

A wife is dear for the sake of desire; truly, sons are not dear for the sake of desire for sons, but sons are dear for the sake of desire for the Self. Truly, wealth is not dear for the sake of desire for wealth, but wealth is dear for the sake of desire for the Self. Truly, [the Brahman is not dear for the sake of desire for the Brahman...]

It is not for the sake of desire that the Brahmin becomes dear, but for the sake of one's own self that the Brahmin becomes dear; indeed, it is not for the sake of desire that the Kshatriya becomes dear, but for the sake of one's own self that the Kshatriya becomes dear;
indeed, it is not for the sake of desire that the worlds become dear, but for the sake of one's own self that the worlds become dear.

Verily, it is not for the sake of the gods that the gods are dear; rather, it is for the sake of the Self that the gods are dear. Verily, it is not for the sake of beings that beings are dear; rather, it is for the sake of the Self that beings are dear.

Beings are dear, but it is not for the sake of all that everything becomes dear; rather, it is for the sake of the Self that everything becomes dear. Indeed, the Self, O Maitreyī, should be seen, heard, reflected upon, and meditated upon. For by seeing, hearing, reflecting upon, and realizing the Self, this [world]—

All is known. 14.5.4.[6] Brahman would desert him who knows Brahman as other than the Self; Kshatra would desert him who knows Kshatra as other than the Self; the worlds would desert him who knows the worlds as other than the Self.
The gods desert him who knows the gods as other than the Self; beings desert him who knows beings as other than the Self;

everything deserts him who knows everything as other than the Self. This Brahminhood, this Kshatriyahood, these worlds, these gods, these beings, this whole world—all this is what this Self is. 14.5.4. [7]
Just as when a drum is being beaten, one cannot grasp the external sounds; rather, by grasping the drum or the striking of the drum, the sound is grasped.
Just as when a lute is being played, one cannot grasp the external sounds; rather, by [grasping] the lute...

By grasping the lute-player, the sound is grasped. Just as when a conch is being blown, one cannot grasp the external sounds [separately], but by grasping the conch, the sound of the conch-blower is grasped.

Just as from a fire of damp wood that has been kindled various clouds of smoke issue forth, even so, my dear, the Ṛgveda, Yajurveda, Sāmaveda, Atharvāṅgirasa, Itihāsa, Purāṇa, the sciences, the Upaniṣads, verses, aphorisms, explanations, and commentaries are the breath of this great Being; these indeed belong to Him alone.

All exhalations. 14.5.4.[11] Just as the ocean is the single point of convergence for all waters, so the skin is the single point of convergence for all tactile sensations; so the two nostrils are the single point of convergence for all odors; so [the tongue is the single point of convergence] for all tastes.
In this way, the tongue is the single point of convergence for all forms; the eye is the single point of convergence for all sounds; the ear is the single point of convergence for all thoughts;
the mind is the single point of convergence for all Vedas; and the two hands are the single point of convergence for all actions.

Just as the feet are the single point of convergence for all paths, so the organ of generation is the single point of convergence for all joys; so the anus is the single point of convergence for all excretions; so speech is the single point of convergence for all branches of knowledge. 14.5.4 [12]

Just as a lump of salt, when thrown into water, dissolves completely into the water so that it cannot be taken up again, yet wherever one may take [the water], it is salty— just so, my dear, this great being, infinite and boundless, consisting of nothing but a mass of consciousness, arises from these elements and vanishes back into them; after death, there is no more [conscious existence].
"O Āre, I say that there is consciousness," said Yājñavalkya.

Maitreyī said: "In this very matter, my lord, you have bewildered me by saying that there is no consciousness after death. Yājñavalkya said: "O Āre, I am not speaking a bewildering thing; indeed, this is sufficient for understanding."

For where there is duality, as it were, there one sees another; there one smells another; there one speaks to another; there one hears another; there one thinks of another; there one perceives another. But where for him everything has become the Self alone, by what and whom should he see? By what and whom should he smell? By what and whom...? 14.5.4. [16]
"Whom should one salute? By what means, and who, should one hear? By what means, and who, should one think? By what means, and who, should one discern?

By what means should one discern that by which all this is discerned? O friend, by what means should one discern the knower? By what means should one discern? This earth is honey for all beings, and all beings are honey for this earth.

And that person consisting of light and consisting of immortality who is in this earth, and that person consisting of light and consisting of immortality who is here with respect to the body (adhyātma)—this very one is the Self; this is the immortal, this is Brahman, this is all. 14.5.5. [2]

These waters are honey for all beings, and all beings are honey for these waters; and this person within these waters, consisting of brilliance and immortal, and this person within the self consisting of semen,
consisting of brilliance and immortal.

This fire is honey for all beings, and all beings are honey for this fire; and that person consisting of splendor and consisting of immortality who is in this fire, and that person consisting of speech, consisting of splendor, and consisting of immortality who is with reference to the self (adhyātma)— [14.5.5].
This space is honey for all beings, and all beings are honey for this space;
and that radiant, immortal person who is in this space, and that radiant, immortal [person] who is the space within the heart—[these two are one]. 14.5.5. [5]
This wind is honey for all beings, and all beings are honey for this wind;

and that person consisting of light and consisting of immortality who is in this wind, and that person consisting of light and consisting of immortality who is the vital breath (*prāṇa*) here in the self—[he is the same]. 14.5.5 [6]
This Āditya is honey for all beings, and all beings are honey for this Āditya.

And that person consisting of splendor and consisting of immortality who is in this Āditya, and that person consisting of splendor and consisting of immortality who is here in the self with respect to the eye—[these are one]. 14.5.5 [7]

This moon is honey for all beings, and all beings are honey for this moon; and this person who consists of splendor and consists of nectar within this moon, and this person who consists of splendor and consists of nectar within the self as the mind— 14.5.5 [8].
These quarters are honey for all beings; all beings are honey for these quarters.
And this person, consisting of splendor and consisting of immortality, who is in these quarters, and he who is the one pertaining to the ear within the self—[these two are one].
The one who is in the echo, consisting of light and immortal. 14.5.5 [9]:
This lightning is honey for all beings, and all beings are honey for this lightning;
and that person who is in this lightning, consisting of light and immortal, and he who is within the self (adhyātma).
The radiant one consists of light and is immortal. 14.5.5.
[10] This thunder is honey for all beings, and all beings are honey for this thunder;
and that person who is in this thunder, consisting of light and immortal, and that person who is within the self, consisting of sound—[these are honey for one another].
The sun is honey, consisting of splendor and immortal nectar. 14.5.5.

[11] This dharma is honey for all beings, and all beings are honey for this dharma; and that person who consists of splendor and immortal nectar within this dharma, and he who is within the self (adhyātma)—[these are honey].
The Dharma is full of splendor and immortal. 14.5.5 [12].
This truth is honey for all beings, and all beings are honey for this truth;
and that person who is full of splendor and immortal within this truth, and he who is so within the self (adhyātma).

That [Self] of yours is full of splendor and immortal. 14.5.5.[13] This human being is honey for all beings, and all beings are honey for this human being; and that person who consists of splendor and is immortal within this human being, and that which is the self (adhyātma).

This human being, consisting of splendor and immortal, [is honey]. 14.5.5. This Self is honey for all beings, and all beings are honey for this Self; and that person who consists of splendor and is immortal within this Self, and this Self itself.
This person, consisting of light and consisting of immortality—this indeed is that which is the self; this is the immortal, this is Brahman, this is all. 14.5.5.
[15] Now, this self is the overlord of all beings, the king of all beings; it is just as follows:

Just as all the spokes are fixed in the nave and the rim of a chariot wheel, even so in this Self (ātman) are fixed all vital breaths (prāṇas), all worlds, all gods, all beings, and all these selves. 14.5.5 [16] This, indeed, is that honey which Dadhyañc Ātharvaṇa spoke to the two Aśvins; seeing this, the seer (ṛṣi) declared:
"O Heroes, for the sake of gain, I proclaim that powerful deed of yours, like thunder proclaiming rain, since Dadhyañc Ātharvaṇa, with the head of a horse, declared this honey to you.
This indeed is that honey which Dadhyañc Ātharvaṇa declared to the Aśvins; seeing this, the seer spoke:
