This indeed is that honey which Dadhyañc Ātharvaṇa spoke to the two Aśvins. Seeing this, a seer declared: "He has become the counterpart of every form; that is his form for the sake of being perceived. Indra moves in many forms through his powers of illusion (*māyā*); for his bay steeds (*harayaḥ*) are yoked, ten times a hundred. These [steeds] are indeed he, and these are indeed ten and a hundred.

There are many thousands and indeed infinite [worlds]; this very Brahman is without beginning, without end, and without exterior—this Self is Brahman, the experiencer of all; such is the instruction. 14.5.5. [20] Now, the lineage: This [tradition] we [have received] from Śaurpaṇāyya; Śaurpaṇāyya from Gautama; Gautama from Vātsya; Vātsya...
From Vātsya and Pārāśarya; Pārāśarya from Sāṃkṛtya and Bhāradvāja; Bhāradvāja from Audavāhi and Śāṇḍilya; and Śāṇḍilya from Vaijavāpa and Gautama; and Gautama from Vaijavāpāyana.

From Vaiṣṭapureya, [it came] from Vaiṣṭapureya; from Śāṇḍilya and Rauhiṇāyana, [it came] from Rauhiṇāyana; from Śaunaka and Ātreya, [it came] from Raibhya; from Pautimāṣyāyaṇa and Kauṇḍinyāyana, [it came] from Kauṇḍinyāyana;
from Kauṇḍinya, [it came] from Kauṇḍinya; from Kauṇḍinya, [it came] from Kauṇḍinya.
From Kauṇḍinya and Āgniveśya;
Āgniveśya from Saitava; Saitava from Pārāśarya; Pārāśarya from Jātūkarṇya; Jātūkarṇya from Bhāradvāja;
Bhāradvāja from both Bhāradvāja and Āsurāyaṇa; and Gautama from Gautama.
From Bhāradvāja [it came to] Bhāradvāja; from Vaijavāpāyana, Vaijavāpāyana; from Kauśikāyani, Kauśikāyani; from Ghṛtakauśika, Ghṛtakauśika; from Pārāśaryāyaṇa, Pārāśaryāyaṇa;
from Pārāśarya, Pārāśarya; from Jātūkarṇya, Jātūkarṇya; from Bhāradvāja, Bhāradvāja.
From Bhāradvāja and from Āsurāyaṇa and from Yāska; Āsurāyaṇa from Traivaṇi; Traivaṇi from Aupajandhani; Aupajandhani from Āsuri; Āsuri from Bhāradvāja; Bhāradvāja from Ātreya. 14.5.5 [22]
Ātreya from Māṇṭi; Māṇṭi from Gautama; Gautama from Gautama; Gautama from Vātsya;
Vātsya from Śāṇḍilya; Śāṇḍilya from Kaiśorya Kāpya; Kaiśorya Kāpya from Kumārahārita; Kumārahārita from Gālava; Gālava from Vidarbhī Kauṇḍinya; Vidarbhī Kauṇḍinya from Vatsanapāt.
From Bābhrava came Vatsanapāt Bābhrava; from Pathas Saubhara came Panthas Saubhara;
from Ayāsya Āṅgirasa came Ayāsya Āṅgirasa; from Ābhūti Tvāṣṭra came Ābhūti Tvāṣṭra;
from Viśvarūpa Tvāṣṭra came Viśvarūpa Tvāṣṭra; and from the two Aśvins came Dadhyañc.
From Atharvan came Dadhyañc Ātharvaṇa; from Atharvan Daiva came Atharvan Daiva; from Mṛtyu Prādhvaṃsana came Mṛtyu Prādhvaṃsana; from Pradhvaṃsana came Pradhvaṃsana;
from Ekarṣi came Ekarṣi; from Viprajitti came Viprajitti; from Vyaṣṭi came Vyaṣṭi; from Sanāru came Sanāru; from Sanātana came Sanātana.
From Sanaga came Sanaga; from Parameṣṭhin came Parameṣṭhin; from Brahmā came Brahmā; Brahmā is self-existent. Homage to Brahmā!
Janaka of Videha performed a sacrifice at which much was given as sacrificial fees. There, the Brahmins of the Kurus and Pañcālas...
They had attained full realization. Now, Janaka of Videha felt a desire to know: "Who among these Brahmins is the most learned in the Vedas?
He enclosed a thousand cows and tied ten gold coins to the horns of each one.
They became [silent]. He said to them, "Venerable Brahmins, let him among you who is most proficient in the Veda (brahmiṣṭha) drive these cows away.
Those Brahmins did not dare.
Then Yājñavalkya said to his own pupil, "Sāmaśrava, my dear, drive these [cows] away. So he did.

He made [himself] the *hotṛ* priest; those Brahmins were indeed incensed, saying, "How can he declare himself the most proficient in sacred knowledge (*brahmiṣṭha*) among us? (14.6.1). Now, Āśvala was the *hotṛ* priest of Janaka of Videha. He questioned him, saying: "Yājñavalkya, are you indeed the most proficient in sacred knowledge among us? He replied: "We pay homage to the one who is most proficient in sacred knowledge."
"We were indeed seekers of cattle," said Hotr Āśvala, and he resolved to question him right then and there.

"O Yājñavalkya," he said, "since all this is seized by death, all this is overtaken by death, by what means does the sacrificer free himself from the reach of death? "By the Hotṛ priest, by fire, and by speech; for speech is the Hotṛ of the sacrifice."
Now, this speech is that axle, this fire is that Hotṛ priest; that is liberation, that is complete liberation.

"Yājñavalkya," he said, "since all this is pervaded by day and night, and all this is encompassed by day and night, by what means does the sacrificer, having attained [them], become completely liberated from day and night?"
"Thus, through the Adhvaryu priest, who is the eye, and through the sun, which is the eye—for the Adhvaryu is indeed the eye of the sacrifice;
that which is this eye is yonder sun, he is the Adhvaryu, he is liberation, he is complete liberation.
Yājñavalkya, he said, "Since all this is pervaded by the fortnights of the waxing and waning moon..."

"By what means does the sacrificer, who is seized by the bright fortnight and the dark fortnight, obtain release from the attainment of the bright and dark fortnights? By means of the Brahman-priest, by means of the mind, by means of the moon.
For the mind is indeed the Brahman-priest of the sacrifice; that which is this mind is yonder moon, it is the Brahman, it is the release."
[The section on] Liberation (sātimukti): 14.6.1.

[8] He said, "O Yājñavalkya, since this intermediate space (*antarikṣa*) is as if without support, by what means does the sacrificer ascend to the heavenly world? "By the Udgātṛ priest, by Vāyu, and by the vital breath (*prāṇa*). "But the vital breath, indeed..."

"The Udgātṛ of the sacrifice—this breath here is Vāyu; he is the Udgātṛ; that is liberation (mukti); that is complete liberation (atimukti). These are the liberations (atimokṣas). Now, the correspondences (sampadas). "Yājñavalkya," he said, "with how many ṛc-verses will this Hotṛ perform today in this sacrifice? "With three."
"What are those three? "The invitatory verse (*puro'nuvākyā*), the offering verse (*yājyā*), and the recitation verse (*śasyā*) as the third. "What does one win by means of them?
"One wins the world of earth by the invitatory verse, the world of the intermediate space by the offering verse, and the world of heaven by the recitation verse.
"Yājñavalkya," he said, "how many oblations will this Adhvaryu priest offer today in this sacrifice? "Three."

What are those three? Those oblations which, when offered, blaze up; those oblations which, when offered, overflow; and those oblations which, when offered, settle down. What does one win by them? By those oblations which, when offered, blaze up, one wins the world of the gods, for the world of the gods is, as it were, ablaze.
By those oblations which, when offered, overflow, one wins the world of men, for the world of men overflows, as it were. By those oblations...
They rest upon the world of the fathers; by means of them, one conquers that [world], for the world of the fathers is, as it were, below.

"Yājñavalkya," he said, "with how many deities will this Brahman priest protect the sacrifice from the south today? "With one. "Which is that one? "The mind alone. For the mind is infinite, and the Viśvedevas are infinite."

"The All-Gods (Viśve Devāḥ) are indeed infinite; by that [knowledge], he wins the world. 14.6.1.[12] "Yājñavalkya," he said, "how many *stotriya* hymns will this Udgātṛ chant today at this sacrifice? "Three," he replied. "Which are those three?
"The *puro'nuvākyā*, the *yājyā*, and the *śasyā* as the third. This is with respect to the deities (*adhidevatam*). Now, with respect to the self (*adhyātmam*):"

"What are those eight that are internal? "The out-breath (*prāṇa*) is the invitatory verse (*puronuvākyā*); the in-breath (*apāna*) is the offering verse (*yājyā*); the diffused breath (*vyāna*) is the recitation (*śasyā*).

What does one win by means of them? "Whatever here exists that is endowed with breath. Thereupon, Aśvala the Hotṛ ceased questioning. Then Jāratkārava Ārtabhāga questioned him. "Yājñavalkya," he said, "how many *grahas* (seizers) are there?"
"How many are the *atigrahas*? "There are eight *grahas* and eight *atigrahas*. Which are those eight *grahas* and eight *atigrahas*?
"Breath (*prāṇa*) is indeed a *graha*; it is seized by exhalation (*apāna*) as its *atigraha*, for by means of exhalation one smells odors."

The tongue is indeed a grasper; it is seized by taste as the over-grasper, for by the tongue one perceives tastes. Speech is indeed a grasper; it is seized by name as the over-grasper, for by speech one utters names.
The eye is indeed a grasper; it is seized by form as the over-grasper, for by the eye one sees forms.

The ear, indeed, is a grasper; it is seized by sound as the over-grasper, for by means of the ear one hears sounds. 14.6.2.[7] The mind, indeed, is a grasper; it is seized by desire as the over-grasper, for by means of the mind one desires objects of desire. 14.6.2.[8] The hands, indeed, are a grasper; they are seized by action as the over-grasper, for by means of the hands one performs actions. 14.6.2.[9]
"The skin, indeed, is a grasper; it is seized by touch as the over-grasper, for by means of the skin one perceives touches. Thus there are eight graspers and eight over-graspers.
"Yājñavalkya," he said, "since all this is food for death, who is that deity to whom [it belongs]?"
"Death is food. Now, fire is indeed death; water is its food. He conquers recurrent death.
Yājñavalkya, he said, "When this person dies, what does not leave him? "The name," [he replied].
"The name is indeed infinite, and the Viśvedevas are infinite. By means of that, he wins an infinite world—yes, by means of that he wins an infinite world."

"Yājñavalkya," he said, "when this person dies, do his vital breaths (*prāṇāḥ*) depart from him, or not? "No, no," said Yājñavalkya; "they are merged right here. He swells, he becomes bloated; bloated, he lies dead.
"Yājñavalkya," he said, "when this person has died, into what does his speech merge? Into the wind."

"The breath [goes] to the sun, the eye to the sun, the mind to the moon, the ear to the quarters, the body to the earth, the self to space, the herbs to the body hair, and the trees to the hair of the head; blood and semen are deposited in the waters.
Where then does this person come to be? Come, my dear, take my hand. (14.6.2)
"O Ārtabhāga," he said, "let us two alone consider this; let us not discuss this in public. So they went out and deliberated. Whatever they spoke of there, they spoke of only action;
and whatever they praised, they praised only action: "One becomes virtuous by virtuous action and evil by evil action. Then...

Thus, Ārtabhāga Jāratkārava ceased questioning. 14.6.3. Then Bhujyu Lāhyāyani questioned him. "Yājñavalkya," he said, "we were wandering as students among the Madras. We came to the house of Cula Kāpya; he had a daughter who was possessed by a Gandharva."

We asked him, "Who are you? He replied, "I am Sudhanvan Āṅgirasa. When we asked him about the ends of the worlds, then we said to him, "Where have the Pārikṣitas gone? Where have the Pārikṣitas gone? That is what I ask you, Yājñavalkya: where have the Pārikṣitas gone? 14.6.3 [2]

He said: "He indeed said that; he told you where those go who have performed the horse sacrifice. But where do those who have performed the horse sacrifice go? This world is thirty-two *ratha-ahnus* (chariot-days) in extent; the earth extends twice as far around this world, and the ocean extends twice as far around that earth."

As thin as the edge of a razor or the wing of a fly—through such a narrow space as that Indra, having become a bird of prey, delivered them to Vāyu; Vāyu, having placed them within himself, brought them to where the Pārikṣitas were.
Thus indeed he praised Vāyu alone; therefore, Vāyu alone is the individual manifestation (vyaṣṭi), Vāyu is the universal manifestation (samaṣṭi).
"He who knows this attains the totality, conquers repeated death, and reaches a full lifespan. Thereupon, Bhujyu Lāhyāyani ceased questioning.
Then Kahoḍa Kauṣītakeya questioned him; "O Yājñavalkya," he said.

"Explain to me that Brahman which is immediate and direct, that Self which is within all. "This Self of yours is the one within all. "Which one, Yājñavalkya, is within all? "He who transcends hunger and thirst, sorrow, delusion, old age, and death. Having known this very Self, the Brāhmaṇas [renounce] the desire for sons and the desire for wealth."

Having risen above the desire for worldly objects, they then lead the life of a mendicant. For the desire for sons is indeed the desire for wealth, and the desire for wealth is the desire for worldly objects; these two are truly one and the same desire. Therefore, a wise man, having become disillusioned with wisdom, should abide in childlike simplicity; and having become disillusioned with both childlike simplicity and wisdom, he then becomes a sage, transcending both the state of non-sagehood and sagehood.

"Then, having become silent, he is a Brāhmaṇa. By what means would he be a Brāhmaṇa? He becomes exactly such as that by which he would be [a Brāhmaṇa], for one who knows thus. Thereupon, Kahoḍa Kauṣītakeya ceased questioning.
Then Uṣasta Cākrāyaṇa questioned him, saying, "O Yājñavalkya! he said.
"Explain to me that Brahman which is immediate and direct, the Self (Ātman) that is within all. "This Self of yours is within all.
"Which one, Yājñavalkya, is within all? "He who breathes in with the prāṇa—that is your Self, within all.
He who breathes out with the apāna—that is your Self, within all. He who breathes through with the vyāna—that is your Self, within all."
"He who breathes out with the out-breath—that is your Self, which is within all. He who breathes equally with the equalizing breath—that is your Self, which is within all.
Uṣasta Cākrāyaṇa said: "Just as one might say, 'That is a cow,' or 'That is a horse,' so indeed has this been pointed out. Tell me that Brahman which is immediate and direct, that Self..."

"Explain to me that which is within all. "This Self of yours is the one within all. "Which one, Yājñavalkya, is within all? "He whom you cannot see by sight, yet who sees sight; whom you cannot hear by hearing, yet who hears hearing; whom you cannot think by thought, yet who thinks thought; whom you cannot know by cognition, yet who knows cognition—this Self of yours is the one within all. Everything other than this is afflicted (mortal). Thereupon...
Uṣasta Cākrāyaṇa then desisted.

Then Gārgī Vācaknavī questioned him. She said, "Yājñavalkya, since all this is woven to and fro upon the waters, upon what are the waters woven to and fro? "Upon the wind, Gārgī. "Upon what is the wind woven to and fro?"

"Yoked across and lengthwise, Gārgī, it is woven in space itself. "In what, then, is space woven across and lengthwise? "In the worlds of the intermediate region, Gārgī. "In what, then, are the worlds of the intermediate region woven across and lengthwise? "In the world of heaven, Gārgī. "In what, then, is the world of heaven woven across and lengthwise?
"In the worlds of the sun, Gārgī. "In what, then, are the worlds of the sun woven across and lengthwise?"
"In the worlds of the moon, O Gārgī," [he said]. "In what, then, are the worlds of the moon woven to and fro? "In the worlds of the stars, O Gārgī.
"In what, then, are the worlds of the stars woven to and fro? "In the worlds of the gods, O Gārgī. "In what, then, are the worlds of the gods woven to and fro?
"In the worlds of the Gandharvas, O Gārgī. "In what, then, are the worlds of the Gandharvas woven to and fro?"

"In the worlds of Prajāpati, Gārgī," [he said]. "In what, then, are the worlds of Prajāpati woven to and fro? "In the worlds of Brahman, Gārgī. "In what, then, are the worlds of Brahman woven to and fro? He said, "Gārgī, do not ask beyond this, lest your head shatter apart. These deities are not to be questioned beyond; you are questioning too far, Gārgī. Do not ask beyond this! Thereupon, Gārgī [fell silent].
Vācaknavī ceased.
Then Uddālaka Āruṇi questioned him. "Yājñavalkya," he said, "we were staying among the Madras in the house of Patañcala Kāpya, studying the sacrifice. His wife was possessed by a Gandharva."

We asked him, "Who are you? He replied, "I am Kabandha Ātharvaṇa. He said to Patañcala Kāpya and the ritualists, "Do you know, O Kāpya, that thread by which this world, the other world, and all beings are strung together? Patañcala replied.
"Kāpya replied, 'I do not know that, O Venerable Sir.
He said to Patañcala Kāpya and the ritualists: 'Do you, Kāpya, know that Inner Controller who controls this world and the other world, and all beings from within?'"
Patañcala Kāpya said, "Venerable sir, I do not know him.

He said to Patañcala Kāpya and the ritualists: "O Kāpya, whoever knows that thread and knows that inner controller—he is a knower of Brahman, he is a knower of the worlds, he is a knower of the gods, he is a knower of the Vedas, he is a knower of sacrifices, he is a knower of beings..."

"He who knows the Self knows all"—this he said to them; that I know. If you, Yājñavalkya, not knowing that thread and that Inner Controller, drive away the Brahman-cows, your head shall fall off. "I do indeed know, O Gautama, that thread and that Inner Controller," [said Yājñavalkya]. "Whoever this may be..."
"He might say, 'I know the Vedas. [The other] should say, 'Tell me how you know them.
"Vāyu, O Gautama, is that thread. By Vāyu, O Gautama, as by a thread, this world, the next world, and all beings are held together. Therefore, O Gautama, when a man [dies]..."
"They say he is a ghost because his limbs have fallen apart; for they are held together, O Gautama, by the thread of wind.
"It is even so, Yājñavalkya. Speak of the Inner Controller.
"He who dwells in the earth, yet is within the earth, whom the earth does not know, whose body is the earth, who..."

He who dwells within the earth, yet is other than the earth, whom the earth does not know, whose body is the earth, and who controls the earth from within— he is your Self, the Inner Controller, the Immortal. He who dwells within the waters, yet is other than the waters, whom the waters do not know, whose body is the waters, and who controls the waters from within— he is your Self, the Inner Controller, the Immortal.
He who dwells in fire, yet is within fire, whom fire does not know, whose body is fire, who controls fire from within—he is your Self, the Inner Controller, the Immortal. 14.6.7.
He who dwells in space, yet is within space, whom space does not know, whose body is space, who...
He who dwells within space, yet is distinct from space, whom space does not know, whose body is space, and who controls space from within— he is your Self, the Inner Controller, the Immortal.

He who dwells within the wind, yet is distinct from the wind, whom the wind does not know, whose body is the wind, and who controls the wind from within— he is your Self, the Inner Controller, the Immortal.

He who, dwelling in the sun, is within the sun, whom the sun does not know, whose body the sun is, who controls the sun from within; [14.6.7.13] he who, dwelling in the moon and the stars, is within the moon and the stars, whom the moon and the stars do not know, whose...

The body is the moon and the stars, yet He who is within the moon and the stars is Yama. 14.6.7.[14] He who, dwelling in the quarters, is internal to the quarters; whom the quarters do not know, whose body is the quarters, and who is internal to the quarters—He is Yama.

He who dwells in lightning, yet is within lightning, whom lightning does not know, whose body is lightning, and who controls lightning from within; [14.6.7.16] He who dwells in thunder, yet is within thunder, whom thunder does not know, whose body is thunder...
"He who, dwelling within the body, controls the body from within—he is your Self, the inner controller, the immortal.
This is with respect to the deities. Now, with respect to the worlds:
"He who, dwelling in all the worlds, is internal to all the worlds, whom all the worlds do not know, whose..."
"He who dwells in all worlds, yet is within all worlds, and who controls all worlds—he is your Self, the Inner Controller, the Immortal.
Thus far with respect to the worlds;
now with respect to the Vedas: "He who dwells in all the Vedas, yet is within all the Vedas..."
Thus [is he] with respect to the Vedas; now, with respect to sacrifice:
"Abiding in all sacrifices, yet internal to all sacrifices"—thus indeed is he with respect to sacrifice. Now, with respect to the elements: Maitri Upaniṣad 14.6.7 [19-20].

He who, dwelling within all beings, is distinct from all beings; whom all beings do not know; whose body all beings are; who controls all beings from within—he is your Self, the Inner Controller, the Immortal. Thus with respect to the elemental realm (adhibhūta); now with respect to the personal realm (adhyātma). 14.6.7 [21]

He who dwells in the vital breath (*prāṇa*), yet is within the vital breath, whom the vital breath does not know, whose body is the vital breath, who controls the vital breath from within—he is your Self, the Inner Controller, the Immortal. 14.6.7 [22] He who dwells in speech (*vāk*), yet is within speech... 14.6.7 [23]
He who dwells in the eye, yet is within the eye; he who dwells in the ear, yet is within the ear; he who dwells in the mind, yet is within the mind.
He who, dwelling in the skin, is within the skin; he who, dwelling in heat, is within the heat; he who, dwelling in darkness, is within the darkness.
He who, dwelling in the semen, is within the semen; [14.6.7.30] He who, dwelling in the self, is within the self;
unseen yet seeing, unheard yet hearing, unthought yet thinking, unknown yet knowing—there is no other seer, there is no other [hearer].
"There is no other hearer, there is no other thinker, there is no other knower; this is your Self, the inner controller, the immortal. Whatever is different from this is subject to suffering.
Thereupon, Uddālaka Āruṇi ceased [questioning].
Then Vācaknavī said: "Venerable Brahmins, come now, let me question this Yājñavalkya with two questions."

"I shall ask two questions; if he will answer them for me, then truly none among you shall ever defeat him in this debate on Brahman. But if he will not answer them for me, his head shall shatter apart. "Ask then, Gārgī," [he said]. 14.6.8. [2]

She said: "O Yājñavalkya, just as a Kāśyan or a Vaidehan nobleman, the son of a prominent family, might rise up having strung his bow and taken two arrow-fitted, enemy-piercing shafts in his hand, even so have I risen up against you with two questions. Answer them for me."
"Ask, Gārgī," he said.

She replied: "Yājñavalkya, that which is above the sky, that which is below the earth, that which is between these two, heaven and earth, and that which they call the past, the present, and the future—in what are all these woven back and forth?"

He said: "O Gārgī, that which is above the sky, that which is below the earth, that which is between these two, heaven and earth, and that which they call the past, the present, and the future—in space, all that is woven, warp and woof. She said: "Homage to you, Yājñavalkya, who has unraveled this for me. Hold fast to another question; ask it. He asked: "Ask."

"Gārgī," he said. She replied, "Yājñavalkya, that which is above the sky, that which is below the earth, that which is between these two, heaven and earth, and that which they call the past, the present, and the future— in what, then, is all that woven to and fro?"

He said: "O Gārgī, that which is above heaven, that which is below the earth, that which is between these two, heaven and earth, and that which they call the past, the present, and the future—across all this, space alone is woven like warp and woof.
"Upon what, then, is space woven like warp and woof? [14.6.8]

He said: "O Gārgī, this indeed is that syllable which the Brāhmaṇas declare as neither gross nor subtle, neither short nor long, neither red nor oily, neither shadowy nor dark, neither air nor space, unattached, intangible, odorless, tasteless, without eyes, without ears, without voice, without mind, and devoid of light."

It is without breath, without mouth, without name, without lineage; it is ageless, immortal, fearless, deathless, stainless, soundless, unmanifested, unenclosed, without before, without after, without interior, without exterior; it does not reach anything, nor does anything reach it. 14.6.8 [9]
"Under the governance of this Imperishable, O Gārgī, heaven and earth stand held apart; under the governance of this Imperishable, O Gārgī, the sun and the moon stand held apart;
under the governance of this Imperishable, O Gārgī, days and nights, half-months, months, seasons, and years stand held apart."

Or, O Gārgī, by the command of that Imperishable, some rivers flow eastward from the white mountains; others flow westward; and in whatever direction they may go, it is by the command of that Imperishable, O Gārgī, that humans praise the one who gives, the gods depend upon the sacrificer, and the ancestors depend upon the giver of oblations. 14.6.8 [10]

"Or, Gārgī, whoever in this world offers oblations, gives gifts, or performs austerities without knowing this Imperishable—even if for many thousands of years—his world is indeed finite. Or, Gārgī, whoever departs from this world without knowing this Imperishable is pitiable; but he who departs from this world after having known this Imperishable, Gārgī—"
"O Gārgī, this very syllable is unseen yet the seer, unheard yet the hearer, unthought yet the thinker, unknown yet the knower; there is nothing other than this. (Brāhmaṇa 14.6.8[11])
"There is no other seer, there is no other hearer, there is no other thinker, there is no other knower— this indeed is that Imperishable, O Gārgī,
in which the ether is woven like warp and woof.
She said, "Venerable Brahmins, you should consider yourselves fortunate enough to receive a mere salutation from me."

"Be released; indeed, none of you shall ever defeat him in a debate concerning Brahman. Thereupon, Vācaknavī ceased questioning him. Then Vidagdha Śākalya asked him: "How many gods are there, Yājñavalkya? He [Yājñavalkya] replied with this very *nivid* (enumeration of deities):
"He reached as many as are mentioned in the *Nivid* of the *Vaiśvadeva*: 'Three hundred and three, and three thousand and three.
'Om,' he said. 'How many gods are there, Yājñavalkya? 'Thirty-three. 'Om,' he said. 'How many gods are there, Yājñavalkya?'"

"Six," he said. "Yes," he replied. "How many gods are there, Yājñavalkya? "Three," he said. "Yes," he replied. "How many gods are there, Yājñavalkya? "Two," he said. "Yes," he replied. "How many gods are there, Yājñavalkya? "One and a half," he said. "Yes," he replied. "How many gods are there, Yājñavalkya? "One," he said. "Yes," he replied. "Which are those three and three hundred?"
"Three and three thousand," [he said]. He replied: "These are merely their manifestations; there are actually only thirty-three gods. "Which are those thirty-three?
"The eight Vasus, the eleven Rudras, and the twelve Ādityas—those are thirty-one; and Indra and..."
"Prajāpati and the thirty-three.

"Who are the Vasus? "Agni and the earth, Vāyu and the intermediate space, Āditya and the sky, and the stars—these are the Vasus; for in these all this wealth (vasu) is placed, and they indeed cause all this to dwell (vāsayante)."

Because they cause all this to dwell, therefore they are called the Vasus. (14.6.9.5) Who are the Rudras? These ten vital breaths in a person, with the self as the eleventh—when they depart from this mortal body, they cause one to weep; because they cause one to weep (*rodayanti*), therefore they are called the Rudras. (14.6.9.6)
"Who are the Ādityas? "The twelve months of the year; these are the Ādityas, for they go along taking up (ādadataḥ) all this [world].
Because they go along taking up all this, therefore they are called Ādityas.
"Who is Indra? Who is Prajāpati? "Indra is indeed the thunder, and Prajāpati is the sacrifice. "Who is he?"
“‘Thunder’—is that ‘the thunderbolt’? ‘What is the sacrifice?’—‘The cattle.
[14.6.9.8] “Which are the six? “Fire and earth, wind and the intermediate space, the sun and the sky;
for these indeed are all this as the six. [14.6.9.9]

"Who are those three gods? "These very three worlds, for within them all these gods reside. "Who are the two gods? "Food and breath. "Who is the one-and-a-half? "This one who blows [the wind]. Regarding this, they say: "Since this [wind] blows as only one, how then is it 'one-and-a-half'? [The answer is: "Because in this [wind], this..."
"Everything is one-and-a-half; by what is it one-and-a-half? Which is that one god? He is called 'That Brahman'.

"Yājñavalkya, he who knows that person whose abode is the earth, whose world is the eye, whose light is the mind, and who is the ultimate resort of every self—he indeed would be a knower. Do you know him, Yājñavalkya? "I do indeed know him."

"The person whom you call the ultimate refuge of every self—that very person who is embodied (śārīra)—tell me, Śākalya, who is his deity? "Women," he said. 14.6.9 [12] He whose abode is forms, whose world is the eye, whose light is the mind—that person indeed...

"One should know him as the ultimate resort of every self; he indeed would be a knower, O Yājñavalkya. "I do indeed know that person, the ultimate resort of every self, of whom you speak—he who is that person in the sun.
Tell me, Śākalya, who is his deity? "The eye," he said. 14.6.9 [13]
"He whose abode is space itself, whose world is the eye, whose self is the mind—he who is this person in the wind, he is that very one.
Tell me, Śākalya, what is his deity? "The vital breath (prāṇa)," he said.
"He whose abode is desire itself, whose world is the eye, whose self is the mind—he who is that person in the moon, he is that very one."

"Tell me, Śākalya, who is his deity? "The mind," he said. "He whose abode is fire, whose world is the eye, and whose self is the mind—he is this very person in the fire. Tell me, Śākalya, who is his deity? "Speech," he said.

"Darkness alone is his abode, the eye his world, and the mind his [source]. As for this person who consists of shadow—tell me, Śākalya, what is his deity? "Death," he said. "Water alone is his abode, the eye his world, and the mind his [source]. As for this person who is in the waters—tell me..."

"Śākalya, who is its deity? "Varuṇa," he said. 14.6.9 [18] "The one whose abode is semen, whose world is the eye, and whose self is the mind—that person who consists of sons, Śākalya, tell me, who is his deity? "Prajāpati," he said. 14.6.9 [19]
"Śākalya," said Yājñavalkya, "have these Brahmins indeed made you their charcoal-burner?

"Yājñavalkya," said Śākalya, "since you have spoken over these Brahmins of the Kurus and Pañcālas, what do you know as Brahman? "I know the quarters together with their gods and their foundations. "In that you know the quarters together with their gods..."
[They are] well-established.
14.6.9.[21] "Which deity are you in this eastern direction? "The deity Aditya. "In what is that Aditya established? "In the eye.
"In what, then, is the eye established? "In forms (rūpa), for by means of the eye one perceives forms."

"Wherein do forms become established? "In the heart," he said. "For by means of the heart one knows forms; indeed, in the heart alone forms become established. "Is it even so, Yājñavalkya? (14.6.9) "With which deity are you associated in this southern direction? "With Yama as my deity. "In whom is that Yama established?"
"Regarding the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*): on what is the sacrificial fee established? "On faith (*śraddhā*).
"For when one has faith, then one gives the sacrificial fee; thus, on faith indeed the sacrificial fee is established.
"On what then is faith established? "On the heart (*hṛdaya*). "For with the heart one has faith; [it is] on the heart..."
"Faith alone is established," [he said]. "Just so, Yājñavalkya.

(14.6.9) "What deity are you in this western direction? "Varuṇa is my deity. "On what is Varuṇa established? "On the waters. "On what are the waters established? "On semen. "On what is semen established?"
"It exists," he said. "In the heart. Therefore they say that what is born is a likeness [of its parent], as if it had slipped from the heart, as if it were fashioned from the heart;
for in the heart alone the seed is established. "It is even so, Yājñavalkya.
"What deity are you in this northern direction? "Soma is my deity. "In what is Soma established?"

Regarding the initiation: "In what is initiation established? "In truth. Therefore, they say to one who has been initiated, "Speak the truth," for initiation is indeed established in truth. "In what is truth established? "In the heart," for by means of the heart one knows the truth; for truth is indeed established in the heart.
"It is established in truth," [he said]. "Just so, Yājñavalkya. (14.6.9) "Which deity are you in this fixed direction? "Agni is my deity. "On what is that Agni established?
"On speech. "On what is speech established? "On the mind. "On what is the mind established?"
"It exists," [he said]. "In what, then, is the heart established?
"It is in *ahallikā*," Yājñavalkya replied. "If you were to think it existed elsewhere than in us, then either dogs would eat it or birds would tear it apart."

"But on what are you and the self established? "On the out-breath (prāṇa). "On what is the out-breath established? "On the in-breath (apāna). "On what is the in-breath established? "On the inter-breath (vyāna). "On what is the inter-breath established? "On the up-breath (udāna). "On what is the up-breath established? "On the equalizing breath (samāna). 14.6.9 [28]

"He is this: 'Not this, not that. He is ungraspable, for he is not grasped; he is indestructible, for he is not destroyed; he is unattached and unfettered; he does not cling, nor is he afflicted. These are the eight abodes, the eight worlds, and the eight persons.
I ask you about that person of the Upanishads who, having driven out and then withdrawn those persons, has transcended them."
"If you do not explain that to me, your head shall fall off. Śākalya did not know this;
his head fell off, and thinking them to be something else, thieves carried away his bones.
Then Yājñavalkya said, "Venerable Brahmins, let whoever among you desires it question me; let everyone [question me]."
"Or rather, ask him among you who desires [to answer]; I shall ask him for you, or I shall ask all of you. Those Brahmins did not dare.
He questioned them with these verses: "As is a tree, a lord of the forest, so indeed is a man; this is no falsehood. Of him..."

The leaves are its body hairs; the outer bark is its skin. From its very skin flows blood, and from the skin comes the sap; therefore, when it is struck, the sap flows out like [resin] from a tree that has been cut.

Its flesh is the sapwood, its sinews are the tough inner bark; the bones within are the heartwood, and the marrow is made like the pith. (9) Just as a tree, when cut down, springs up again from its roots even more luxuriantly, so too does a mortal, when cut down by death, [arise again]. 14.6.9 [33]

From what root does it sprout? Do not say "from semen," for that is produced from the living; once born, it is not born again. Who, indeed, would produce it anew? A tree is surely one that grows from a seed; after death, there is rebirth from something else. If they were to uproot the tree along with its very roots, it would not grow again.

"Does a mortal, once cut down by death, sprout again from some root? Knowledge and bliss are Brahman, the supreme goal of the giver of wealth who stands firm as one who knows it. Janaka of Videha was sitting [in his assembly hall], when Yājñavalkya arrived. Janaka of Videha said to him:

"Yājñavalkya, for what purpose have you wandered about, eating food while not studying the Vedas? "For both reasons, O Emperor," he replied, "and also because someone told me, 'Let us hear what another has said to you. "Udaṅka Śaulvāyana told me: 'The vital breath (prāṇa) indeed is Brahman. As..."

"One who has a mother, one who has a father, and one who has a teacher should speak thus; so said Cūlāyana: 'Brahman is indeed prāṇa. [The other asked: 'For what could there be for one who is without prāṇa? [Cūlāyana replied:
'But he did not tell you its abode or its support. [The other said: 'This, O Emperor, is only one-quarter.'"

"Tell us that, Yājñavalkya. "Space itself is its abode; space is its foundation. One should meditate upon it as 'the dear' (priya). "What is its dearness, Yājñavalkya? "The vital breath (*prāṇa*), O Emperor," he said. "For the sake of the vital breath, O Emperor, one performs sacrifices for which one should not sacrifice, and accepts gifts for which one should not accept them; even there, the fear of death arises in whatever direction one goes."

"It is for the sake of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), O Emperor, that one desires; the vital breath, O Emperor, is indeed the supreme Brahman. The vital breath does not abandon him, and all beings flow toward him. Having become a god, he goes to the gods—he who, knowing this, worships it thus. "I shall give you a thousand [cows] with an elephant as the bull," [said Janaka].
Janaka, the King of Videha, said this. Yājñavalkya replied: "My father thought that one should not take [gifts] without having first instructed [his pupil].
Who was it, and what did he say to you?
"He told me, after defeating me, 'Śailina said: Speech indeed is Brahman. As one who possesses a mother, a father, and a teacher would speak, so did he speak."

Tacaílina said: "Speech, indeed, is Brahman. "Tell me, what would one gain by merely saying that? He replied: "But he did not tell you its abode or its support. "It has but one foot, O Emperor. "Tell us that, Yājñavalkya! "Speech is its abode, space is its support; one should meditate upon it as 'Intelligence' (prajñā). "What is its deity?"
"Understanding, O Yājñavalkya? "Speech itself, Your Majesty," he said. "For by speech, Your Majesty, a kinsman is recognized;

the Ṛgveda, the Yajurveda, the Sāmaveda, the Atharvāṅgirasa, history, the Purāṇas, the sciences, the Upaniṣads, verses, aphorisms, explanations, and commentaries—all these, Your Majesty, are recognized by speech alone. Speech indeed, Your Majesty, [is understanding]."
The supreme Brahman does not abandon him; all beings flow toward him.
Having become a god, he goes to the gods—he who, knowing this, meditates upon this.
Varku Vārṣṇa said to me: "The eye, indeed, is Brahman," just as...
"One who has a mother, one who has a father, and one who has a teacher may speak thus; so did Vārṣṇa say: 'The eye, indeed, is Brahman. [The other said: 'What could there be for one who does not see?
But he did not tell you its abode or its support. [Vārṣṇa replied: 'This, O Emperor, is only one-quarter.'"
"Tell us that, Yājñavalkya. "The eye itself is the abode, space is the foundation;
one should meditate upon this as 'the True'. "What is its truthfulness, Yājñavalkya? "The eye itself, O Emperor," he said.
"For when someone sees with the eye, O Emperor, people say, 'Have you seen? If he says, 'I have seen,' that becomes the truth. The eye, indeed, is [the truth]."
The Sovereign is the Supreme Brahman; the eye does not desert him, and all beings flow toward him. 14.6.10.
[10] Having become a god, he goes to the gods—he who, knowing this, meditates upon it as such. 14.6.10. [11] Gardabhīvipīta Bhāradvāja said to me: "The ear, indeed, is Brahman," just as...

"One who has a mother, one who has a father, and one who has a teacher should speak thus. Bharadvāja said, "The ear, indeed, is Brahman. [Janaka asked: "What would become of one who does not hear? He replied, "I have told you that, but he did not tell me its abode or its support. [Janaka said: "This [Brahman], O Emperor, is only one-footed. 14.6.10. [12]
"Tell us that, Yājñavalkya. "The ear, indeed, is its abode; space is its foundation. One should meditate upon it as 'the Infinite' (Ananta).
"What constitutes its infinity, Yājñavalkya? "The quarters of space themselves, O Emperor," he said.
"Therefore, O Emperor, whichever quarter one goes toward, one never reaches its end, for the quarters are infinite. The quarters are the ear; the ear, O Emperor, is indeed the quarters."
The supreme Brahman does not forsake him; all beings flow toward him.
Having become a god, he goes to the gods—he who, knowing this, meditates upon this. Satyakāma Jābāla said to me: "Mind indeed is Brahman," just as...

"One who has a mother, one who has a father, and one who has a teacher should speak thus; so Satyakāma spoke: 'The mind, indeed, is Brahman. [The teacher said: 'For what could there be for one who is without a mind? [Satyakāma replied: 'But he did not tell me its abode and its support. [The teacher said:
'This [Brahman], O Emperor, is indeed one-footed.'"

"Tell us that, Yājñavalkya. "The mind alone is its abode, space is its foundation; one should worship it as bliss. "What constitutes its blissfulness, Yājñavalkya? "The mind alone, O Emperor," he said. "For with the mind, O Emperor, one desires a woman. From her a son is born who is like him; that is bliss. The mind, O Emperor, [is indeed bliss]."
The supreme Brahman does not abandon him; all beings flow toward him.
Having become a god, he goes to the gods—he who, knowing this, meditates upon it as such. Vidagdha Śākalya said to me: "The heart, indeed, is Brahman," just as...

"One who has a mother, one who has a father, or one who has a teacher should speak thus; so did Akalya say: 'Brahman is indeed the heart. [The other asked: 'What would there be for one who is heartless? He replied: 'He told you that, but he did not tell you its abode or its support. [The other said: 'This, O Emperor, is but one-quarter. 14.6.10 [18]
"Tell us that, Yājñavalkya. "The heart itself is the abode, and space is its foundation;
one should meditate upon it as 'Stability'. "What is this stability, Yājñavalkya? "The heart itself, O Emperor," he said.
"The heart indeed, O Emperor, is the foundation of all beings, for by the heart all beings are established."

"The heart, O Emperor, is indeed the supreme Brahman; the heart does not desert him, and all beings flow toward him. Having become a god, he goes to the gods—he who, knowing this, venerates it thus. I shall give a thousand [cows] with a bull as the eleventh," [he said].
Janaka of Videha said. Yājñavalkya replied: "My father was of the opinion that one should not accept a gift without having first instructed.
Then Janaka of Videha, descending from his seat of kusha grass, said: "Homage to you, Yājñavalkya; instruct me further."

"Teach me," he said. He [the teacher] replied: "Just as indeed, O Emperor, one who is about to travel a great distance would prepare a chariot or a boat, even so you have prepared yourself with these secret doctrines (*upaniṣad*). Being thus honored, wealthy, learned in the Vedas, and instructed in the secret doctrines, where will you go when you are released from here? "I do not know," he replied.
"O Venerable One, may you know where I shall go. "Then indeed, I shall tell you where you will go," he said.
"Let the Venerable One speak.
He replied: "This person who is here in the right eye is indeed named Indha; him, this Indha—"

They call him "Indra" by means of an indirect designation, for the gods, as it were, prefer the indirect to the direct and dislike what is manifest. 14.6.11[3] Now, this person in the left eye is his wife, Virāj. That which is the space within the heart is the place where these two converse. And that which is within the heart is their food.
Then there is this lump of blood, which serves as their covering—this network-like thing within the heart.
And this is their path, the way for movement, which rises upward from the heart as a channel.
These indeed are his channels called the *hitā*; they are like a hair split a thousandfold. By means of these...
It flows toward these outflows; therefore, it becomes as if more secluded from this body-self.

Of this very person, the eastern direction consists of his forward vital breaths (*prāṇas*); the southern direction consists of his rightward vital breaths; the western direction consists of his backward vital breaths; the northern direction consists of his upward vital breaths; and the zenith consists of his upward vital breaths.
The downward direction is the downward vital breaths; all directions are all the vital breaths.
This very Self is "not this, not this"—it is ungraspable, for it is not grasped; it is indestructible, for it is not destroyed; it is unattached and unfettered, for it is neither attached nor bound.
"It trembles, O Janaka, for you have indeed reached the state beyond fear," said Yājñavalkya. Janaka, the King of Videha, replied:
"Salutations to you, Yājñavalkya! May fearlessness come to you; for you, O Blessed One, have taught us that which is beyond fear. Here are the people of Videha, and here am I."

Yājñavalkya went to Janaka of Videha, thinking, "I shall speak with him on equal terms. Now, when Janaka of Videha and Yājñavalkya had conversed together regarding the Agnihotra sacrifice, Yājñavalkya granted him a boon. He chose the right to ask any question he desired; Yājñavalkya granted it to him. Then the Emperor himself asked the first question. 14.7.1. [2]

"Yājñavalkya, what is the light of this person? "The light of the sun, O King," he said, "for by the light of the sun alone this person sits, moves about, performs his work, and returns. "Just so, Yājñavalkya. "When the sun has set, Yājñavalkya, what is the light of this person? "The light of the moon, O King," he said.

He said: "By the moon alone as his light, this person sits, moves about, performs work, and returns. "It is just so, Yājñavalkya. (14.7.1) "Yājñavalkya, when the sun has set and the moon has set, what light does this person have?"
"Fire is his light, O Emperor," Yājñavalkya replied. "By fire as his light, he sits, moves about, performs his work, and returns.
"It is just so, Yājñavalkya.
"When the sun has set, Yājñavalkya, when the moon has set, and the fire has gone out, what light does this person have?"
"Speech is the light, O Emperor," he said. "For by speech as his light, this person sits, moves about, performs work, and returns.
Therefore, O Emperor, even where one's own hand cannot be discerned, one still goes on there as soon as speech rises up. "It is just so, Yājñavalkya. (14.7.1)

"When the sun has set, Yājñavalkya, when the moon has set, when the fire has gone out, and speech has been stilled, what light does this person have? "The self is his light, O Emperor," he said. "By the light of the self alone, he sits, moves about, performs his work, and returns. 14.7.1. [7]

"What is the self? It is this person consisting of consciousness, who is the light within the heart among the vital breaths. Being the same [in both states], he moves between both worlds; as if meditating, as if moving about, becoming a dreamer endowed with intelligence, he transcends this world. 14.7.1 [8]
This person, indeed, when being born and entering a body, becomes joined with evils;
when departing and dying, he leaves behind the evils, the forms of death.
Of this very person, there are indeed two stations: this world and the station of the other world.
The third state is the junction, the place of dream; standing in that intermediate state, one perceives both places—this world and the world beyond. 14.7.1.
[10] Now, as he proceeds toward that state of the world beyond, having traversed that path, he encounters all evils.

And he sees joys; for when he is here in this state of sleep, having taken a measure from this all-encompassing world, having himself struck it down and himself fashioned it, he sleeps by his own radiance, by his own light. Herein, this person becomes self-luminous. 14.7.1 [11]
There are no chariots there, no draft animals, and no roads, yet he creates chariots, draft animals, and roads;
there is no joy, no delight, and no rapture there, yet he creates joy, delight, and rapture; there are no pools, rivers, or lotus ponds there, yet he creates pools, rivers, and lotus ponds.
For he is the creator who emits [the world].

Regarding this, there are these verses: "Having struck down the bodily [self] with sleep, the Unsleeping one looks upon the sleeping senses; taking the light, he returns again to his place—the golden, solitary swan, the person. (14.7.1.13)
Protecting his lower nest with his vital breath (*prāṇa*), the immortal one, having moved outside the nest, goes wherever he desires as an immortal—the golden, singular swan of the person (*puruṣa*).
In the state of dream, moving through high and low [realms], the god assumes many forms; he sports, as it were, with women.
Rejoicing and laughing, as it were, even while seeing terrors;
(14.7.1.15) "They see his pleasure grove, yet no one sees him.
They say that one should not wake him when he is sleeping, for it is difficult to treat the one whom he does not attend to. (14.7.1.16)
Moreover, they say: "This [state] of his is indeed the very region of waking; for whatever he sees while awake, those same things he sees while asleep.
"In this state, this person becomes self-luminous"—"It is even so, Yājñavalkya. "I give you a thousand [cows], O Venerable One; speak further only for the sake of liberation. 14.7.1. [17]

Having enjoyed himself and wandered about in that state of dream, and having seen both good and evil, he hastens back again according to the rule and according to his source, toward the waking state itself. Whatever he sees there, he does not carry with him; for this person is unattached.
"So it is indeed, Yājñavalkya. I give you a thousand [cows], O Blessed One;
speak further for the sake of liberation alone.
"Just as a great fish moves along both banks, the near and the far, even so does this [Self]."
The person moves back and forth between these two ends: the state of dream and the state of waking.

Just as in this sky a hawk or a falcon, having flown about and become weary, folds its wings and remains poised for its nest, even so this person hastens toward that end where, when asleep, he does not know anything at all.
He desires no desire at all, nor does he see any dream whatsoever.
These channels of his, called the *hitā*, exist with a fineness like that of a hair split a thousandfold;
they are filled with white, blue, brown, green, and red [fluids]. Then, when it seems as though they are striking him...

As if being conquered, as if by an elephant, he trembles; as if falling into a pit—whatever fear he perceives while waking, that he considers to be fear here due to ignorance. But where he thinks, "I am indeed this all," like a king, like a god—that is his supreme world. Then, where, asleep, he desires no desire whatsoever, nor [perceives] anything...
He does not even dream.

This, indeed, is his form which consists of the self, in which all desires are fulfilled, which has attained all its desires, and which is free from desire. Just as a man embraced by a beloved wife knows nothing without nor within, even so this embodied self.

Embraced by the intelligent Self (prājña ātman), one knows nothing external and nothing internal. This, indeed, is his form that transcends the bright, free from evil, fearless, and devoid of sorrow. Here, a father becomes no father, a mother no mother; worlds become no worlds, gods no gods, and the Vedas no Vedas; sacrifices become no sacrifices. Here, a thief becomes no thief.
The slayer of an embryo is not a slayer of an embryo; the Paulkasa is not a Paulkasa; the Caṇḍāla is not a Caṇḍāla; the ascetic is not an ascetic; the mendicant is not a mendicant.
For at that time he has transcended all worlds and is untouched by merit and untouched by evil.

Verily, that which he does not see there—he, though seeing, does not see that which is to be seen; for there is no loss of the vision of the seer, because of its imperishability. But there is not a second thing existing there, other than himself, separate from him, which he might see.
When he does not smell there, it is because, though smelling, he does not smell that which is to be smelled;
for there is no loss of the smeller’s power of smelling, since it is indestructible. However, there is no second thing, distinct from him, that he might smell. 14.7.1 [25]

Indeed, when he does not taste, it is because, though knowing, he does not taste that flavor; for there is no loss of the power of tasting in the taster, because of his imperishability. Yet, there is nothing second to him, nothing else separate from him, that he might taste.
Indeed, when he does not speak, it is because, though speaking, he does not speak that which is to be spoken; for there is no loss of the power of speech in the speaker.

It exists because it is imperishable; yet there is no second thing, other than it and separate from it, that one could speak of. (14.7.1 [27]) Indeed, when one does not hear that, it is because, though hearing, one does not hear what is to be heard; for there is no loss of the hearing of the hearer, because it is imperishable. Yet there is no second thing, other than it and separate from it, that one might hear. (14.7.1 [28])

Verily, when one does not think that [which is his own Self], he indeed thinks that which is to be thought; yet he does not think it, for there is no loss of the thinker’s power of thinking because of its imperishability. But there is not a second thing existing there, distinct from him, which he might think. 14.7.1 [29]
