From Viśvarūpa, the son of Tvaṣṭṛ; from Viśvarūpa, the son of Tvaṣṭṛ, [the knowledge went] to the Aśvins;
from the Aśvins to Dadhyañc Ātharvaṇa; from Dadhyañc Ātharvaṇa to Atharvan Daiva; from Atharvan Daiva to Mṛtyu Prādhvaṃsana; from Mṛtyu Prādhvaṃsana to Pradhvaṃsana.

From Ekarṣi [came] Ekarṣi; from Viprajitti, Viprajitti; from Vyaṣṭi, Vyaṣṭi; from Sanāru, Sanāru; from Sanātana, Sanātana; from Sanaga, Sanaga; from Parameṣṭhin, Parameṣṭhin; from Brahmā, Brahmā. To the self-existent Brahmā, salutation! 14.8.1.

"Full is that, full is this; from the full, the full arises. When the full is taken from the full, the full alone remains. "Om, Kha is Brahman; Kha is the ancient one; Kha is Vāyu; Kha," so said Kauravyāyaṇīputra. This is the Veda which the Brāhmaṇas know; by means of this, that which is to be known is known. 14.8.2.1.

There were three classes of Prajāpati’s offspring who lived the life of a student of sacred knowledge (brahmacarya) with their father Prajāpati: the gods, the humans, and the asuras. (14.8.2) Having completed their studentship, the gods said, "May your lordship speak to us. He spoke this single syllable to them: "Da! "Do you understand? he asked. "We understand," they replied. "What have you understood? he asked. "You told us: 'Be self-controlled' (dāmyata)," they said. He said, "Yes (om)."
"You have understood," [he said].

14.8.2.[3] Then the men said to him, "May your honor speak to us. To them he spoke this very syllable, "Da. "Have you understood? "We have understood," they said. "What did you understand? "You told us 'Give' (datta). "Yes," he said, "you have understood. 14.8.2.[4]

Then the Asuras said to him, "May your honor speak to us. He spoke this very syllable to them: "Da. [They asked: "Have you understood? [He replied: "We have understood. [They said: "You have told us 'Be merciful' (dayadhvam). [He said: "Yes," he replied, "you have understood. This very same divine voice, the thunder, repeats it: "Da-da-da"—"Be self-controlled, give, be merciful."

"Be compassionate"—thus one should learn these three: self-restraint, generosity, and compassion. Vāyu is the immortal breath; the body ends in ashes. Oṃ! O Kratu, remember! O Kliba, remember! O Agni, lead us by a good path to wealth, O God who knows all ways; drive away from us the sin that leads astray.
"Let us offer you the most abundant speech of homage.

This heart is Prajāpati; this is Brahman; this is all. This "Heart" consists of three syllables: *hṛ* is one syllable; for one who knows thus, both his own people and others bring offerings to him. *Da* is one syllable.
Both his own people and others give [gifts] to him who knows thus; "yam" is one syllable—he who knows thus goes to the heavenly world.
That indeed was this very thing; it was the Truth itself. He who knows thus that great, first-born Yakṣa...

"He who knows that Brahman is Truth conquers these worlds; he has indeed conquered them today. Thus one knows this great, first-born Yakṣa: "Brahman is Truth. For Brahman is indeed Truth. In the beginning, this world was only water. Those waters produced Truth. Truth [produced] Brahman, and Brahman [produced] Prajāpati.
Prajāpati [created] the gods. Those gods venerate "Truth" (satya). This "Truth" consists of three syllables:
*sa* is one syllable, *ti* is one syllable, and *am* is one syllable. The first and the last syllables are Truth.
That falsehood which is in the middle is this very falsehood surrounded by truth; it becomes, indeed, an abundance of truth.
Falsehood does not harm one who knows this.
That which is that truth is yonder sun—the person who is in this orb, and also this [person here].

In the right eye is a person; these two are established in one another. Indeed, this [sun] is established in this [eye] by means of its rays, and this [eye] is established in that [sun] by means of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*). When he is about to depart, he sees this orb as pure; these rays do not return to him. 14.8.6[4]
Of this person who is in that orb, "Bhūḥ" is the head—there is one head and this syllable is one;
"Bhuvaḥ" is the two arms—there are two arms and these two syllables; "Svar" is the two feet—there are two feet and these two syllables.
His secret name (upaniṣad) is "Ahaḥ. He who knows this destroys evil and leaves it behind. 14.8.6[5]
Now, as for this person who is in the right eye: "Bhūḥ" is his head; the head is one, and this syllable is one.
"Bhuvaḥ" is his two arms; the arms are two, and these two syllables are two. "Svaḥ" is his foundation; the foundations are two, and these two syllables are two.
His secret name (*upaniṣad*) is "Aham" (I). He who knows this slays evil and leaves it behind. 14.8.7.
"Lightning is Brahman," they say. Because it flashes (*vidāna*), it is lightning; he who knows that "lightning is Brahman" flashes away from all evil.
Lightning indeed is Brahman.
This person consists of mind, his essence is light, and he is true. Within his heart, he is like a grain of rice or a grain of barley.
Verily, this person within the inner self—he is the controller of all, the lord of all, the sovereign of all;
he rules over all this, whatever exists. He who knows thus [attains this].
One should meditate upon speech as a cow. It has four udders: the utterance *svāhā*, the utterance *vaṣaṭ*, the utterance *hanta*, and the utterance *svadhā*.
The utterance *svadhā* constitutes her two breasts upon which the gods subsist: the *svāhā*-utterance and the *vaṣaṭ*-utterance.
Humans [subsist on] the *hanta*-utterance, and the ancestors on the *svadhā*-utterance. Her breath is the bull, and her mind is the calf.
This is indeed Agni Vaiśvānara, who is within the person, by whom this food is cooked—that which is eaten here.
This is its sound which one hears when one covers the ears; when he is about to depart [from this world], he does not hear that sound.
This is indeed the supreme austerity: when one who is ill suffers. He who knows thus wins the supreme world.

"Truly, this is the supreme austerity: when they carry the deceased to the forest; he who knows this indeed conquers the supreme world. Truly, this is the supreme austerity: when they place the deceased upon the fire; he who knows this indeed conquers the supreme world. (14.8.12)

When a person indeed departs from this world, he comes to Vāyu. There, Vāyu makes way for him like the hole of a chariot wheel; through that, he ascends upwards. He comes to Āditya. There, Āditya makes way for him like the hole of a drum; through that, he ascends upwards. He comes to Candramas. There, he [Candramas]...
There he moves about as the space within a drum; by that [space] he ascends upward, reaches the world of heaven free from sorrow, and dwells therein for eternal years.
(14.8.13) "Food is Brahman," say some; but that is not so, for food putrefies without life-breath (*prāṇa*). "Life-breath is Brahman," say some.
They say that this is not so; for the vital breath (*prāṇa*) does indeed wither without food. However, these two deities, having become one, attain the supreme state.
Regarding this, Prātṛda once said to his father: "What good thing could one do for one who knows thus? What indeed could one do for him?"
"He might do what is improper," he said, "O Prātṛda, do not [fear]. But who, having become one with these two, goes to the supreme state?
To him he then spoke this: "Vi. Food indeed is "vi," for all these beings are pervaded (*viṣṭa*) by food. "Ram. Food indeed is "ram," for all these beings delight (*ramante*) in food.
The vital breath (*prāṇa*) is indeed *ram*. For in the vital breath all these beings are delighted (*ratāni*).
Indeed, all beings enter into him and all beings delight in him who knows this. 14.8.14[1]
The *uktha* is breath; for the *uktha* is indeed breath, since breath raises up all this.
For him who knows the *uktha*, a hero stands ready to rise up, and he wins union with and residence in the same world as the *uktha*.
14.8.14 [2] Breath is indeed the *yajus*; for by breath all these beings are joined (*yujyante*). Indeed, all things are joined for him.
The beings attain preeminence through the Yajus; he who knows this conquers union with it and residence in the same world as it.

14.8.14[3] The Sāman is indeed breath; for breath holds all these beings together (samyañci). Indeed, all beings strive for preeminence in this [breath]. He who knows this conquers union with the Sāman and residence in the same world as it. 14.8.14[4]

The ruling power (*kṣatra*) is indeed breath; for breath indeed protects the ruling power from being harmed. He who knows this attains the full measure of the ruling power and wins union with and residence in the same world as the ruling power. 14.8.15.
[1] "Earth, atmosphere, heaven"—these are eight syllables. Indeed, one *gāyatrī* verse-foot consists of eight syllables.
This is indeed her foot; he who knows this foot of hers thus wins as much as there is in these worlds.
"The Ṛcs, the Yajus, the Sāmans"—these are eight syllables. Indeed, one foot of the Gāyatrī consists of eight syllables. This is that [foot]. 14.8.15[2]
This indeed is its [the Gāyatrī’s] very self. He who knows this foot of hers thus wins as much as there is of this threefold knowledge (trayī vidyā).
“Prāṇa, apāna, vyāna”—these are eight syllables. Indeed, one foot of the Gāyatrī consists of eight syllables;
this indeed is its [the Gāyatrī’s] very self. He who knows this foot of hers thus wins as much as there is of this living world (prāṇi).

Now, this very fourth, visible foot of hers is that which shines beyond the dust (*parorajas*), namely, he who burns [the sun]. For what is fourth is the "fourth," and it is "visible" because he is, as it were, visible; and it is "beyond the dust" because he burns high above all the dust. In this very way, one who knows this foot of hers thus shines with prosperity and fame. 14.8.15. [5]
This very Gāyatrī is established upon that fourth, visible foot, which is beyond the dust of the atmosphere; it is indeed established upon Truth.

The eye is Truth, for the eye is indeed Truth. Therefore, if two people should come disputing, one saying "I saw" and the other "I heard," one would say to him who says "I saw": [you speak the truth].
One should have faith in that alone. That truth is indeed established in strength; strength is breath, and it is established in breath.
Therefore, they say: "Strength is more powerful than truth. Thus, this Gāyatrī is established with respect to the self (the body).

This very [verse] is called *gāyatrī* because it protects (*tatré*) the vital breaths (*prāṇāḥ*), for the vital breaths are indeed the *gayas*. Since it protects the vital breaths there, it is named *gāyatrī*. That which he recites is this very same one; it protects the vital breaths of him for whom he recites it. Now, some recite that *Sāvitrī* as an *anuṣṭubh*, saying, "The *anuṣṭubh* is speech; thus we recite speech. But one should not do so.
One should perform [the sacrifice] with the Gāyatrī alone; one should recite only the Gāyatrī. Even if one were to accept many gifts, it would not equal even a single foot of the Gāyatrī.
If one were to accept these three worlds full of wealth, he would obtain only this first foot of hers. Then...
Whatever extent this triple knowledge (trayī vidyā) extends, whoever were to receive it all, he would obtain this second foot of it;
and whatever living beings exist here, whoever were to receive them all, he would obtain this third foot of it;
but its fourth, visible foot, which is beyond the dust—that is he who shines yonder—it cannot be obtained by anyone at all, so how much less [the rest]?
One should accept only this much. 14.8.15. [10] Its liturgy is: "O Gāyatrī, you are one-footed, two-footed, three-footed, four-footed; you are footless, for you do not go.
Homage to your fourth, visible foot, which is beyond the dust! May so-and-so not reach that [which is yours]. (Regarding) whom...

"May he hate him; may this desire of his not be fulfilled"—this desire indeed does not come to fruition for one against whom he thus offers salutation, whether thinking, "I have attained that," or "I have reached that.
Janaka of Videha said this to Buḍila Āśvatarāśvi: "Now, what indeed..."

"Then why, having become an elephant, do you carry her? "O King, I did not know her mouth," he said. 14.8.15 [12] "Fire indeed is her mouth; for whatever they place into the fire, even if it be much, it all—"
It burns that away; even so, one who knows this, even if he should do much evil, consumes it all and becomes pure, cleansed, ageless, and immortal.
Śvetaketu Āruṇeya once went to the assembly of the Pañcālas. He approached Jaivali.
Seeing Pravāhaṇa attending upon [his father], he addressed him, saying, "O boy! He replied, "Yes, sir.
"Have you been instructed by your father? "Yes," he said.
"Do you know how these creatures, when they depart, go in different directions? "No," he said. "Do you know how this..."

"Do they return again to this world? "No," he said. "Do you know how that world is not filled up, even though many people go there again and again? "No," he said. "Do you know on which oblation being offered, the waters, having become human speech, arise and speak?"
"No," he said, "do you know the starting point of the path of the gods or of the path of the fathers—that which, having performed it, one enters upon the path of the gods or the path of the fathers?
For have we not heard the word of the seer: 'I have heard of two paths—the path of the fathers and that of the gods, as well as of mortals'? (14.9.1)

"Into these two, this whole trembling world moves—that which is between the father and the mother," he said. "Of these, I do not know even one. 14.9.1. Then they invited him to stay the night; disregarding the invitation to stay, the boy ran away. He...
He came to his father and said to him, "Father, you surely told me before that we had been instructed;
how is it, O Sumedhas, that a mere kinsman of the royal class asked me five questions and I did not know even one of them?
He replied, "Which ones were they? and he recited the beginnings of those questions.
He said, "My dear, you should know us thus: whatever I know, all that I have told you. But come, let us go there and live the life of a religious student (brahmacarya). You yourself go. 14.9.1. [7]
Gautama came to where Pravāhaṇa Jaibali was; he offered him a seat, brought water for him, and then presented him with the guest-offering (*argha*).
He said, "We shall grant a boon to you, Gautama. He replied, "This boon has already been granted to me, which—"
"But you spoke these words in the presence of the prince; tell them to me.
He said, "Gautama, among the boons for the gods, speak for men.
He said, "It is well known that I possess gold, cattle, horses, female slaves, and excellent chariots."
"Regarding our garments, may you not be one who withholds from us that which is much, endless, and boundless.

"Indeed, Gautama, I approach you through the proper ritual channel (*tīrtha*)," he said. "I am approaching your ladyship," [the other replied]. Formerly, they used to approach [a teacher] merely by word. 14.9.1. He, having announced his arrival, said: "In this way, Gautama, do not fail us, nor your ancestors."
"Since this knowledge has never before dwelt with any Brāhmaṇa, I shall indeed tell it to you; for who would refuse one who speaks thus?
"That world, O Gautama, is indeed the fire. The sun is its fuel, the rays are its smoke, the day is its flame, and the moon is its embers."
The coals are the stars, and the sparks are the [minor] constellations. Into this very fire, the gods offer faith (*śraddhā*).
From that oblation, King Soma arises.
Parjanya, O Gautama, is indeed the fire; the year is its fuel, and the clouds are its smoke.
Lightning is its flame, thunder its embers, and hailstones its sparks. Into this very fire the gods offer Soma;
from that oblation rain comes into being. 14.9.1.
[14] This world, indeed, is the fire, O Gautama. Of this fire, the earth is the fuel, wind the smoke, night the flame, and the quarters the embers.
The intermediate directions are the sparks. Into this very fire, the gods offer rain; from that offering, food comes into being.
Man, indeed, is the fire, O Gautama. His opened mouth is the fuel, his breath is the smoke, his speech is the flame, and his eye is the embers.
The ear is the sparks; into this very fire the gods offer food, and from that oblation semen comes into being. 14.9.1.
[16] Woman, indeed, is the fire, O Gautama; her lap is the fuel, and her hair is the smoke.

The womb is its fire; what it performs within is its embers; its pleasures are its sparks. Into this very fire the gods offer semen; from that oblation a person comes into being. He is born; he lives as long as he lives.
Then, when he dies, they carry him away to the fire. 14.9.1. [17]

In that case, fire itself becomes the fire; the fuel is the fuel, the smoke is the smoke, the flame is the flame, the embers are the embers, and the sparks are the sparks. Into this very fire, the gods offer the person. From that oblation, a person of radiant complexion comes into being. 14.9.1 [18]
Those who know this thus, and those who, in the forest, venerate truth with faith—they pass into the light; from the light, into the day;
from the day, into the waxing fortnight; from the waxing fortnight, into the six months during which the sun moves northward; and from those months...
From the world of the gods he goes to the sun; from the sun, to the realm of lightning. A person consisting of mind comes from that realm of lightning and leads them to the worlds of Brahman.
In those worlds of Brahman they dwell as supreme beings in supreme distances. For them there is no returning here again. 14.9.1 [19]
Now, those who win the world by means of sacrifice, charity, and austerity, they pass into the smoke;
from smoke, into the night;
from the night, into the waning fortnight; from the waning fortnight, into those six months during which the sun moves southward.
From the months they go to the world of the fathers; from the world of the fathers to the moon. Having reached the moon, they become food.
There the gods consume them, just as they consume King Soma with the words, "Swell up! Wane away!
When that [merit] of theirs is exhausted, they emerge into this very space; from space to air, and from air to rain.

Upon falling as rain, they reach the earth and become food; thus do they revolve again and again. But those who do not know these two paths become worms, moths, and whatever is biting. Verily, he who knows the eldest and the best becomes the eldest and the best among his own people.

Breath indeed is the eldest and the best; he who knows this becomes the eldest and the best among his own people, and even among those for whom he desires to be so. (14.9.2) He who knows the most excellent (*vasiṣṭhā*) becomes the most excellent among his own people; speech indeed is the most excellent, and thus he becomes the most excellent.
It belongs to his own people for one who knows thus. 14.9.2.
[3] He who truly knows the foundation stands firm on level ground and stands firm on difficult terrain. Sight, indeed, is the foundation;
for by means of sight one stands firm on both level ground and difficult terrain. One stands firm on level ground; one stands firm on level ground.
He who knows this in the *Durga* [section], 14.9.2[4].

He who indeed knows the attainment (*sampad*)—whatever desire he desires, that is attained for him. The ear, verily, is the attainment; for in the ear all these Vedas are fully contained. Whatever desire he desires, that is attained for him.

He who knows thus desires [his wishes]. 14.9.2.[5] Verily, he who knows the abode becomes the abode of his own people and the abode of other men. The mind, indeed, is the abode. He who knows thus becomes the abode of his own people and the abode of other men. 14.9.2.[6]

He who knows procreation indeed procreates with offspring and cattle; semen is procreation. He who knows this procreates with offspring and cattle. 14.9.2. These vital breaths, disputing among themselves as to who was the best, went to Brahmā, saying, "Which of us is the most excellent?"
"Whichever of you, upon departing from this body, makes it seem worse, that one among you shall be the most excellent.
Speech departed. Having been away for a year, it returned and said, "How were you able to live without me?
They replied, "Just as mute people live without speech—breathing with the breath, seeing with the eye, hearing with the ear..."
"By the ear have we become wise, by the mind have we been procreated, and by semen have we thus lived," said Speech, and she entered back [into the body].
Then the Eye departed. Having stayed away for a year, it returned and said, "How were you able to live without me?
They replied, "Just as the blind, though not seeing with the eye, lived on by means of breath, speaking by means of speech..."
"Listening with the ear, knowing with the mind, and procreating with semen—in this way we have lived," [said the eye], and so it entered back.
Then the ear departed; having stayed away for a year, it returned and said, "How were you able to live without me?"

"Let us live," they said. "Just as the deaf, though not hearing with the ear, yet breathe with the breath, speak with speech, see with the eye, know with the mind, and procreate with semen—even so have we lived. Thereupon, the ear entered [the body]. 14.9.2. [11]

The mind departed; having stayed away for a year, it returned and said, "How were you able to live without me? They replied, "Just as the ignorant and deluded live—breathing with the vital breath, speaking with speech, seeing with the eye, hearing with the ear, and procreating with semen—even so have we lived. Thereupon, the mind entered back in.
Then the mind departed. After staying away for a year, it returned and said, "How were you able to live without me?
They replied, "Just as eunuchs live without procreating, breathing with the breath and speaking with speech."
"Seeing with the eye, hearing with the ear, and knowing with the mind—thus have we lived," [they said]; and so the semen entered.
Then, as the vital breath (*prāṇa*) was about to depart, it was like a great, well-bred horse from the Sindhu region.
"He pulled out the pegs of the tethering post. In this very way, he pulled out these vital breaths from him.
They said, 'O Venerable One, do not depart! We shall certainly not be able to live without you. 'Then offer me tribute,' [he said]. 'So be it,' [they replied].
Then Speech said, "Insofar as I am the most excellent (*vasiṣṭhā*), so are you the most excellent. Then the Eye said, "Insofar as I..."

“I am the foundation; you are that foundation,” he said to the ear. “Insofar as I am attainment, you are that attainment,” he said to the mind. “Insofar as I am the abode, you are that abode,” he said to semen.
“Insofar as I am procreation, you are that procreation,” he said to it. [The other asked: “What is my food? What is my clothing? [He replied: “Whatever there is here.”

"From dogs, from worms, from insects and moths—this is your food; water is your clothing. Indeed, for one who knows this food of the breath (*anasya annam*), no food is ever eaten that is not food, nor is anything received that is not food.
Those learned in the Vedas (*śrotriyāḥ*) who know this rinse their mouths before eating and rinse their mouths after eating; thus they make this very breath-food non-naked.
Those who perform [these rites] think thus: therefore, one who knows this should sip water before eating and sip water after eating; thereby he makes that very food non-naked.
Now, he who desires, "May I attain greatness," [should sacrifice] during the northern course of the sun, in the waxing fortnight, on an auspicious day.

Having observed the *upasad* vow for twelve days, and having collected all kinds of herbs and fruits in a vessel made of *udumbara* wood, whether a shallow cup (*kaṃsa*) or a bowl (*camasa*), he sweeps the ground around the fire, smears it with cow-dung, kindles the fire, prepares the clarified butter according to the prescribed ritual procedure, and at a male constellation, having mixed the mash, he offers it as an oblation. 14.9.3. [2]
O Jātavedas, as many gods as there are among you who strike down the desires of a man from every side—to them I offer this portion;
may they, being satisfied, satisfy me with my desires. Svāhā!
I worship you with a stream of clarified butter, you who lie across, saying, "I am the supporter."
He offers the third oblation with the verses: "To the one who wins over, svāhā! O Prajāpati, these [beings] are not other than you, svāhā! (14.9.3).

Having offered into the fire with the formulas, "To the eldest, svāhā! To the best, svāhā!", he pours the residue into the stirred drink (mantha) with the formula, "To the out-breath, svāhā! To the most excellent, svāhā! Then, having offered into the fire with the formulas, "To the eye, svāhā! To prosperity, svāhā!", he offers to the ear.
"Oblation to the abode, svāhā!"—thus [he offers] into the fire; "Oblation to the mind, svāhā! Oblation to procreation, svāhā!"—thus into the fire; "Oblation to semen, svāhā!"—thus into the fire.
14.9.3.[5] "Oblation to what has been, svāhā!"—thus into the fire;
"Oblation to what will be, svāhā!"—thus into the fire; "Oblation to the All, svāhā!"—thus into the fire; "Oblation to the Whole."

“Svāhā!”—he offers into the fire. “To the earth, svāhā!”—he offers into the fire. “To the intermediate space, svāhā!”—he offers into the fire. “To the sky, svāhā!”—he offers into the fire. “To the quarters, svāhā!”—he offers into the fire. “To the Brahman, svāhā!”—he offers into the fire. “To the Kṣatra, svāhā!”—he offers into the fire. 14.9.3.[7]

"Bhūḥ svāhā!"—in the fire; "Bhuvaḥ svāhā!"—in the fire; "Svaḥ svāhā!"—in the fire; "Bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ svāhā!"—in the fire. [14.9.3.8] "To Agni, svāhā!"—in the fire; "To Soma, svāhā!"—in the fire; "To Tejas, svāhā!"—in the fire; "To Śrī..."

Having offered oblations into the fire with "Svāhā! to Agni, "Svāhā! to Lakṣmī, "Svāhā! to Savitṛ, "Svāhā! to Sarasvatī, "Svāhā! to the Viśvedevas, and "Svāhā! to Prajāpati, he pours the remnants into the mash. 14.9.3. [9]

Then he touches it, saying: "Thou art moving; thou art flaming; thou art full; thou art firm; thou art the single assembly; thou art the *hiṅ* uttered; thou art the *hiṅ* being uttered; thou art the *udgītha*; thou art the *udgītha* being sung; thou art the *śrāvaṇa*; thou art the *pratyāśrāvaṇa*;
thou art moist and yet ablaze; thou art pervasive; thou art abundant; thou art light; thou art food."
"Thou art the end; thou art the absorber," [he says].
14.9.3.[10] Then he lifts it up: "Unripe art thou; for unripe is it in me. He indeed is the king, the ruler, the overlord;
may he, as king, ruler, and overlord, make me one. 14.9.3.[11]

Then he sips from it with the verse: "That most excellent splendor of Savitṛ; the winds blow honey for the one who follows the Law; the rivers flow with honey; may the plants be sweet for us. Bhūḥ! Svāhā!
(14.9.3.12) "We meditate upon the splendor of the god; honeyed be the night and the dawns; honeyed be the earthly realm. (Madhu)
"May Heaven be our father; may the Earth be ours; Svāhā! (14.9.3.13).
"May he who shall impel our thoughts [be ours]; may the Lord of the Forest be honey-sweet for us; may Sūrya be honey-sweet;
may the cows be honey-sweet for us; Svarga! Svāhā! And he recites the entire *Sāvitrī* verse, and all [the other verses].

Having recited all the *madhumatī* verses and the *vyāhṛtis*, and finally saying, "May I become this All; Bhūr Bhuvaḥ Svaḥ Svāhā," he sips water, washes [his hands], and lies down behind the fire with his head toward the east. 14.9.3.
At dawn, he worships the sun, saying: "I am the unique lotus of the quarters."
"May I become the unique white lotus among men"—having returned by the same way he came and sitting behind the fire, he mutters the *vaṃśa* (lineage).
Having told this very same thing to his pupil Vājasaneya Yājñavalkya, Uddālaka Āruṇi said: "And whoever..."
“If one were to sprinkle water on a withered stump, would not shoots be born and leaves sprout?
Thus indeed did Vājasaneya Yājñavalkya teach this to his pupil Madhuka Paiṅgya;
and Madhuka Paiṅgya taught this to his pupil Cūḍa Bhāgavitti.
Cūḍa Bhāgavitti taught this very same [knowledge] to Jānaki Āyasthūṇa as a pupil.
Jānaki Āyasthūṇa taught this very same [knowledge] to Satyakāma Jābāla as a pupil.
Satyakāma Jābāla, having taught this very same [knowledge] to his pupils, said: "Even if one were to [apply this] to a withered stump..."
"One should sprinkle [the seeds], so that shoots may arise and leaves may sprout. One should not teach this very [instruction] to one who is not a son or a pupil. 14.9.3.
There are four things made of udumbara wood: a cup of udumbara, a dipping-spoon of udumbara, and fuel of udumbara.
The two stirring-sticks for the *audumbarī* post [are made of udumbara wood].
14.9.3.[22] There are ten kinds of cultivated grains: rice, barley, sesame, beans, millet, panic seed, wheat, lentils, chickpeas, and vetch;
having ground these together with curd and honey...
He sprinkles with ghee; he offers an oblation of clarified butter.
Of these beings, the earth is the essence; of the earth, water; of water, plants; of plants, flowers;
of flowers, fruits; of fruits, man; of man, semen.
Prajāpati reflected: "Come now, I shall provide a support for him. He created a woman; having created her, he approached her from below.
Therefore, one should approach a woman from below, for she is indeed prosperity (*śrī*). He drew forth from himself this pressing-stone facing eastward and sent it forth toward her. 14.9.4. [3]
Her altar is the vulva, her hair is the sacrificial grass (*barhis*), her skin is the two pressing-skins, and the kindled fire is between her thighs—namely, the two testicles.

As great as is the world of one who performs the *Vājapeya* sacrifice, so great is the world of him who, knowing this, engages in sexual intercourse; he appropriates the merit of women. But he who, not knowing this, engages in sexual intercourse...
His women practice [this], and they take away his merit. 14.9.4.
[4] Knowing this, Uddālaka Āruṇi indeed said this; knowing this, Nāka Maudgalya indeed said this; knowing this, Kumārahārita indeed said this: "Many young men..."
"Brahmin-like men who lack self-control and are devoid of merit depart from this world, they who practice vulgar laughter while ignorant of this [teaching].
(14.9.4) "Much indeed is this semen that spills for one whether sleeping or waking; he should touch it or recite a mantra over it. (14.9.5)

"Whatever semen of mine has today spilled upon the earth, whatever has flowed into the plants, or into the waters—this semen I take up again; may my virility return to me, may my splendor return, may my fortune return; may the sacrificial fires return to their respective places. Having said this, he takes it up with his ring finger and thumb, and places it between his breasts or between his eyebrows.
He should wipe [his face].
(14.9.4.6) Now, if he should see his own reflection in water, he should consecrate it with the mantra: "In me be splendor, sensory power, fame, wealth, and merit. (14.9.4.7)

This woman who has removed her soiled garment is indeed the Fortune (*Śrī*) of women; therefore, one should approach and address a renowned woman who has removed her soiled garment. If she does not yield to him, he may, if he wishes, purchase her [with wealth].
If she still does not yield to him, he may, if he wishes, strike her with a staff or with his hand and pass by her, saying: "By your organ..."
"By glory he takes away glory"—thus he indeed becomes inglorious.

14.9.4.[8] If he should desire a woman, thinking, "May she love me," he should have his purpose accomplished with her, join mouth to mouth, touch her private parts, and mutter: "From the limb you arise, from the heart you are born; you are that [soma]."
"You are astringent-limbed; intoxicate me like one who has been struck by a poisoned arrow.

[14.9.4.9] Now, if he desires that she should not conceive, having performed the ritual act with her and joining mouth to mouth, he should first breathe out upon her and then breathe in, saying: "With my organ, I take away your seed. Thus, she becomes indeed seedless. [14.9.4.10]

Now, if one should desire, "May she conceive," having prepared the object for her, he should join mouth to mouth and exhale and inhale [upon her], saying: "With my faculty, with my seed, I place seed in you. She becomes pregnant.
Now, if one should have a lover for his wife and should hate him, he should kindle a fire in a raw earthen vessel and [place it] against the grain.
Having spread out a bed of reeds, he should offer upon it these three reed-shafts with their points turned backward, dipped in clarified butter, [saying]:
"In my kindled fire you have offered; I seize your hope and expectation, O So-and-so!"—here he utters the name.
"In my kindled fire you have offered; I seize your sons and cattle, O So-and-so!"—here he utters the name. "In my kindled fire you have offered..."

"I take your out-breath and in-breath, O so-and-so"—thus he takes his name. Deprived of his senses and stripped of his merit, he departs from this world, whomsoever a Brahmin who knows this curses. Therefore, one who knows this should not seek to jest with the wife of a learned Vedic scholar (śrotriya), for such a knower becomes a superior being. 14.9.4 [12]

Now, if one should find that his wife has reached her menses, she shall not drink from a bronze vessel for three days and shall remain in unwashed clothes; neither a *vṛṣala* nor a *vṛṣalī* shall touch her.
At the end of the three nights, having bathed, he should have rice grains pounded.
(14.9.4) If he should desire, "May a fair-skinned son be born to me, may he recite the Veda, and may he reach a full lifespan," [he should offer] milk-rice.

Having cooked [the rice], the two masters should eat it with clarified butter in order to procreate. (14.9.4) Now, if one should desire, "May a son be born to me who is tawny and reddish-brown, who shall study the two Vedas, and who shall live his full span of life," he should cook rice with curd. (14.9.4)
Now, if one should desire, "May a son be born to me who is dark-complexioned with red eyes, who shall recite the three Vedas,
and who shall live his full span of life," he should have rice cooked with milk.
Then, if one should desire, "May a daughter be born to me who is wise and who shall live her full span of life," he should have rice cooked with sesame seeds.

Now, if one should desire, "May a son be born to me who is wise, victorious, capable in assembly, a speaker of words that ought to be heeded, who shall study all the Vedas and live his full span of life," they should have rice cooked with meat and eat it with clarified butter; being thus empowered, they should procreate, using either beef or the meat of a bull. 14.9.4 [18]

Then, at the very break of dawn, having performed the rites with clarified butter according to the procedure for the *sthālīpāka* (cooked-rice offering), he offers a portion of the *sthālīpāka* with the formula:
"To Agni, Svāhā! To Anumati, Svāhā! To the god Savitṛ of true impulsion, Svāhā! Having offered and drawn out [the remainder], he eats;
he gives the other [portion] to her. Having washed his hands and filled a water-vessel, he [sprinkles] her with it.

He sprinkles her three times with the mantra: "Arise from here, O Viśvāvasu! Seek another woman who is more fertile; go back to your own wife. (14.9.4) Then he approaches her, saying: "I am he (Ama), you are she (Sā).
You are she, I am he. I am Sāman, you are Ṛc. I am heaven, you are earth. Come, let us two unite; let us both deposit seed for the sake of a male child."
"For the sake of sons and wealth" (14.9.4.20).

Then he causes her thighs to spread apart with the words, "May Heaven and Earth open wide. Having placed his member within her and joined mouth to mouth, he strokes her three times in the direction of the hair with the mantra: "May Viṣṇu prepare the womb; may Tvaṣṭṛ..."
May Prajāpati, the Ordainer, fashion and infuse forms; may he place the embryo within you. O Sinīvālī, bestow an embryo;
O Pṛthuṣṭukī, bestow an embryo. May the two divine Aśvins, wreathed with lotuses, place an embryo within you.
With the two golden fire-drills by which the divine Aśvins churned [the fire], we place that embryo within you.

"In the tenth month for birth, as the earth pregnant with fire, as the sky pregnant with Indra, as the wind is the embryo of the quarters—so do I place the embryo within you, [Name]," thus he pronounces her name. When she is about to give birth, he sprinkles her with water: "As the wind stirs a lotus pond on every side, even so [stir] yours."
"Let the embryo stir; let it come forth with the placenta. This stall for Indra has been prepared, with a barrier and an enclosure.
O Indra, drive it out along with the embryo and the covering! (14.9.4).
When [the child] is born, having kindled the fire and placed [the child] on his lap, he brings speckled butter into a bronze vessel and, taking portions of the speckled butter...

In this [fire], prospering and increasing, one offers a thousand [oblations] in his own home. May he not neglect its attendance; may he be blessed with offspring and cattle, svāhā! With my mind, I offer the vital breaths into you, svāhā!
(14.9.4)[24] Whatever I have overdone in this rite, or whatever I have done here deficiently—may Agni Sviṣṭakṛt, the wise one, make it well-offered.
"May he offer it well; Svāhā! (14.9.4[25]).
Then he performs the rite for long life: placing [his mouth] near the boy's right ear, he says "Speech! Speech! three times.
Then he gives him a name, saying, "Thou art Veda. This shall be his secret name. Then [he gives him] curds and honey.
Having mixed clarified butter with gold that is not separated [from it], he makes him eat it, saying: "Bhūḥ! I place you in me;
Bhuvaḥ! I place you in me; Bhūr-bhuvaḥ-svaḥ! I place everything in you. (14.9.4) Then he touches him, saying: "Become a stone, become an axe, become unmelting gold; for you are indeed the self."
"You are named Son; live for a hundred autumns. (14.9.4.27) Then he addresses his mother: "You are Iḍā, belonging to Mitra and Varuṇa; you have given birth to a hero among heroes.
May you be possessed of heroes, she who has made us possessed of heroes. (14.9.4.28)

Then, having handed him over to his mother, she gives him the breast with [the verse]: "That breast of thine which is inexhaustible, which is refreshing, which bestows jewels, finds wealth, and is most bountiful; that by which thou nourishest all desirable things—O Sarasvatī, bring that here for him to suck. (14.9.4)

Regarding him, they say: "Truly, you have become a great-grandfather; truly, you have become a great-great-grandfather. You have indeed reached the highest pinnacle in prosperity, fame, and the splendor of sacred knowledge (*brahmavarcasa*), since a son has been born to a Brahmin who knows thus. Now follows the lineage: This [lineage] we [derive] from Bhāradvājīputra; Bhāradvājīputra [from his father].
From Vātsīmāṇḍavīputra, [it was received] by Vātsīmāṇḍavīputra; from Pārāśarīputra, by Pārāśarīputra; from Gārgīputra, by Gārgīputra; from Pārāśarīkauṇḍinīputra, by Pārāśarīkauṇḍinīputra;
from Gārgīputra, by Gārgīputra; from another Gārgīputra, by [that] Gārgīputra; from Bāḍeyīputra, by Bāḍeyīputra.
From Mauṣikīputra, [the lineage comes] Mauṣikīputra; from Hārikarṇīputra, Hārikarṇīputra;
from Bhāradvājīputra, Bhāradvājīputra; from Paiṅgīputra, Paiṅgīputra; and from Śaunakīputra, Śaunakīputra. 14.9.4 [31]
From Kāśyapībālākyāmāṭharīputra, [the lineage descends] to Kāśyapībālākyāmāṭharīputra;
from Kautsīputra, to Kautsīputra;
from Baudhīputra, to Baudhīputra; from Śālaṅkāyanīputra, to Śālaṅkāyanīputra.
From Vārṣagaṇīputra [descended] Vārṣagaṇīputra; from Gautamīputra [descended] Gautamīputra;
from Ātreyīputra [descended] Ātreyīputra; from Gautamīputra [descended] Gautamīputra; from Vātsīputra [descended] Vātsīputra;
from Bhāradvājīputra [descended] Bhāradvājīputra; from Pārāśarīputra [descended] Pārāśarīputra.
From Vārkāruṇīputra, [the lineage comes from] Vārkāruṇīputra; from Ārtabhāgīputra, Ārtabhāgīputra;
from Śauṅgīputra, Śauṅgīputra; from Sāṃkṛtīputra, Sāṃkṛtīputra;
from Ālambīputra, Ālambīputra; from Ālambāyanīputra, Ālambāyanīputra.
From Jāyantīputra, [descends] Jāyantīputra; from Māṇḍūkāyanīputra, Māṇḍūkāyanīputra;
from Māṇḍūkīputra, Māṇḍūkīputra; from Śāṇḍilīputra, Śāṇḍilīputra;
from Rāthītarīputra, Rāthītarīputra; from the two Krauñcikīputras, the two Krauñcikīputras.
From Vaidabhṛtīputra, [the lineage comes from] Vaidabhṛtīputra; from Bhālukīputra, Bhālukīputra;
from Prācīnayogīputra, Prācīnayogīputra; from Sāṃjīvīputra, Sāṃjīvīputra; from Kārśakeyīputra, Kārśakeyīputra. 14.9.4. [33]
From Prāśnīputra Āsurivāsina; Prāśnīputra from Āsurāyaṇa;
Āsurāyaṇa from Āsuri; Āsuri from Yājñavalkya; Yājñavalkya from Uddālaka; Uddālaka from Aruṇa;
Aruṇa from Upaveśi; Upaveśi [from...].
Kuśri from Vājaśravas; Vājaśravas from Jihvāvān Bādhyoga; Jihvāvān Bādhyoga from Asita Vārṣagaṇa; Asita Vārṣagaṇa from Harita Kaśyapa;
Harita Kaśyapa from Śilpa Kaśyapa; Śilpa Kaśyapa from Kaśyapa Naidhruvi; Kaśyapa Naidhruvi from Vāk.

From Vāgambhiṇī came Ambhiṇī; from Āditya came these white *yajus* formulas, which are proclaimed by Yājñavalkya Vājasaneya. For this [soma] is indeed the seed of milk brought together with brilliance.
For this is the seed of milk that has been brought; may we obtain its milking, higher and ever higher.
"Samām"—by this he indeed invokes this very blessing. Then they purify themselves at the *cātvāla* pit; the significance (*bandhu*) of that is the same as before. 14.3.1.
Now, therefore, regarding the sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*). He gives a gold coin weighing a hundred *mānas* to the Brahman priest.
For the Brahman is seated, while gold is something lying down; therefore, he gives a gold coin weighing a hundred *mānas* to the Brahman.
Now, that cow which milks the *gharma* he gives to the *adhvaryu*.
For the *gharma* is, as it were, heated, and the *adhvaryu* goes forth as if heated; therefore he gives her to the *adhvaryu*.
Then, that cow which milks the sacrificial food (*vrata*) for the sacrificer he gives to the *hotṛ*. For the *hotṛ* is the sacrifice, and the sacrifice is...

Therefore, the sacrificer gives her to the Hotṛ. Now, as for this cow that milks the fast-food for the wife, he gives her to the Udgātṛs; for it is the work of the wife indeed that the Udgātṛs perform here, and therefore he gives her to the Udgātṛs.
Now, he who either recites this or consumes it enters this life and this light.
His observance of the vow is the same as that prescribed for the creation. Indeed, this sacrifice is the self of all beings and of all the gods; following its success—
The sacrificer prospers with offspring and cattle; indeed, he whose *gharma* vessel breaks apart is deprived of offspring and cattle. In this case, the expiation is as follows:
he offers a full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*). The full is indeed everything; by means of everything, he thus heals whatever has been torn asunder.

"Of the sacrifice, Svāhā! To the vital breaths together with their overlord!"—the mind, indeed, is the overlord of the vital breaths, for in the mind all the vital breaths are established; thus, by means of the mind itself, he heals whatever in the sacrifice has been torn asunder.
"To Earth, svāhā!"—Earth indeed is the abode of all the gods;
thus he heals with all these deities whatever in the sacrifice has been torn asunder.
"To Agni, svāhā!"—Agni indeed is the self of all the gods.
By means of all these deities he heals whatever in the sacrifice has been torn asunder.
"To the atmosphere, svāhā!"—the atmosphere is indeed the abode of all the gods;
thus, by means of all these deities, he heals whatever in the sacrifice has been torn asunder.

"To Vāyu, svāhā!"—Vāyu, indeed, is the self of all the gods; thus he heals with all these deities whatever in the sacrifice has been torn asunder. "To Dyaus, svāhā!"—Dyaus, indeed, is the abode of all the gods.
By means of all these deities he heals whatever in the sacrifice has been torn asunder. "Svāhā to Sūrya!"—Sūrya is indeed the self of all the gods;
thus, by means of all these deities, he heals whatever in the sacrifice has been torn asunder.
"To the quarters, svāhā!"—the quarters are indeed the abode of all the gods;
thus he heals by means of all these deities whatever in the sacrifice has been torn asunder.
"To the Moon, svāhā!"—the Moon is indeed the self of all the gods.
By means of all these deities he heals whatever in the sacrifice has been torn asunder.
"Svāhā to the constellations!"—the constellations are indeed the abode of all the gods;
thus, by means of all these deities, he heals whatever in the sacrifice has been torn asunder.
"To the waters, svāhā!"—the waters, indeed, are the abode of all the gods;
thus he heals by means of all these deities whatever in the sacrifice has been torn asunder.
"To Varuṇa, svāhā!"—Varuṇa, indeed, is the self of all the gods.
By means of all these deities he heals whatever in the sacrifice has been torn asunder.
With the formulas, "To the navel, svāhā! To the purified one, svāhā!"—these are undefined; for Prajāpati is undefined, and the sacrifice is Prajāpati.
Thus, he heals Prajāpati himself, who is the sacrifice.

These libations are thirteen; for there are indeed thirteen months in a year, and the year is Prajāpati, and the sacrifice is Prajāpati; thus he heals this very Prajāpati, the sacrifice. With "Svāhā to Speech! he places the mouth in him; with "Svāhā to Breath! Svāhā to Breath! he places the two nostrils.

Thus he places this in him: "To the eye, svāhā! To the eye, svāhā!"—he thereby places the two eyes in him. "To the ear, svāhā! To the ear, svāhā!"—he thereby places the two ears in him. There are seven of these oblations; for there are these seven vital breaths in the head; it is these very ones that he places in him.

He offers the supreme *pūrṇāhuti* oblation; for the full is indeed everything, and by means of everything he heals whatever in the sacrifice has been torn asunder. With the words, "The desire of the mind, the intention,"—for by the mind all this is attained—he heals it by means of the mind itself.

"Whatever has been omitted from the sacrifice, may I obtain the truth of speech"—for by speech indeed all this is obtained; it is by means of speech that he heals whatever has been omitted from the sacrifice.
"May the form of the cattle, the essence of food, glory, and prosperity rest within me."

With "Svāhā," he thus invokes a blessing. Then, having ground that [clay] and the spare clay together with fine earth, he prepares it according to the prescribed ritual procedure and bakes it according to the prescribed ritual procedure for the purpose of setting it aside. Now, whichever of the two spare pieces is firm, with that one he should proceed.

The Pravargya is indeed the year; the year is everything, and the Pravargya is everything. When it is heated, that is spring; when it has grown warm, that is summer; when it has swelled, that is the rainy season. Indeed, when the rains swell, then all the gods and all beings subsist upon them. Verily, for him, the rains swell.
Thus he knows this: these worlds are indeed the Pravargya;

for these worlds are everything, and the Pravargya is everything. When it is heated (pravṛkta), that is this world; when it has shone forth (rucita), that is the intermediate world; when it has swelled (pinvita), that is yonder world. Or rather, when...
That world swells, and all the gods and all beings live upon it; indeed, that world swells for him who knows this thus.
These deities are indeed the Pravargya: Agni, Vāyu, and Āditya. All these deities are indeed everything.

The Pravargya is that [vessel]: when it is heated, it is Agni; when it has shone forth, it is Vāyu; when it has swelled, it is yonder Āditya. And when yonder Āditya swells, then all the gods and all beings subsist upon him. Yonder Āditya indeed swells for him who knows this thus. 14.3.2.25

The Pravargya is indeed the sacrificer; his self, offspring, and cattle are it. The sacrificer is everything, and the Pravargya is everything. When it is heated, that is the self; when it has been made radiant, that is the offspring; when it has been made to swell, that is the cattle. For when the cattle swell, then all the gods and all beings live upon them; indeed, they cause them to swell for him.

The cattle are those who know this thus. 14.3.2.26 The Agnihotra is indeed the Pravargya; the Agnihotra is everything, and the Pravargya is everything. When it has been placed on the fire, that is the *pravṛkta*; when it has been ladled out, that is the *rucita*; when it has been offered, that is the *pinvita*. Indeed, when the Agnihotra...
It swells; then all the gods and all beings live upon it as it swells. Indeed, the *agnihotra* swells for him who knows this.
The *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices are the *pravargya*; the *darśapūrṇamāsa* are everything, and the *pravargya* is everything. He...

That which is placed upon [the fire] is for Pravṛkta; that which is near is for Rucita; that which is offered is for Pinvita. When the New and Full Moon sacrifices swell, then all the gods and all beings subsist upon them. Indeed, the New and Full Moon sacrifices swell for him who knows this thus. 14.3.2.28

The Cāturmāsyas are indeed the Pravargya; the Cāturmāsyas are everything, and the Pravargya is everything. When it has been placed on the fire, that is the *pravṛkta*; when it has been set down, that is the *rucita*; when it has been offered, that is the *pinvita*. For when the Cāturmāsyas overflow (*pinvante*), then all the gods and all beings subsist upon them; they indeed overflow.
For him who knows this, there are the Cāturmāsya sacrifices.

The Pravargya is indeed the Paśubandha; the Paśubandha is everything, and the Pravargya is everything. When it has been placed on the fire, that is the *pravṛkta*; when it has been set down, that is the *rucita*; when it has been offered, that is the *pinvita*. When indeed...
The animal sacrifice overflows; then all the gods and all beings subsist upon it. Indeed, the animal sacrifice overflows for him who knows this thus.
The Pravargya is indeed Soma; Soma is everything, and the Pravargya is everything. It is he [who is everything].

When it is pressed, it is "set forth"; when it is drawn up, it is "delighted"; when it is offered, it is "swollen. For when Soma swells, then all the gods and all beings partake of him. Indeed, Soma swells for that man who knows this thus; and for him, no sacrifice remains unperformed that is lacking the *pravargya* rite.
Thus he knows this. Now, indeed, he enters this life-span and this light who either recites this or consumes it;
his observance of the vow is that which [is prescribed] at the creation.
